1.overview:
God speaks, and a dark, empty, water-covered world becomes ordered and full. Over six days he makes light, sky, land, and plants, then fills those spaces with lights, birds and fish, animals, and finally humankind, male and female, made in his image and blessed to rule the earth. Each day closes with the same refrain of evening and morning.

The account ends at 2:3, not 1:31. The chapter break came centuries later, and it cuts off the seventh day, when God rests and makes the day holy. Read with 2:1–3 attached, the story ends in rest rather than in the creation of man.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses. In Moses 1–2 the account comes to Moses by revelation, with the command to write it (Moses 1:40; 2:1). Many scholars assign it to a later priestly writer drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Moses 1 sets the vision after the burning bush and before Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Moses 1:17, 25–26).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Biblical chronology places Adam about 4000 BC; Archbishop Ussher's 1650 reckoning, long printed in KJV margins, gives 4004 BC. D&C 77:6 speaks of the earth's seven thousand years of “temporal existence.”

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel, whether in the wilderness (traditional view) or in exile in Babylon (common scholarly view).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 2:4–25 (a second creation account), Moses 2, Abraham 4.

1.hermeneutics:
Babylon's creation epic, *Enuma Elish*, has the same pieces as Genesis 1: primeval waters, a sky that holds water back above, land below. There the god Marduk gets them by killing the sea goddess Tiamat and splitting her body in half, and humans are made from a slain god's blood to do the gods' work. Genesis keeps the pieces and drops the war. The “deep” (*tehom*, a word related to Tiamat's name) is just water. God gives an order and it is done, and the humans he makes are blessed and fed (vv. 28–29), not put to work for him.

On day four the sun and moon go unnamed. They are “the greater light” and “the lesser light.” Across the region the sun was a god (Babylon's Shamash, Egypt's Ra), and the common Hebrew word for sun, *shemesh*, matches the Babylonian god's name. Genesis also makes them on day four, after light already exists on day one. A listener raised among sun worshipers would hear a demotion: these are lamps hung up to keep the calendar.

“Image of God” was royal language. Egyptian and Assyrian texts call the king the image of a god, and kings set up statues of themselves in conquered lands to mark whose land it was. Genesis gives that title to every human, male and female, and the rule it grants is over animals and the earth, not over other people.

structure.summary: Parallel panels (A B C / A′ B′ C′) inside a frame. Not a chiasm.

open.text: God created the heaven and the earth

close.text: Heaven and earth finished; day 7, rest

notes: Verse 2 names two problems: the earth is formless (*tohu*) and empty (*bohu*). Days 1–3 solve the first by making spaces. Days 4–6 solve the second by filling them. Day 7 sits outside both panels; nothing is made.

**Repetition to watch:** “And God said” (10 times), “it was so,” “God saw that it was good” (7 times, missing on day 2, raised to “very good” on day 6), “the evening and the morning.” Day 7 has no evening-and-morning line.
**Sevens:** Verse 1 has 7 Hebrew words and verse 2 has 14. “God” (*Elohim*) appears 35 times in 1:1–2:3.

Genesis is organized by headings that read “these are the generations of…” (Hebrew *toledot*). The first one is 2:4, so 1:1–2:3 stands in front of all of them as a prologue to the book. It opens the primeval history (chapters 1–11), which runs from creation to the scattering at Babel before narrowing to one family, Abraham's.

**Echoes later in the Torah:** The seventh day becomes the Sabbath command, grounded in creation (Exodus 20:11). When the tabernacle is finished, the wording echoes 2:1–3: all the work is finished, Moses looks on it, and he blesses the people (Exodus 39:32, 43).

traditions.text: In the Restoration account, Genesis 1 is not a stand-alone text but part of a larger vision. Moses sees the earth and every soul on it, asks why these things are so and by what God made them, and is told that God has made “worlds without number” through the Only Begotten. The creation account follows as the answer, introduced with “write the words which I speak.” The Lord also warns that men will take words from Moses' book and promises to raise up one like Moses to restore them, which Latter-day Saints read as Joseph Smith.

A second Restoration version told as a plan: “the Gods” take counsel, organize, and form, and each “day” is a “time.” In 4:18 the Gods “watched those things which they had ordered until they obeyed,” and Abraham 3:4 sets the Lord's reckoning at a thousand years to a day. Where Genesis reports what happened, Abraham describes what was planned and then carried out.

He argued that the Hebrew *bara* means to organize, “the same as a man would organize a ship,” and that element had an existence as long as God himself. He also read the Bible's opening words as the head of the Gods bringing forth the Gods, a council that matches the plural “Let us” of v. 26 and Abraham 4:26.

A retelling of Genesis framed as dictation from the angel of the presence to Moses on Sinai, the same setting Moses 1 gives. It fills in what Genesis leaves out: the angels, the spirits over wind, cloud, and snow, and the deep were all created on the first day. It counts 22 works of creation and matches them to the 22 generations from Adam to Jacob, so creation and Israel's family line have the same shape. The Sabbath, Jubilees says, was first kept by God and the highest angels before any human kept it.

A Jewish philosopher in Egypt who read Genesis through Greek philosophy. He says God did not need six days, since he could make everything at once; six is used because it is the first “perfect” number, the sum of its factors (1 + 2 + 3), and order requires number. He reads the man of 1:27 as an ideal, spiritual pattern and the man of 2:7 as the earthly one, which resembles Moses 3:5's spiritual-then-natural creation.

Opens his *Antiquities* with a plain retelling of creation, then stops on one detail: Moses wrote “one day,” not “the first day.” Josephus says he could explain why but saves it for a later book on causes that he never wrote.

The rabbis treated the “work of creation” (*ma'aseh bereshit*) as guarded knowledge, taught to no more than one student at a time. The same passage warns against asking what is above, below, before, and after. Pirkei Avot asks why the world was made with ten sayings when one would have done, and answers that it raises the cost of destroying the world and the reward for sustaining it.

Lists ten things created on the first day, among them heaven and earth, light and darkness, wind and water, and the measure of day and night. Rabbi Elazar adds that the light of day one, which exists before the sun, let a person see from one end of the world to the other. God hid it away because of the wicked generations of the Flood and Babel and stored it for the righteous in the world to come.

Takes the wisdom of Proverbs 8 (“as one brought up with him,” 8:30) to be the Torah and reads the Hebrew *amon* as “artisan,” one of several meanings it offers. God looked into the Torah and created the world from it, the way an architect builds from plans. Creation follows a written design that existed before the world.

His commentary opens by asking why the Torah begins with creation instead of with Israel's first commandment (Exodus 12). His answer: so that if the nations accuse Israel of taking Canaan, Israel can reply that the whole earth is God's and he gives land to whom he pleases.

Reads the six days as prophecy. With the Lord a day is a thousand years, so in six thousand years he will bring all things to an end, and the seventh day is the rest that follows his coming. D&C 77 uses the same seven-thousand-year frame for the earth's temporal history.

Sees the three days before the sun and moon as a type of God, his Word, and his Wisdom, and uses the word *Trias* for it, usually counted the earliest surviving use of the term. He also notes that plants appear on day three, before the heavenly bodies, so that philosophers could not credit growth to the stars and leave God out.

Takes up the same detail as Josephus and gives two reasons for “one day.” It fixes day and night together as a single unit of time, and it points to eternity, the one day without evening that the Psalms call the eighth day. His sermons on the six days were the most read Christian commentary on Genesis 1 for centuries.

Argued the days are not days like ours, since the sun does not exist until day four. He proposed that God created all things at once, and the six days teach the order of creation to minds that understand things in sequence. He also warned Christians against defending readings of Genesis that conflict with what people can plainly observe of the world.

A Babylonian priest who wrote his people's history in Greek. His creation account survives only in quotes by later writers. In it, Bel cuts the sea-woman Thalatth in two, making the earth from one half and the heavens from the other, then takes off his own head so the other gods can mix his blood with earth to make humans. It shows the Babylonian story that Genesis 1 stands against (see Hermeneutics).

2.overview:
God finishes the heavens and the earth, rests on the seventh day, and blesses it (vv. 1–3). Then the story starts again from the ground up. Before any plant has grown or rain has fallen, the LORD God shapes a man from dust and breathes life into him. He plants a garden in Eden, watered by a river that splits into four, and puts the man there to work it, with one tree forbidden. None of the animals the man names is a fit partner, so God builds a woman from his side. The man greets her as “bone of my bones,” and the two are naked and unashamed.

The real seam falls at v. 4, not at the chapter break. A new heading begins, God is now called “the LORD God,” and the order of events changes: the man comes first, then the garden, the animals, and the woman. The camera has moved from the sky to the soil.

2.hermeneutics:
In the Babylonian *Atrahasis* epic the gods grow tired of digging canals and working the land, so the birth goddess mixes clay with the flesh and blood of a slain god to make humans who will carry the gods' workload. Genesis 2 starts from the same worry: there is “not a man to till the ground” (v. 5). The LORD God also works the clay like a potter, much as Egypt pictured the god Khnum shaping people on a wheel. But no god dies here, and what fills the clay is God's own breath. The man does work (v. 15), yet God plants the garden first and lets him eat freely from it (v. 16). He is a gardener in God's garden, not a laborer standing in for tired gods.

Ancient Near Eastern gods lived where the waters rise. At Ugarit the high god El dwells at the source of the two rivers, and in *Gilgamesh* the hero reaches a garden of the gods whose trees bear gemstones. Eden fits that picture: a river rises there and becomes four, and the land nearby has gold, bdellium, and onyx (vv. 10–12). Israel later used the same imagery for God's house. A spring outside Jerusalem was named Gihon (1 Kings 1:33), and Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from under the temple (Ezekiel 47:1). First hearers would take Eden as the place where God lives, with the man set inside it, more than as a point on a map.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, hinged by a small chiasm at v. 4.

No plant, no rain, no man; the man formed
The garden planted; the man placed and commanded
“Not good” answered: animals, then the woman

notes: Verse 4 turns “heavens and earth” around into “earth and heavens,” a hinge between the two accounts. What follows looks at the earth first.
**The divine name:** from v. 4 through 3:24, God is “the LORD God” (*YHWH Elohim*) 20 times. The plain word “God” returns only when the serpent and the woman talk about him (3:1–5).
**Man and ground:** the man (*adam*) is formed from the ground (*adamah*). “Ground” comes 8 times in 2:4–3:24, ending with the man sent out to till it (3:23).
**“Not good”:** after the seven verdicts of “good” in chapter 1, the first thing God calls not good is the man alone (v. 18).

Verses 1–3 finish the creation account that began at 1:1. Verse 4 opens the first *toledot* heading, “these are the generations of the heavens and of the earth,” and that unit runs to 4:26, where the next heading begins (5:1). Each such heading introduces what came out of the thing named; here, the human story that grows out of heaven and earth.
**Echoes:** Hebrews 4:4 quotes v. 2 to speak of a rest that still remains for God's people. The Bible ends where this chapter begins, with a river and the tree of life (Revelation 22:1–2).

traditions.text: Joseph Smith's revision adds what Genesis 2:5 lacks: the Lord God created all things “spiritually, before they were naturally upon the face of the earth,” and all the children of men were first created in heaven. Adam becomes the first flesh on the earth (3:7), and plants and animals are called living souls. The command about the tree gains a line on agency (3:17), and God speaks of the help meet to his Only Begotten (3:18).

Here the Gods form the man's body and put his own spirit into it before breathing life into him. Abraham explains the “day” of the warning in v. 17 as the Lord's time, reckoned by Kolob, because Adam had not yet been given his own reckoning. The order also differs: the woman is formed before the animals are named, and the chapter ends with “there was found an help meet for him.”

A revelation to missionaries visiting the Shakers, who renounced marriage, answers them with v. 24. Marriage is ordained of God, “they twain shall be one flesh,” and this is so the earth can answer the end of its creation and be filled with people according to their creation before the world was made.

The angel of the presence tells Moses that the animals were brought to Adam over five days of the second week, one class each day. Adam was created in the first week and Eve shown to him in the second, and Adam entered the garden after forty days, Eve after eighty. Jubilees reads this as the origin of the purification periods after childbirth (Leviticus 12), because the garden is holier than all the earth.

After the seventh day, he says, Moses “begins to talk philosophically,” as if v. 4 changes the kind of writing. He explains Adam as “red,” made from red earth, and names the four rivers as the Ganges, Euphrates, Tigris, and Nile, so that Eden waters the whole known world.

Judges warning witnesses in a capital case explain why God made one man alone. Whoever destroys a single life is counted as destroying a whole world, since a world came from Adam. No one can say his ancestor outranks another's, and all people are stamped from one seal yet no two are alike.

One rabbi says the first human was made male and female in one body, reading 5:2 with 1:27. Another says God made him with two faces and then sawed him in two. When challenged with the “rib” of v. 21, he answers that the same Hebrew word means the side of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:20), so God took one of Adam's two sides.

The standard Aramaic translation renders the end of v. 7 so that man became a speaking spirit instead of a living soul. Animals also breathe; speech is what marks the man, and in vv. 19–20 his first act is to name.

Asked whether a man may divorce his wife for any cause, Jesus answers from Genesis instead of from Moses' divorce law. He sets 1:27 beside v. 24 and draws his own conclusion: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” Divorce was allowed because of hard hearts, he says, but the garden shows how it was from the beginning. D&C 49 makes the same appeal to v. 24.

Paul quotes v. 7, “The first man Adam was made a living soul,” and sets Christ against him as the last Adam, a life-giving spirit. He adds that the natural comes first and the spiritual afterward, a statement about bodies and resurrection that reverses the order of Moses 3:5.

Paradise is a real place on earth, since it was planted “eastward” and “out of the ground”; Eden, he says, means delight, and the Gihon reappears in Egypt as the Nile. God made the woman from the man's rib so that no one could claim one god made the man and another the woman, and so their love for each other would be greater.

Reads v. 25 as a sign of youth. Adam and Eve were naked and unashamed because they had been created only a short time before and did not yet understand bearing children; they had first to come to adult age. Theophilus likewise calls Adam an infant in the garden (2.25).

3.overview:
The serpent, craftiest of the animals, asks the woman what God really said about the trees. She answers, adding that they may not even touch the tree in the middle of the garden, and the serpent tells her they will not die but become like gods. She eats, gives to her husband, and both see that they are naked. When the LORD God walks in the garden they hide. Questioned, the man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent. God curses the serpent and the ground, announces pain in childbirth and toil in the fields, clothes the couple in skins, and sends them out east, with cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life.

Watch the questions. God asks “Where art thou?” and “Who told thee?” and lets each one answer before he passes sentence. Death is announced, but the two walk out of the garden alive and clothed by the God they disobeyed.

3.hermeneutics:
Two Babylonian stories turn on lost immortality. In *Gilgamesh* (Tablet XI) the hero dives for a plant that makes the old young again, and on the way home a snake smells it, carries it off, and sheds its skin. In *Adapa*, the sage Adapa is summoned before the sky god Anu and offered the bread and water of life, but he refuses them, because his patron god Ea had warned him they would be deadly; he goes home mortal. Ancient hearers knew the pattern: humans come within reach of endless life and lose it by a trick or a misunderstanding. Genesis keeps the snake and the food of life but moves the cause. Nobody steals the tree of life or refuses it on bad advice. It is closed off after a choice made with full warning (2:17).

Winged guardians of mixed form stood at the doors of Assyrian palaces and temples: huge bulls or lions with human heads and wings, set there to watch the way in. Israel's cherubim belong to the same family. Their wings spread over the ark (Exodus 25:18–22), they were woven into the veil before the most holy place (Exodus 26:31), and the temple's entrance faced east (Ezekiel 47:1). When God places cherubim at the east of the garden (v. 24), an Israelite would recognize the furnishings of a sanctuary. Eden is guarded the way the holy of holies was guarded, and being driven out of it reads like being sent out of God's house.

structure.summary: The chapter moves in sequence; the trial scene (vv. 9–19) is a small chiasm.

rows.label: C
rows.text: The serpent, never questioned, is cursed

notes: The questions go man, woman; the sentences come back serpent, woman, man. Only the serpent and the ground are cursed (vv. 14, 17); the man and the woman are not.

**“Eat”:** the verb comes 17 times in the Hebrew of this chapter. It begins with fruit from the trees and ends with the serpent eating dust and the man eating bread by the sweat of his face (vv. 14, 17–19).

**Eyes and knowing:** the serpent promises opened eyes and the knowledge of good and evil (v. 5). Their eyes do open, and what they know is that they are naked (v. 7). God's last speech grants the point (v. 22).

The chapter sits in the middle of the first *toledot* unit (2:4–4:26). Chapter 2 builds the garden and the couple; chapter 3 loses the garden; chapter 4 follows the family outside it, where the ground already resists the man and brother kills brother.

**Echoes:** Paul reads the chapter as the entry of sin and death through one man (Romans 5:12). Revelation answers its last scene: the tree of life stands open in the city and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:2–3).

traditions.text: Genesis never says who stands behind the serpent. Moses 4 begins before the world: Satan offered to redeem all mankind so that not one soul would be lost, in exchange for God's honor, while the Beloved Son said, “Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever.” Satan sought to destroy man's agency and was cast down; then he put the temptation into the serpent's heart, not knowing the mind of God.

Lehi tells his son that the forbidden fruit stood in opposition to the tree of life so that man could act for himself. Had Adam not transgressed, he and Eve would have stayed in the garden in innocence, with no children, no misery, and no joy. His summary is the Book of Mormon's best-known line on this chapter: “Adam fell that men might be,” and men exist to have joy.

After the expulsion, Moses 5 records what Genesis never does: how Adam and Eve came to see the Fall. Adam blesses God because his eyes are now opened, echoing the serpent's promise in v. 5. Eve says that without their transgression they would never have had children or known good and evil and “the joy of our redemption.”

Alma explains the cherubim and flaming sword to his son. Had Adam eaten of the tree of life at once, he would have lived forever with no space to repent, and the plan of salvation would have been frustrated; the guard granted a probationary time. Irenaeus reached a similar reading in the 2nd century (below).

Adam and Eve tend the garden for seven years before the serpent comes, on the seventeenth day of the second month, the same date Genesis gives for the Flood (7:11). Eve covers herself with fig leaves before she gives the fruit to Adam. On the day he leaves, Adam offers incense, and the mouths of all the animals are closed; until then they had all spoken one language.

Also assumes the animals once shared one language, and says the serpent acted out of envy at the couple's happiness. In his telling God takes away the serpent's speech, puts poison under its tongue, removes its feet, and tells people to aim their blows at its head, his reading of v. 15.

Notices that God forbade eating (2:17) but the woman reports that they may not even touch the tree (v. 3). Adding to God's words is a fence built taller than what it protects, and it falls. The serpent pushed her against the tree, and when she did not die from touching it, told her she would not die from eating either.
traditions.cite: Genesis Rabbah 19:3; compare Avot de-Rabbi Natan 1

traditions.text: Outside the garden Adam stands forty days in the Jordan and Eve in the Tigris to repent, until Satan, disguised as an angel, deceives her a second time. Satan then explains his hatred: when Adam was made in God's image he refused Michael's order to bow to a younger being, vowed to set his seat above the stars, and was cast out. Moses 4 also places Satan's fall before the Fall, for a different reason.

Written after Rome destroyed the temple, it laments that Adam's sin reached everyone after him: “O thou Adam, what hast thou done?” The writer adds that the fall was not Adam's alone but belongs to all who came from him.

Through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, so death passed to all. Adam is “the figure of him that was to come,” the one man whose act is undone by the obedience of another. Moses 6:54 adds a Restoration reading of the same question: the Son of God has atoned for original guilt.

The first writer known to set Eve beside Mary. Eve, a virgin, received the serpent's word and brought forth disobedience and death; Mary, a virgin, received the angel's word with faith and joy. Irenaeus later puts it as a knot: what Eve tied by unbelief, Mary untied by faith (Against Heresies 3.22.4).

Reads Adam's rough fig-leaf girdle as the first act of repentance. God drove him from the tree of life out of pity, so that sin would not be immortal; death set a limit to it. Theophilus of Antioch similarly calls the expulsion a kindness and “Where art thou?” an opening for confession (To Autolycus 2.26).

Holds that the open act grew from a hidden one: pride came first, and the fruit was its result. He reads 1 Timothy 2:14 to mean Adam was not fooled by the serpent but would not be parted from his only companion. The excuses of vv. 12–13 he counts worse than the eating, since each blames another and no one asks for pardon.

4.overview:
Eve bears Cain and then Abel. Cain farms, Abel keeps sheep, and both bring offerings; the LORD accepts Abel's and not Cain's. God warns the angry Cain that sin is crouching at his door, but Cain kills his brother in the field and answers God's question with “Am I my brother's keeper?” The ground that drank Abel's blood will no longer yield to Cain, and he goes out a wanderer, protected by a mark. His descendants build the first city and begin herding, music, and metalwork, until Lamech boasts of killing a man and claims seventy-sevenfold vengeance. The chapter ends with a new son, Seth, and with people beginning to call on the name of the LORD.

Count the word “brother.” In vv. 2–11 Abel is called Cain's brother seven times, and God's question presses it home: “Where is Abel thy brother?”

4.hermeneutics:
Sumerian poets liked contests between a shepherd and a farmer. In *Dumuzid and Enkimdu* the goddess Inana must choose a husband. She prefers the farmer, her brother urges the shepherd, and the shepherd sets his milk, cheese, and wool against the farmer's grain and beer. The quarrel ends with the farmer offering friendship and gifts. Genesis sets up the same pair and the same comparison of produce (vv. 3–4), but here God chooses, and he gives no reason anyone can see. The Sumerian contest ends in a wedding; this one ends with a brother dead in a field.

Mesopotamians credited the arts of civilization to divine sages. Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek, reports that a fish-man named Oannes came up out of the sea and taught people writing, crafts, the founding of cities and temples, laws, and farming. Genesis gives the same kinds of firsts to ordinary human beings: Cain builds the first city, and his descendants begin tent-dwelling herding, music on harp and pipe, and work in bronze and iron (vv. 17–22). No divine teacher hands them down, and the line that invents them starts with a murderer and ends in Lamech's boast.

Babylonian texts know a *rabisu*, a lurking spirit posted at the entrance of a house. God's warning uses a related Hebrew verb: sin is “crouching” at the door (v. 7; KJV “lieth”), waiting with its desire for Cain. The image puts sin outside Cain as something he can still master.
