Seth and Enos; people call on the LORD

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence: a story, then two family lines.
notes: **“Brother”:** seven times in vv. 2–11, Hebrew and KJV alike, then once more for Jubal (v. 21).
**Sevens:** Cain is to be avenged sevenfold, Lamech seventy-sevenfold (vv. 15, 24). Lamech is the seventh name from Adam in Cain's line, matching Enoch, the seventh in Seth's (5:18–24; Jude 14).
**“Ground”:** six times. Cain tills it, offers its fruit, and then it opens its mouth for Abel's blood and refuses Cain its strength (vv. 2, 3, 10–12, 14).
**Echoes of chapter 3:** “Where is Abel thy brother?” recalls “Where art thou?” (3:9), and the desire that sin has for Cain, which he must rule, repeats the words of 3:16.

The chapter closes the first *toledot* unit (2:4–4:26). Cain's line leads nowhere after Lamech; Seth's line begins in vv. 25–26 and is taken up by the next heading, “the book of the generations of Adam” (5:1).

**Echoes:** Jesus answers Lamech's seventy-sevenfold vengeance with forgiveness “until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22), and Hebrews sets the blood of Jesus beside Abel's blood, which still speaks (Hebrews 12:24).

traditions.text: In the Restoration text Cain's trouble starts before the offering. He asks, “Who is the Lord that I should know him?” and loves Satan more than God, and Satan commands him to make the offering. God's warning in v. 7 is expanded: Satan desires to have Cain, and Cain will be called Perdition, for he was also before the world.

Cain swears an oath of secrecy with Satan, takes the title Master Mahan, “master of this great secret, that I may murder and get gain,” and boasts after the killing that his brother's flocks are now his. Lamech later enters the same covenant and kills Irad for revealing it, which explains his song in vv. 23–24. The Book of Mormon traces later secret oaths back to the same source (Helaman 6:26–27; Ether 8:15).

Explains why the offerings were treated differently. Abel offered the firstlings of the flock by faith in the coming atonement; Cain brought fruit of the ground and could not offer in faith, because sacrifice was a type of the shedding of the Only Begotten's blood. Moses 5:5–7 gives the same rule to Adam: offer the firstlings as a likeness of the Son's sacrifice.
traditions.cite: Letter to the Church, Evening and Morning Star, 1834; Moses 5:5–7

traditions.text: Dates the murder to the third jubilee of the world and names Cain's wife: Awan, his sister. Adam and Eve mourn Abel for twenty-eight years before Seth is born. Cain dies when his house falls on him: he had killed Abel with a stone, and stones kill him, which Jubilees makes a law of the heavenly tablets.

The Hebrew of v. 8 reads oddly, “Cain said to Abel” with no words reported. This Aramaic paraphrase supplies them: Cain says the world is ruled with favoritism and that there is no judgment, no judge, and no world to come, and Abel answers that there is. The argument ends with Cain driving a stone into his brother's forehead.

Asks the same question about v. 8: what did they quarrel over? One answer: they divided the world, one taking the land and the other the movable goods, until each claimed what the other stood on or wore. Others say they fought over where the temple would stand, or over a twin sister born with Abel.

Notes that v. 10 says “bloods” in the plural. Cain was charged with Abel's blood and the blood of all the descendants Abel would have had. Judges cited this to warn witnesses in capital cases that a false testimony kills generations.

Says God preferred Abel's milk and firstlings because they grew naturally, over the produce Cain forced from the ground as a covetous man. Exiled, Cain grew rich by robbery, invented weights and measures, set boundaries on land, and walled the first city. Moses 5:31 also makes gain Cain's motive.

On his tour of the places of the dead, Enoch hears one spirit crying out to heaven. The angel Raphael tells him it is Abel, who keeps accusing Cain until Cain's seed is gone from the earth. Hebrews 11:4 says Abel “being dead yet speaketh.”

Reads v. 8 as an allegory of the soul. On a close reading, he says, Cain killed himself: the soul that destroys its love of God dies to virtue. Abel is both dead and alive, since his blood still cries out, and a man who no longer existed could not speak.
traditions.cite: That the Worse Attacks the Better 47–48

traditions.text: Explains Lamech's song with a tradition from the Midrash. Lamech was blind, and his son Tubal-cain, leading him, mistook Cain for an animal; Lamech shot, killed Cain, and then struck his son dead in his grief. His wives left him, and vv. 23–24 are his plea that he acted without intent. Moses 5:47–50 gives a different victim and motive.

Hebrews lists Abel first among the faithful: by faith he offered a better sacrifice than Cain, and though dead he still speaks. First John says Cain belonged to the wicked one and killed because his own works were evil while his brother's were righteous. Jude warns against those who have “gone in the way of Cain.”

Builds his City of God on this chapter. Cain, the firstborn, belongs to the earthly city and builds one; Abel, a pilgrim, builds none. He sets the first murder beside Rome's founding, when Romulus killed his brother Remus, and says Cain killed out of the envy the wicked feel toward the good.

5.overview:
A new heading, “the book of the generations of Adam,” recalls that God made humankind in his likeness, male and female, and named them. Then ten generations run from Adam to Noah in a fixed form: the father's age when his son is born, the years he lives after that, his total years, and “and he died.” The ages are enormous; Methuselah reaches 969. Two entries break the pattern. Enoch walks with God and is not said to die: “he was not; for God took him” (v. 24). Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring comfort from the toil of the cursed ground (v. 29). The list ends with Noah's three sons.

The refrain carries the meaning. “And he died” closes eight of the entries, so the sentence of 3:19 lands name after name. Enoch's is the one entry where it never comes.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; Moses 6:5–8 says a genealogy and book of remembrance were kept from Adam's day.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith received Moses 6:5–25 and 8:1–12, his revision of this chapter, between November 1830 and February 1831. Between them sits Enoch's ministry (Moses 6:26–7:69).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly proposals range from the 10th to the 5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: By the Hebrew numbers the Flood comes 1,656 years after Adam's creation (Ussher: 4004 to 2348 BC). The Greek Septuagint numbers stretch the span to over 2,200 years; the Samaritan Pentateuch shortens it to 1,307.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Genesis names no place. D&C 107:53 sets Adam's last blessing of his descendants in the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman, which D&C 116 places at Spring Hill, Missouri.

5.hermeneutics:
The Sumerian King List opens with the rulers before the flood: eight kings in five cities who reigned 241,200 years in all, the first of them, Alulim of Eridu, for 28,800 years. Then the flood sweeps over, and the reigns that follow drop to hundreds of years and later to ordinary lengths. Genesis 5 shares that frame: a fixed list of long-lived men between creation and the flood, with lifespans shrinking afterward (11:10–32). But its numbers are far smaller, since no one reaches a thousand years, and its men are fathers, not kings of cities. The list records births and deaths, not reigns, and every life ends.

The seventh king in the Sumerian list, Enmeduranna, ruled Sippar, the city of the sun god. Later Babylonian tradition says the gods Shamash and Adad brought this king, as Enmeduranki, into their presence and taught him the secrets of heaven and earth, the divination arts that Babylonian diviners claimed to inherit from him. Enoch is also seventh, his 365 years match the days of a solar year, and he too is brought near to God. Genesis gives him no secret technique and no guild of heirs. He “walked with God,” and the text says nothing more about how.

breakdown.label: Heading: God made humankind in his likeness
Adam: Seth born in Adam's own likeness
Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, and Jared
Enoch walks with God; God takes him
Methuselah: the longest life, 969 years
Lamech names Noah, hoping for comfort
Noah and his three sons

structure.summary: No strong pattern; a ten-member list repeats one formula.

rows.text: Creation recalled: likeness, male and female, blessing
Six entries in the full formula, each ending “and he died”
Two more entries ending “and he died”

notes: **The formula:** each entry gives the age at a son's birth, the years after, the total, and “and he died,” eight times in all (vv. 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 27, 31). Noah's entry stays open until 9:29.
**Enoch, seventh from Adam:** where the others “lived,” he “walked with God” (vv. 22, 24). The phrase appears once more, for Noah (6:9).
**Likeness handed on:** God made man “in the likeness of God” (v. 1); Adam fathers Seth “in his own likeness, after his image” (v. 3).
**One speech:** Lamech's words at Noah's birth (v. 29) are the only speech in the chapter, and they look back to the cursed ground of 3:17.

Verse 1 opens the second *toledot* heading, “the book of the generations of Adam.” It starts over from creation, passes over Cain's line, and carries Seth's line to Noah. The unit closes at 6:8 with Noah finding grace, and the Flood begins under the next heading at 6:9.
**Echoes:** 1 Chronicles opens Israel's history with these names (1 Chronicles 1:1–4), and Luke runs Jesus' genealogy back through them to “Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38).

traditions.text: Before the list begins, Moses 6 says a book of remembrance was kept in the language of Adam, and that children were taught to read and write. Genesis 5 is presented as that record, “a genealogy… of the children of God.” Where Luke calls Adam the son of God, Moses 6:22 says the same, adding that God himself conversed with him.

Turns the genealogy into a priesthood line, giving each patriarch's age at ordination by Adam: Seth at 69, Enos at 134, Enoch at 25. Enoch's 65 years, his age at Methuselah's birth in v. 21, become the age when Adam blessed him, and his 365 years of walking with God bring him to 430 when he is translated. Lamech is ordained by Seth and Noah, at ten, by Methuselah.

Three years before Adam's death he gathers Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, and Methuselah in the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman. The Lord appears, they call Adam “Michael, the prince, the archangel,” and Adam prophesies to the last generation; these things were written in the book of Enoch. In 1839 Joseph Smith identified Adam with Daniel's Ancient of Days, who will again call his children together in council.

The Restoration text gives Enoch's 365 years to his city as well: “all the days of Zion” in Enoch's time were 365 years, and then God received Zion up into his bosom. Methuselah is not taken, so that Noah can come from Enoch's line. Moses 8:12 also differs from v. 32: Noah fathers Japheth at 450, Shem at 492, and Ham at 500.

Quotes vv. 22–24 and says God reserved Enoch from death and appointed him a ministry to terrestrial bodies. He adds that Enoch appeared to Jude, as Abel did to Paul, which is how Jude could quote him. Translation, he taught, is a power of the priesthood.
traditions.cite: Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 October 1840 (Joseph Smith Papers)

traditions.text: Enoch is the first man to learn writing and to record the signs of heaven by their months, and he spends six jubilees with the angels. Then he is taken into the garden of Eden, where he still writes down the judgment of the world. Jubilees also explains Adam's 930 years: he died seventy short of a thousand, a single “day” of the Lord, fulfilling “in the day that thou eatest” (2:17).

A collection of books in Enoch's name that grew from v. 24. Enoch is “hidden” among the holy ones, called the scribe of righteousness, and finally raised on chariots of the spirit so that he is no longer counted among the living. Its opening prophecy of the Lord coming with ten thousands of his holy ones is the passage Jude quotes.

This Aramaic paraphrase of v. 24 says Enoch served in truth before the Lord, was withdrawn from the dwellers on earth, and ascended to the firmament, where he was named Metatron, the great scribe. It merges the Enoch of Genesis with the heavenly scribe of the Enoch books.

Takes the opposite line. Some rabbis read v. 24 as death: Enoch wavered between righteous and wicked, so God took him while he was still righteous. When sectarians argued that his death is never mentioned, Rabbi Abahu pointed to Ezekiel 24:16, where God's “taking” means death. Rashi repeats this reading.

His ages follow the longer Greek numbers (Adam 230 at Seth's birth), and of Enoch he says death was not written because he “departed and went to God.” He defends the long lives: they were beloved of God, ate better food, and needed six centuries to track the stars' great year. He also says Seth's descendants carved their discoveries on pillars of brick and stone to survive fire and flood.

Hebrews follows the Greek wording of v. 24: Enoch “was not found, because God had translated him,” having pleased God. Jude counts him seventh from Adam and quotes his prophecy of judgment, words found in 1 Enoch 1:9.

Notices that by the Septuagint's numbers Methuselah outlives the Flood by fourteen years, though only eight people were saved. He rejects the claim that the Jews altered their text, and on matters of fact follows the Hebrew, by which Methuselah dies in the Flood year.

Sets Berossus' kings beside Genesis 5. Both count ten generations from the first man to the flood, he says, and Berossus' flood hero is the man the Hebrews call Noah. He calls Berossus' hundreds of thousands of years incredible and suggests the Babylonian “sar” measured some much shorter unit.

A Babylonian priest who wrote in Greek. He lists ten kings from Alorus, the first, to Xisuthrus, in whose reign the great flood came, and gives them 120 sars, or 432,000 years. His list survives only through later writers such as Alexander Polyhistor and Eusebius.
traditions.cite: Berossus in Eusebius, Chronicon 1; Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)

6.overview:
As people multiply, “the sons of God” take wives from “the daughters of men,” and the LORD limits man's days to 120 years. The Nephilim (KJV “giants”) are on the earth, the mighty men of old. God sees that every imagination of the human heart is only evil, regrets making man, and resolves to wipe out people and animals, but Noah finds grace. A new heading introduces Noah, a just man who walks with God, on an earth corrupt and full of violence. God tells him to build an ark of gopher wood, 300 cubits long, and to bring his family, pairs of every kind of animal, and food. Noah does all that God commands.

Watch what God sees. In chapter 1 he looked at what he had made and saw that it was good. Here he looks again and sees wickedness (v. 5) and a corrupt earth (v. 12), and the sight grieves him at his heart.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith received Moses 8:13–30, his revision of vv. 1–13, in February 1831. In it Noah preaches repentance and baptism, and the giants seek his life.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly proposals range from the 10th to the 5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The Flood comes in Noah's 600th year (7:6), 1,656 years after Adam by the Hebrew numbers: about 2350 BC (Ussher, 2348 BC).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Moses 8:13–30 (vv. 1–13). Outside the Bible: the flood stories of *Atrahasis*, *Gilgamesh* XI, and Berossus.

6.hermeneutics:
Ancient hearers knew stories of heroes born of gods and women. Gilgamesh, the great hero of Mesopotamia, is two-thirds god and one-third man. Hesiod's *Works and Days* calls the heroes of the age before his own a race of demigods, and at Ugarit the members of the divine council are the sons of El. Against that background vv. 1–4 sound like the opening of a heroic age, with “mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” Genesis gives those heroes four verses, no names, and no deeds, and moves straight to God's verdict on the world they filled.

In the Babylonian *Atrahasis* epic the gods send plague, drought, and famine, and at last a flood, because multiplying humans make so much noise that the god Enlil cannot sleep. After the flood the gods hold human numbers down another way, with barren women and infant death. Genesis also ties the flood to human increase (v. 1) and sets a limit on human life (v. 3), but God's reason is moral: wickedness, corruption, violence (vv. 5, 11). He is not kept awake. He grieves (v. 6).

In *Gilgamesh* XI the flood hero Utnapishtim builds a cube, about 120 cubits on each side, with seven decks. Noah's ark is 300 by 50 by 30 cubits with three decks (vv. 15–16), a long box six times as long as it is wide. The Babylonian vessel looks like a temple floating on the water; Noah's looks like something meant to ride it out.

breakdown.label: Sons of God, daughters of men, and the Nephilim
God sees the evil and grieves; Noah finds grace
Heading: Noah, just and walking with God; three sons
A corrupt and violent earth; the end announced
Instructions for the ark
Flood, covenant, passengers, and food
Noah does all that God commands

structure.summary: Chiasm: the opening of Wenham's palistrophe for the Flood (6:10–9:19), abridged. Verses 1–9 stand before it.
notes: This chapter holds only the first six members. Wenham's full pattern has fifteen on each side of 8:1; members G to O (7:1–8:13) are left out here. Verses 1–8 belong to the Adam unit and sit outside the pattern.

**Corrupt and destroy:** one Hebrew verb, *shachat*, comes five times in vv. 11–17. The earth “was corrupt,” all flesh “had corrupted” its way, and God will “destroy” them: the sentence matches the deed.

**Seeing:** the sons of God “saw” the daughters (v. 2), God “saw” the wickedness (v. 5) and “looked” on the corrupt earth (v. 12), all one verb, the same one as “God saw that it was good” in chapter 1.

Verses 1–8 close the unit headed “the book of the generations of Adam” (5:1), ending in grief and in grace for one man. Verse 9 opens the next *toledot*, “the generations of Noah,” which runs to his death at 9:29; the line of his sons begins at 10:1.

**Echoes:** Jesus says the days before his coming will be like the days of Noah, with people eating, drinking, and marrying until the Flood came (Matthew 24:37–39). Hebrews counts Noah's ark-building as an act of faith (Hebrews 11:7).

traditions.source: Moses 8 on the sons of God
traditions.text: The Restoration text turns vv. 1–2 around. Noah and his sons hearken to the Lord and are called the sons of God; it is the daughters of Noah's sons who marry the sons of men. Later the unrepentant claim the title for themselves: “Behold, we are the sons of God,” they tell Noah, and their children are the mighty men of renown.

Noah is ordained after God's own order and preaches faith, repentance, and baptism in the name of Jesus Christ. The 120 years of v. 3 become a deadline with a condition: if men do not repent, the floods will come. The giants seek his life, and the Lord protects him.

Verse 6 says God was grieved at his heart. In Moses 8 it is Noah whose heart is pained that the Lord made man, and Moses 7 shows Enoch watching the God of heaven weep over the residue of the people, who hate their own blood. Enoch asks how a holy God can weep, and is answered that the whole heavens weep over those who will suffer.

Teaching on priesthood keys, he identified Noah with the angel Gabriel and placed him next to Adam in authority. The Noah of this chapter thus becomes the messenger who later announces births to Zacharias and Mary (Luke 1:19, 26).

The fullest early retelling of vv. 1–4. Two hundred angels, the Watchers, swear an oath together and descend on Mount Hermon in the days of Jared, take wives, and teach charms, metalworking, weapons, and cosmetics. Their giant sons devour humankind until the earth cries out; God sends an angel to warn Noah and has the Watchers bound. The binding oath echoes Cain's secret oath in Moses 5:29.

Says the Watchers first came down in Jared's days to teach people judgment and uprightness, and only later sinned with women. God binds them in the depths and sends a sword among their sons, who kill one another. The 120 years are kept as the limit God sets on man.

Takes the sons of God as angels and compares their sons to the giants of Greek legend. He adds that Noah urged them to change and then left the land because he feared they would kill him and his family, a detail Moses 8:18 shares. God then cut human life to 120 years.

His Greek Bible read “angels of God” in v. 2. Philo says angels, demons, and souls are one kind of being under different names, and the bad ones chase bodily pleasure. The giants of v. 4 are no fable: they stand for earth-born people who live for the body, set against those born of heaven and of God.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rendered “sons of God” as sons of judges, meaning the powerful, and cursed anyone who translated it “sons of God” in Aramaic. Their corruption mattered because the common people follow the great. Other rabbis say they were given long lives to work out the courses of the stars, a reason Josephus also gives for the patriarchs' long lives.

Asks why God, who could save Noah any way he wished, made him build a ship. Building it for 120 years was a sermon: people would ask what it was for, hear that a flood was coming, and perhaps repent. The idea comes from the Talmud (Sanhedrin 108b) and fits Moses 8's picture of Noah as preacher.

Second Peter and Jude speak of angels who sinned or left their own habitation and are held in chains for judgment, a reading close to 1 Enoch. Second Peter calls Noah “a preacher of righteousness,” and 1 Peter says God's patience waited in Noah's days while the ark was being prepared.

Follows the angel reading. The angels broke God's appointment, were captured by love of women, and fathered the demons, who then enslaved humankind through magic, fear, and the demand for sacrifices. The pagan myths about gods, he says, are garbled memories of their deeds.

Rejects the angel reading. The sons of God were Seth's descendants who married Cain's daughters; Scripture calls them flesh in v. 3. He notes that some Septuagint copies read “angels of God,” and sets aside the Enoch books as uncertain in origin and outside the canon.

In the Babylonian account the god Kronos warns Xisuthrus in a dream that a flood will destroy humankind. He is told to bury the writings at Sippar, build a boat, load it with food, birds, and four-footed animals, and board with his family and friends. The Armenian version of Eusebius gives the boat 15 stades by 2.
traditions.cite: Berossus in Eusebius, Chronicon 1; Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)

7.overview:
The LORD tells Noah to enter the ark with his household, taking seven pairs of every clean animal and bird and one pair of the rest, and gives him seven days’ warning. Noah does all he is told. In his six hundredth year, on the seventeenth day of the second month, the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open. Rain falls forty days, the LORD shuts Noah in, and the water rises fifteen cubits over the mountains. Everything on dry land that breathes dies, and the waters prevail 150 days.

Verse 11 runs Genesis 1 backward. The “deep” (*tehom*) of 1:2 breaks loose, the waters God divided above and below the firmament (1:7) pour back together, and the dry land of day three goes under. One family and a boatload of animals are kept “to keep seed alive” (v. 3) for a new start.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign it to later writers drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: The Book of Moses stops at Genesis 6:13 (Moses 8:30), so the Flood itself has no Moses text. Enoch sees Noah build the ark and the floods come in a vision (Moses 7:42–43).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The ages in Genesis 5 and 7:6 put the Flood 1,656 years after Adam. Ussher’s reckoning, printed in many KJV margins, dates it 2349–2348 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: The Babylonian flood stories in *Atrahasis* and *Gilgamesh* tablet XI, and Berossus’ story of Xisuthrus (see Hermeneutics and Traditions).

7.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamia told this story long before Israel did. In *Gilgamesh* tablet XI the flood hero Utnapishtim says he went into his boat and “sealed the entry,” then handed the caulking over to a boatman named Puzur-Amurri. In *Atrahasis* the hero seals the hatch himself with pitch. Genesis gives that job to God: “the LORD shut him in” (v. 16). A listener who knew the older story would notice that Noah does not secure his own rescue. The door is closed from outside.

The gods of *Gilgamesh* lose control of their own storm. They are “cowering like dogs,” fleeing up to the heaven of Anu, while the goddess Ishtar shrieks like a woman in labor. The storm blows six days and seven nights and then stops. Genesis has no frightened deity. God opens the fountains and the windows (v. 11), and the waters keep a schedule: seven days of warning, forty days of rain, 150 days at full height, each dated by Noah’s age like an entry in a chronicle.

In the Babylonian creation epic *Enuma Elish*, Marduk splits the sea goddess Tiamat, makes half of her a cover for the sky, fixes a bolt, posts a watchman, and orders them not to let her waters out. Ancient hearers pictured water held back above the sky by a barrier. “The windows of heaven” (v. 11) are openings in that barrier, and the fountains below are the deep breaking through from beneath. In Genesis 7 both barriers give way at once.

breakdown.label: The LORD’s command: enter, with seven pairs of clean animals
Noah’s household and the animals go in; seven days pass
The dated day: the deep and the heavens burst open
All enter that same day; the LORD shuts Noah in
Forty days: the ark lifts; water covers the mountains
All flesh on dry land dies; only Noah’s company survives
The waters prevail for 150 days
God remembers Noah: the turning point

structure.summary: Chiasm: the Flood’s time spans mirror each other around 8:1. Part of Wenham’s palistrophe across 6:10–9:19.

rows.label: C′
rows.text: At the end of forty days

notes: Gordon Wenham traced a 31-step mirror pattern across 6:10–9:19 with “God remembered Noah” (8:1) at its center. The day counts are its clearest thread: 7, 7, 40, 150 as the water rises, then 150, 40, 7, 7 as it falls. The fuller ladder appears under chapter 8.
Wenham notes the pattern is partly a writer’s choice. The one week of waiting is mentioned twice (vv. 4, 10), balancing the two weeks of waiting at the end (8:10, 12).

**Repetition to watch:** the waters “prevailed” (*gavar*) four times (vv. 18, 19, 20, 24). Noah does “according unto all” God commanded (v. 5), a line repeated in vv. 9 and 16 and first heard at 6:22.

The heading “these are the generations of Noah” (6:9) opens the Flood story, and Noah’s death notice (9:28–29) closes it. Chapter 7 is the rising half: the entry into the ark and the waters at full height. The story turns at 8:1.

**Echoes:** The Hebrew word for the ark, *tevah*, comes back for the basket that carries the infant Moses on the Nile (Exodus 2:3). Jesus compares the days before his coming to the days before “Noe entered into the ark” (Matthew 24:37–39).

traditions.text: Enoch’s vision runs past his own city to the Flood. He sees Noah build an ark and the Lord smile on it and hold it “in his own hand,” while the floods swallow the rest. Enoch weeps and refuses to be comforted until he is shown Noah’s descendants and the coming of the Son of Man. Genesis has the LORD shut Noah in (v. 16); Moses 7 has him holding the ark.

The Jaredite crossing is told as a second ark story. The barges carry food, flocks, herds, and birds, and when waves bury them in the deep no water can hurt them, because they are “tight like unto the ark of Noah.” Moroni’s abridgment assumes readers know Genesis 7.

Joseph F. Smith’s vision opens with 1 Peter 3:18–20, the spirits who were disobedient “in the days of Noah,” and he wonders how Christ could preach to them. He sees that the Lord organized messengers from among the righteous dead to carry the gospel to the spirits in darkness. The people drowned in v. 23 are given a further chapter.

Jubilees dates each step. Noah and the animals enter from the new moon of the second month to the sixteenth, and the Lord closes the ark “from without” on the evening of the seventeenth. It counts seven floodgates of heaven and seven mouths of the deep, matching the sevens of the chapter.

Names the month of v. 11: the second month, called Dius by the Macedonians and Marheshvan by the Hebrews, in the autumn. He explains that this was the old order of the year, before Moses made Nisan first for the festivals. He also lists foreign historians who mention the Flood and the ark, among them Berossus and Nicolaus of Damascus.

Two sages split over “the second month.” Rabbi Eliezer counts from Tishri, so the Flood begins in Marheshvan, when the springs rise with the rains. Rabbi Joshua counts from Nisan, putting it in Iyar, the dry season, and says God changed the order of creation to bring the water. Josephus’ dating agrees with Rabbi Eliezer’s.

Reads “because of the waters” (v. 7) to mean Noah went in only when the water forced him; he half believed the warning. On v. 12 he notes the text says “rain” before it says “flood”: God began gently, so the rain could still become a blessing if the people repented. Both readings come from Genesis Rabbah.

The sages taught that the Flood waters were scalding: a generation that sinned in the heat of passion was punished with hot water. Rav Hisda finds the proof in 8:1, where the waters “assuaged,” the verb Esther 7:10 uses when the king’s wrath cools (KJV “pacified”). The same passage says Noah rebuked his neighbors while he built, and they scorned him, asking the old man why he was building an ark.

Peter counts the people saved in the ark, “eight souls,” saved by water, and calls baptism the “like figure.” This makes the Flood the pattern for baptism, a reading Justin and Tertullian develop and D&C 138:9 quotes.

Argues with a Jewish teacher that the eight people in the ark were a sign of the eighth day, when Christ rose from the dead. Noah was saved by wood riding over water, as Christians are saved through water, faith, and the wood of the cross. He also stresses that the water stood fifteen cubits above every mountain, so the whole earth was covered.

Reads the ark as the Church and its measurements as a human body, six times as long as it is wide and ten times as long as it is deep, like 300 by 50 by 30 cubits. The door in its side stands for the wound in Christ’s side. He also answers critics who said the ark was too small, citing Origen’s guess that Moses meant a larger Egyptian cubit, and he warns against reading the story only as history or only as allegory.

At Hierapolis in Syria Lucian heard a Deucalion story in which the earth poured out water and rain fell in torrents. Deucalion put his children and their wives into a huge ark, and boars, horses, lions, serpents, and every other beast came to him “all in couples” and did him no harm. His 1913 editors observed that this is far closer to the Babylonian and biblical stories than to the usual Greek legend, where only Deucalion and Pyrrha survive.
traditions.cite: De Dea Syria 12; Strong and Garstang (1913), note 22

8.overview:
God remembers Noah and sends a wind over the earth. The deep and the windows of heaven are closed, the waters fall, and the ark comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. When the hilltops have shown for forty days, Noah sends out a raven, then a dove three times; the dove brings back an olive leaf and at last stays away. A year and ten days after the Flood began, the earth is dry, and God tells Noah to go out. Noah builds an altar, and the LORD resolves never again to curse the ground or strike every living thing.

The reason God gives for mercy is the reason he gave for the Flood. Before, “every imagination” of man’s heart was “only evil continually” (6:5). Now he will not curse the ground again, “for the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (v. 21). Human nature has not changed; God’s response to it has.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign it to later writers drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith’s translation of Genesis (1830–1831) recasts vv. 20–22: Noah gives thanks, and it is Noah who smells the sweet savor and calls on the Lord (JST Genesis 9:4–6).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The earth is dry in Noah’s 601st year (vv. 13–14), 1,657 years after Adam by the ages in Genesis 5. Ussher’s reckoning gives 2348 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: “The mountains of Ararat” (v. 4) names a region, the land of Urartu in the Armenian highlands north of Mesopotamia, not a single peak.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: *Gilgamesh* tablet XI and *Atrahasis* tablet III (birds, sacrifice, the gods’ response); Berossus on Xisuthrus.

8.hermeneutics:
In *Gilgamesh* tablet XI the boat lodges on Mount Nimush. After seven days Utnapishtim sends out a dove, then a swallow; both come back with no place to perch. Then he sends a raven, which finds the water going down and does not return, and at once he sends everything out in all directions and sacrifices. Genesis has the same signal, a bird that stays away, but the order differs: the raven goes first, then the dove three times, and the olive leaf is the evidence. Noah also waits after the ground is dry (vv. 13–14) until God tells him to leave (vv. 15–16).

Utnapishtim’s offering draws a crowd: “the gods smelled the sweet savor, and collected like flies” over it. In *Atrahasis* they had gone hungry and thirsty through the flood, because no humans were left to feed them. Genesis uses the same phrase, “the LORD smelled a sweet savour” (v. 21), but nothing suggests hunger. In *Gilgamesh* the mother goddess bars Enlil from the meal for sending the flood without thought, Enlil rages that anyone survived, and the god Ea rebukes him. In Genesis the one God who sent the Flood also makes the promise, speaking “in his heart.”

Assyrian records name Urartu as a kingdom around Lake Van in the 9th to 7th centuries BC, and Jeremiah lists “the kingdoms of Ararat” among the northern peoples (Jeremiah 51:27). Mount Nimush lies in the Zagros east of Assyria; Berossus puts the boat in the Cordyaean mountains of Armenia. Each version grounds the ark in the high country north of the flood plain.

breakdown.label: God remembers Noah; a wind; the waters abate
The ark rests on Ararat; the mountaintops appear
The raven, and the dove that finds no rest
The olive leaf; the dove does not return
The ground dries: a year and ten days
God’s command: go out, be fruitful, multiply
Noah’s altar and the LORD’s promise in his heart

structure.summary: Chiasm (palistrophe): Wenham’s 31-step mirror across 6:10–9:19, grouped here into 15 steps, with 8:1 at the center.

rows.label: B
rows.text: Ark built; flood announced; covenant promised

rows.label: D
rows.text: Command to enter; seven days, seven days

rows.label: E
rows.text: Entry; the LORD shuts Noah in

rows.label: F
rows.text: Forty days; waters rise; mountains covered

rows.label: F′
rows.text: Mountaintops seen; waters fall; forty days

rows.label: E′
rows.text: Window opened; raven and dove leave

rows.label: D′
rows.text: Seven days, seven days; command to leave

rows.label: B′
rows.text: Covenant; no more flood; the ark

notes: At the center God “remembered” (*zakar*) Noah (v. 1). The verb returns only twice more in the Flood story, when God promises to remember his covenant (9:15–16).

The wind (*ruach*) of v. 1 is the word for the Spirit moving on the waters in 1:2. After it, land appears, birds fly, and living things are sent out to “be fruitful, and multiply” (v. 17), the steps of creation retraced.
Wenham notes that Noah’s sacrifice (vv. 20–22) stands outside the pattern. The story of the waters ends at v. 19; the altar opens what follows.

Chapter 8 is the falling half of the Flood story (6:9–9:29), from the hinge at v. 1 to dry ground. The closing verses turn from water to worship, and the promise spoken “in his heart” (v. 21) becomes a spoken covenant with a sign in 9:8–17.

**Echoes:** Isaiah recalls the oath that “the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth” as the model for God’s promise not to stay angry with Israel (Isaiah 54:9). The Savior quotes the passage to the Nephites (3 Nephi 22:9).

traditions.text: In the JST, Noah offers his burnt offerings, “gave thanks unto the Lord, and rejoiced in his heart.” Then Noah, not the Lord, smells the sweet savor and says in his heart that he will call on the name of the Lord, so that God will not curse the ground again. The inner resolve of v. 21 becomes Noah’s prayer, much as Josephus has Noah plead that the earth not be flooded again.

Long before the Flood, Enoch hears the earth mourn and asks the Lord to have mercy on Noah and his seed, “that the earth might never more be covered by the floods.” The Lord swears an oath to Enoch to stay the floods and to call upon Noah’s children. In this reading the promise of vv. 21–22 answers a prayer made generations earlier; JST Genesis 9 ties the bow to the same covenant.

Ether taught the Jaredites that after the waters receded from off the face of their land, it became a choice land above all others. He saw there the place of a New Jerusalem to be built for the remnant of Joseph. The drying of the earth (vv. 13–14) becomes the start of a sacred geography in the Americas.

The ark rests “on the top of Lubar, one of the mountains of Ararat.” Noah leaves on the new moon of the third month and first makes atonement for the earth with the blood of a kid, then offers an ox, goat, sheep, salt, turtle-dove, and young dove with oil, wine, and frankincense. The Lord smells the savor and makes his covenant then, in the month Jubilees ties to the Feast of Weeks (see ch. 9).

His version differs from Genesis in small ways: the raven comes back, and the dove returns covered with mud and carrying an olive branch. The Armenians called the landing place the Place of Descent and showed the ark’s remains there. Noah, Josephus adds, feared God would flood the earth every year, so he prayed with his offering that nature would keep its order, and God promised it would.

Reish Lakish gives the raven a voice. It protests that God and Noah both hate it: Noah sent an unclean bird, of which there was only one pair, instead of one of the clean birds kept by sevens, and if it died its kind would be lost. The sages read the raven’s refusal to return (v. 7) as a quarrel.

Reads the olive leaf as the dove’s speech: better that my food be bitter as an olive from the hand of God than sweet as honey from the hand of man. On v. 22 he divides the year into six two-month seasons and infers from “shall not cease” that day and night had stopped during the Flood. Both comments draw on the Talmud and Genesis Rabbah.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 8:11, 22; Eruvin 18b; Genesis Rabbah 34:11

traditions.text: The world “that then was” perished by water, and the present heavens and earth are kept for fire at the day of judgment. Verse 22 promises the earth will last “while the earth remaineth”; 2 Peter supplies the end of that sentence.

After the Flood, “the baptism, so to say, of the world,” a dove brought the olive branch that announced the end of God’s wrath. In the same way the dove of the Holy Spirit comes to the baptized as they rise from the font, bringing God’s peace. Tertullian adds that the world returned to sin and so is destined for fire, as 2 Peter says.

Reads each bird. The raven that does not return is like people defiled by worldly desire; the dove that finds no rest shows that the saints are promised no rest in this world; the olive leaf brought back after seven days stands for the sevenfold Spirit drawing people into one communion. Josephus’ raven comes back; Augustine’s, like the Hebrew text’s, does not.

In the Babylonian priest’s version, Xisuthrus sends out birds three times: first they return finding no food or rest, then they return with mud on their feet, and the third time they stay away. He leaves the boat, sacrifices, and vanishes with his wife, daughter, and helmsman to live with the gods. Pieces of the boat remained in the mountains of the Cordyaeans in Armenia, where people scraped off its bitumen for amulets; Josephus quotes this line.
traditions.cite: Eusebius, Chronicle 1 (from Alexander Polyhistor); Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)

traditions.text: In an essay on animal intelligence, he says the mythographers tell of a dove let out of Deucalion’s ark: its return meant the storm was still raging, and its flying away meant fair weather. He is the only Greek writer to add the dove to the Deucalion story. Lucian’s pairs of animals (ch. 7) and Plutarch’s dove both point to an eastern Flood story reaching Greek readers.

9.overview:
God blesses Noah and his sons with the words first given to Adam, “be fruitful, and multiply,” and now gives them animals for food, with two limits: no eating flesh with its blood, and a reckoning for anyone who sheds human blood, because man is made in God’s image. He makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets his bow in the cloud as its sign. Later Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent. Ham sees and tells his brothers, who cover their father walking backward. Noah curses Canaan, blesses Shem and Japheth, and dies at 950.

The curse falls on Canaan, Ham’s son, and Ham himself is never cursed (v. 25). Why the son pays for the father’s act is a question the text leaves open, and early readers answered it in very different ways.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign it to later writers drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith’s translation of Genesis (1830–1831) expands the laws on blood and ties the bow to God’s covenant with Enoch (JST Genesis 9:10–15, 21–25).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Noah lives 350 years after the Flood (v. 28), dying 2,006 years after Adam by the Hebrew text’s ages. Ussher’s reckoning gives 1998 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Moses 7:49–52 (God’s oath to Enoch to stay the floods); Abraham 1:26–27 (Noah’s blessing and curse in the line of Ham).

9.hermeneutics:
*Atrahasis* ends its flood with the gods limiting humanity so it will not disturb them again. The god Enki has the birth goddess arrange for women who do not bear, a demon who snatches infants from their mothers’ laps, and orders of priestesses who have no children. Genesis ends the other way. God twice commands “be fruitful, and multiply” (vv. 1, 7). The problem before the Flood was violence (6:11), not crowding, and the answer is a law against bloodshed (vv. 5–6).

The Hebrew word for the rainbow, *qeshet*, is the ordinary word for a warrior’s bow. In *Enuma Elish*, after Marduk defeats Tiamat, Anu lifts Marduk’s bow in the assembly of the gods, kisses it, names it, and makes it the Bow-star in the sky. A hearer would see a weapon hung up after battle. In *Gilgamesh* tablet XI, the mother goddess lifts her lapis lazuli necklace after the flood and swears by it never to forget those days. Genesis has a similar token, but God is the one who promises to look on it and remember (vv. 15–16).

*Gilgamesh* ends its hero’s story outside history. Enlil touches the foreheads of Utnapishtim and his wife, makes them “like us, the gods,” and settles them far away at the Mouth of the Rivers. Noah stays human. He works the ground (v. 20), the soil his father Lamech had called cursed (5:29); he gets drunk, curses, blesses, and dies (v. 29). The Flood’s survivor goes on as a man among his descendants.

breakdown.label: Blessing renewed: meat allowed, blood and murder forbidden
God’s covenant with Noah and every living creature
The bow in the cloud, the covenant’s token
Noah’s three sons people the whole earth
Noah’s vineyard and drunkenness; Ham sees, his brothers cover
Noah curses Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth
Noah dies at 950 years

structure.summary: Parallel panels: the closing steps of Wenham’s Flood palistrophe (6:10–9:19) answer its opening steps in reverse order. Verses 20–29 stand outside it.

right.label: C′
right.text: Those who went out of the ark

secondary.title: Small chiasm in v. 6 (Hebrew word order)

notes: **Sevens:** “covenant” (*berit*) occurs seven times in vv. 9–17 (vv. 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17). Earlier in the Flood story it appears only once, in the promise of 6:18.
God will “remember” the covenant (vv. 15, 16), the verb of 8:1 at the center of the Flood story. The bow reminds God as well as people.
In v. 6 the punishment repeats the crime’s words in reverse. **Canaan** is named five times in vv. 18–27, though he plays no part in the scene.

Noah’s death notice (vv. 28–29) uses the formula of the Genesis 5 genealogy, finishing the entry for Noah left open at 5:32 and closing the *toledot* of Noah that began at 6:9. The next heading, the generations of Noah’s sons, follows at 10:1, and v. 19 (“of them was the whole earth overspread”) previews it.
**Echoes:** Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD shining like “the bow that is in the cloud” (Ezekiel 1:28), and John sees a rainbow around God’s throne (Revelation 4:3).

traditions.text: In the JST the covenant of vv. 9–16 is the one God made with Noah’s great-grandfather Enoch. When God looks on the bow he remembers that promise: when Noah’s posterity “shall embrace the truth, and look upward,” Zion will look downward, the heavens will shake with gladness, and the city of Enoch, taken up to heaven, will come down to possess the earth. Moses 7:62–64 describes the same meeting, with Enoch’s city and the latter-day Zion falling on each other’s necks. The bow becomes a sign of Zion as well as a promise about water.

The JST tightens vv. 4–6. Blood is to be shed only for meat to save life, God will require the blood of every beast at their hands, and each man is commanded to preserve his brother’s life, because man is made in God’s image. Revelations of 1831 and 1833 carry the same limits forward: flesh is ordained for food, but woe to the man who “sheddeth blood or that wasteth flesh and hath no need,” and meat is to be used sparingly.

The Book of Abraham says Noah blessed the first Pharaoh, a descendant of Ham, “with the blessings of the earth” and of wisdom, but cursed him as pertaining to the priesthood. In the 19th and 20th centuries this passage and Genesis 9 were used to explain the Church’s priesthood restriction. The Church now disavows the theories that black skin is a sign of divine disfavor or curse.
traditions.cite: Abraham 1:26–27; Gospel Topics, “Race and the Priesthood” (2013)

traditions.text: Noah and his sons swear never to eat blood, and God makes the covenant in the third month. Jubilees says the Feast of Weeks was ordained to renew this covenant every year; Noah’s sons let it lapse after his death until Abraham restored it. Israel’s covenant at Sinai, made in the same month, renews Noah’s.

Noah plants his vines on Lubar, the mountain where the ark rested, and keeps the wine until a festival on the first day of the first month, when he offers sacrifice and drinks with his sons. After the curse, Ham is angry that his son was cursed and leaves his father with Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan to build a city of his own.

The rabbis taught that the descendants of Noah, meaning all humanity, are bound by seven commandments: to set up courts of justice, and not to blaspheme, worship idols, commit sexual sin, murder, rob, or eat a limb torn from a living animal. One school lists castration and mixing species in place of the first two. The bans on blood and murder in vv. 4–6 overlap this list, which Jews call the Noahide laws.

Asks what Ham actually did. Rav and Shmuel each held that it was more than looking; one said Ham castrated Noah. On that view the curse fits: Noah, unable to father a fourth son, cursed Ham’s fourth son, Canaan (10:6).

Ham came laughing to show his brothers their father’s nakedness. Noah, Josephus says, did not curse Ham himself because he was so near in blood, but cursed his posterity, and God laid the curse on the children of Canaan. Justin Martyr gives a different reason for the same outcome (below).

Verse 27 is unclear about who will “dwell in the tents of Shem.” Onkelos makes it God: his Presence (*Shekhinah*) will dwell there. Pseudo-Jonathan makes it Japheth’s sons, who become proselytes and study in the schools of Shem. Jubilees had already read the line as God dwelling with Shem.
traditions.cite: Targum Onkelos and Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 9:27; Jubilees 7:12

traditions.text: The Jerusalem council asks Gentile converts to abstain from things offered to idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood. Many readers have compared the list with the commandments given to all Noah’s descendants in vv. 4–6, since it binds non-Jews without requiring the whole law of Moses.

The Spirit of prophecy, Justin says, would not curse a son whom God had already blessed (v. 1), so the curse began with Ham’s son. He reads vv. 25–27 as history foretold: Shem’s descendants took Canaan’s land, and Japheth’s descendants, the Romans, later took it from them.

Reads the scene as prophecy of Christ. Shem means “named,” and Christ came from him; Japheth means “enlargement,” the Gentile church dwelling in Shem’s tents. Noah’s nakedness signifies Christ’s passion, which Shem and Japheth, the Jewish and Gentile believers, honor by covering it with their backs to the past; Ham stands for heretics.

10.overview:
The sons of Noah become nations. The list runs through Japheth’s line, the coastland peoples to the north and west; Ham’s, including Egypt, Cush, Canaan, and the Mesopotamian kingdom of Nimrod; and Shem’s, from Elam and Assyria to the Arabian tribes of Joktan. Each section closes with the same formula of families, tongues, lands, and nations. Two short notes break the list: Nimrod, a mighty hunter, rules Babel and builds Nineveh, and Peleg is named because “in his days was the earth divided.”

The chapter speaks of many tongues (vv. 5, 20, 31) before the next chapter tells how one language became many. Genesis gives the result first and the cause second, so the Babel story in 11:1–9 reads as a flashback explaining the map drawn here.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign it to later writers drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Undated. Peleg is born 101 years after the Flood (11:10–16); Ussher puts his birth in 2247 BC. The peoples named appear in records of about 1500–600 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The world known to ancient Israel: Greece, the islands, and Anatolia to the north and west; Egypt, Nubia, and Arabia to the south; Mesopotamia and Iran to the east.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 1:4–23 repeats the list. Abraham 1:21–25 traces Egypt’s settlement to a daughter of Ham.

10.hermeneutics:
Many of these names match peoples in Assyrian and other ancient records. Gomer is the Gimirrai, the Cimmerians; Ashkenaz is the Ishkuza, the Scythians; Madai is the Medes; Javan is the Ionian Greeks; Tubal and Meshech are Tabal and Mushki in central Anatolia, named together in Assyrian annals; Kittim is Kition on Cyprus. Mizraim is Egypt, Cush the Nile kingdom south of it, and Caphtor probably Crete. The chapter is a map of the real world as Israel knew it, set out as a family tree.

Nimrod’s cities are the great names of Mesopotamia: Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), and Accad, the capital of Sargon’s empire; then Nineveh and Calah (Kalhu, modern Nimrud), capitals of Assyria. Assyrian kings boasted of hunting, and the palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Calah was lined with reliefs of the king killing lions from his chariot. “A mighty hunter” was the language of Mesopotamian kingship. Micah 5:6 even calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod.” Nimrod stands for the empire-builder, and his first city is Babel.

The table groups peoples by geography and politics, not by language family. Canaan is a son of Ham, placed beside Egypt, though Canaanite speech was so close to Hebrew that Isaiah calls Hebrew “the language of Canaan” (Isaiah 19:18). Elam, whose language was unrelated to Hebrew, is a son of Shem. The modern labels “Semitic” and “Hamitic” borrowed these names much later, and they do not match how Genesis sorts the nations.

breakdown.label: Heading: the generations of Noah’s sons after the Flood
Japheth: the peoples of the coasts and islands
Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Phut, Canaan, and Cush’s sons
Nimrod the mighty hunter and his kingdom
Mizraim’s sons, with the origin of the Philistines
Canaan’s sons and the borders of Canaan
Shem’s line to Eber and Peleg: the earth divided
Joktan’s thirteen sons and their lands
Closing summary: the nations divided after the Flood

structure.summary: Inclusio: a heading (v. 1) and a closing summary (v. 32) frame three family lists, each ending in the same formula.

open.text: The generations of the sons of Noah, after the flood

close.text: The families of the sons of Noah; the nations divided after the flood

notes: **Seventy names:** Japheth’s line has 14 descendants, Ham’s 30, and Shem’s 26, for 70 in all, counting Nimrod but not the Philistines, who appear in a side note (v. 14). Jewish tradition speaks of 70 nations (see Traditions).
**Formula:** each section ends with families, tongues, lands, and nations (vv. 5, 20, 31), and v. 32 gathers them up. The word “nations” (*goyim*) occurs six times, all in these closing lines.
**Order:** Shem’s line comes last because it is the one the book follows (11:10). The two notes that interrupt the list, Nimrod (vv. 8–12) and Peleg (v. 25), both point ahead to Babel.

A new *toledot* heading, “the generations of the sons of Noah” (v. 1), opens the last subsection of the primeval history, which runs through Babel to the end of Shem’s line (11:26). Chapter 10 fans the family out to the whole world; 11:10 narrows it to Shem’s line and 11:27 to Terah’s.

**Echoes:** God promises Abram that in him “all families of the earth” will be blessed (12:3), using the word for the families of this chapter (vv. 5, 18, 20, 31, 32). Ezekiel’s Gog oracle brings back Magog, Meshech, Tubal, Gomer, and Togarmah as invaders from the north (Ezekiel 38:2–6).

traditions.text: Abraham’s record adds a story behind Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. The land was first discovered by a woman, a daughter of Ham named Egyptus, while it was still under water, and she settled her sons there. Her eldest son, Pharaoh, set up Egypt’s first government after the patriarchal order of Ham, seeking to imitate the order of Adam and Noah. Genesis gives Egypt only a name in a list; Abraham gives it a founding story.

Describing the Second Coming, the Lord says the great deep will be driven back into the north countries, the islands will become one land, and the earth will be as it was “before it was divided.” Latter-day Saints have often read this with v. 25, taking the division in Peleg’s days as a division of the land itself. Jubilees and Josephus read the same verse as a division among peoples (below).

When the Jaredites leave the tower, they gather in a valley to the north called Nimrod, “being called after the mighty hunter.” The Book of Mormon assumes the Nimrod of v. 9 as a known figure and places his name on the land near Babel.

Peleg is named because in his days Noah’s children began to divide the earth. Noah draws lots, and his sons take the written portions out of his bosom: Shem receives the middle of the earth, with Eden, Sinai, and Zion; Ham the hot south; Japheth the cold north. The chapter’s geography becomes a deed of inheritance.

After Babel, Canaan sees that the land from Lebanon to the river of Egypt is good and refuses to go to his own lot by the western sea. His father and brothers warn him that he is settling in Shem’s portion and will be cursed for it, but he stays. That, says Jubilees, is why the land is called Canaan, and why Israel’s later claim to it is just.

Matches the names to the peoples of his day: Gomer to the Galatians, Magog to the Scythians, Madai to the Medes, Javan to the Ionians and all Greeks, Meshech to the Cappadocians, Tiras to the Thracians, and Kittim to Cyprus, with its city Citium. He complains that the Greeks renamed the nations so the names would sound Greek. From Eber, he says, the Hebrews take their name, and Peleg was so called because he was born when the nations dispersed to their lands, Peleg meaning “division.”

Deuteronomy 32:8 says God set the bounds of the peoples by the number of the children of Israel. The Targum explains: God cast lots among seventy angels, princes of the nations, and fixed the borders by the seventy souls of Israel who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27). The Talmud says the seventy bulls offered at the Feast of Tabernacles atoned for the seventy nations.

The number seventy became shorthand for all humanity. Rabbi Yohanan taught that at Sinai each word from God’s mouth divided into seventy languages, one for each nation of the table. The same count of seventy nations stands behind the Targum and the Sukkot offerings above.

Both read “mighty hunter before the LORD” (v. 9) as rebellion. The Targum renders it as a mighty rebel before the Lord, adding that no one like Nimrod had lived since the world was created. Rashi says he hunted people’s minds with words, luring them to revolt against God, and that “before the LORD” means to God’s face, on purpose. Josephus likewise makes Nimrod the instigator of Babel (see ch. 11).
traditions.cite: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 10:9; Rashi on Genesis 10:9

traditions.text: Paul tells the Athenians that God made all nations “of one blood” and fixed the times and bounds of their dwelling. Genesis 10 traces every nation to one family, and Paul uses that to argue that God is near to all of them, so that they should seek him. His talk of the bounds of their habitation echoes Deuteronomy 32:8, where God set the bounds of the peoples when he divided the nations.

Counting from his Latin Bible, which follows the Greek text, Augustine finds 73 descendants: 15 from Japheth, 31 from Ham, 27 from Shem; elsewhere he speaks of 72 nations and languages. He reads Nimrod as “a giant hunter against the Lord,” noting that the Greek word can mean either before or against, and takes hunter to mean deceiver and oppressor.

11.overview:
The whole earth speaks one language. Settling on a plain in Shinar, people bake bricks and set out to build a city and a tower with its top in heaven, to make a name for themselves and not be scattered. The LORD comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them, and the city is called Babel. The chapter then traces Shem’s line to Terah, father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran dies in Ur, Abram marries Sarai, who is barren, and Terah sets out for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.

The builders want to “make us a name” (v. 4). In the next chapter God tells Abram, “I will … make thy name great” (12:2). The chapter moves from a name people try to seize to a name God gives, and from the whole earth to one childless couple (v. 30).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign it to later writers drawing on older material.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: The Book of Abraham (published 1842) gives Abraham’s own account of Ur, the famine, and the stop at Haran (Abraham 1–2). The Book of Mormon’s Jaredites leave from “the great tower” (Ether 1:33).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Babel is undated. By the Hebrew text’s ages Abram is born 292 years after the Flood (vv. 10–26); tradition places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Shinar is southern Mesopotamia (Babylonia). Ur of the Chaldees is usually identified with Ur in southern Iraq; Haran lies on the Balikh River in today’s southeastern Turkey.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 1:24–27 (Shem to Abram); Abraham 1–2; Ether 1:33–43.

11.hermeneutics:
Southern Mesopotamia had almost no building stone. People built with sun-dried mud brick and, for lasting works, with kiln-fired brick laid in bitumen, which seeps from the ground in the region. Verse 3 explains this to hearers who lived in stony Canaan: “they had brick for stone, and slime for mortar.” Nebuchadnezzar records that his father raised the walls of Babylon’s great temple tower with “bitumen and baked brick,” the materials of v. 3.

That tower was Etemenanki, “House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth,” a stepped temple platform called a ziggurat. Its builders used the language of v. 4 about it. Nabopolassar wrote that Marduk ordered him to set its foundation on the underworld and make its summit rival the heavens, and his son Nebuchadnezzar claimed to have finished the job. Genesis takes the boast at face value and answers it: the tower meant to reach heaven is so small that the LORD has to “come down” to see it (v. 5).

Babylonians explained their city’s name, *Bab-ili*, as “gate of the god.” In the creation epic *Enuma Elish* the gods themselves mold bricks to build Esagila, Marduk’s temple in Babylon, as a home for the gods. Genesis answers with a Hebrew pun: the city is called Babel because there the LORD “confounded” (*balal*) the language of all the earth (v. 9). The city that called itself the gods’ gateway is named for confusion.

Peleg to Terah: lifespans fall; Abram, Nahor, Haran born

Terah leaves Ur for Canaan but stops and dies in Haran
Abram leaves Haran for Canaan at the LORD’s call

rows.label: G

notes: **Sound play:** “let us make brick” (*nilbenah*, v. 3) and “let us confound” (*navlah*, v. 7) share their letters with *l* and *b* swapped, so God’s plan undoes theirs in their own sounds. Verse 9 adds Babel and *balal*, “confound.”
**Repetition:** “all the earth” (*kol ha’arets*) occurs five times in vv. 1–9 (vv. 1, 4, 8, 9 twice), and “language” (*safah*, literally “lip”) five times (vv. 1, 6, 7 twice, 9).

**Genealogy:** Shem’s line has ten names from Shem to Abram, as Genesis 5 has ten from Adam to Noah, and both end with a father of three sons (5:32; v. 26). This list never totals a life or says “and he died.”

Babel is the last story of the primeval history, and Shem’s *toledot* (v. 10) narrows the seventy names of chapter 10 to one line. A new heading, “the generations of Terah” (v. 27), opens the Abraham cycle, which runs to Abraham’s death (25:11). The chapter straddles the book’s first great seam.

**Echoes:** At Pentecost the crowd is “confounded” because each hears the apostles in his own language (Acts 2:6). Zephaniah promises that God will “turn to the people a pure language” so all can call on the LORD (Zephaniah 3:9).

traditions.text: Jared and his brother leave “the great tower” when the Lord confounds the language. At the brother of Jared’s prayer, their language and their friends’ is not confounded, and the Lord sends them out with flocks “male and female, of every kind” and seed of every kind, like a new ark. The Book of Mormon never uses the name Babel; Omni and Mosiah also date the Jaredite record from the tower.

Mormon names the motive Genesis leaves unspoken. The same being who gave the Gadianton robbers their secret plans put it into the people’s hearts “to build a tower sufficiently high that they might get to heaven,” and he led on those who came from the tower into this land, spreading the works of darkness until they were destroyed. The Jaredites’ end is traced back to Babel.

Abraham’s own account fills in vv. 27–32. His fathers had turned to idols, and he was nearly sacrificed on an altar in Ur. A famine follows, in which his brother Haran dies; Genesis says only that Haran died before Terah in Ur. Terah repents and follows Abraham to Haran, then returns to his idols, which is why he stays there.

The tower took 43 years to build and rose 5,433 cubits and two palms, of brick and asphalt from the springs of Shinar. The Lord and his angels go down to see it, and afterward the Lord sends a great wind that throws it to the ground; its ruin is called “Overthrow.” Peleg’s son Reu is named for the evil of the builders.

God had told Noah’s descendants to spread out and found colonies, and they refused. Nimrod, grandson of Ham, talked them into crediting their own strength, ruled as a tyrant, and vowed to build a tower too high for any flood, as revenge on God. Josephus also quotes the Sibyl: the gods sent winds that overthrew the tower, as in Jubilees.

Rabbi Jeremiah bar Eleazar said the builders split into three parties: one wanted to live at the top, one to worship idols there, and one to make war on heaven, and each was punished in kind. The Targum likewise puts an idol on the summit with a sword in its hand. Both read v. 4 as rebellion, not mere ambition.

Having no stone, the builders burned bricks and raised the tower seven miles high, with a ramp up the east side and down the west. If a man fell and died, no one cared; if a brick fell, they sat down and wept, asking when another would come up. The brick of v. 3 has become worth more than a person.

Terah sold idols, and young Abram smashed them, leaving the club in the hand of the largest. Terah handed him to Nimrod, who threw him into a furnace; Abram came out alive. Haran, who had waited to see who would win, then sided with Abram, was thrown in, and died “before his father” (v. 28). Rashi notes that “Ur” can mean fire; Abraham 1 likewise has Abraham rescued from death in Ur at the hands of idolaters.

Counts ten generations from Adam to Noah and ten from Noah to Abraham, to show God’s patience: each set kept provoking him until the Flood, and the second until Abraham came and received the reward of them all. Josephus also calls Abraham the tenth from Noah.

Stephen says God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran, and that he left Haran after his father died. By the ages in Genesis, Terah was 70 at Abram’s birth (v. 26) and Abram 75 when he left (12:4), so Terah would have lived 60 more years in Haran (v. 32). Ussher resolved the tension by making Abram a later son, born when Terah was 130.

Luke’s genealogy of Jesus runs back through this list but adds a Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah. The addition comes from the Greek Septuagint, whose Genesis 11 has Arphaxad beget Cainan, and Cainan beget Salah. Luke’s Bible was the Greek one.

Preaching on Pentecost, he calls the confusion at Babel praiseworthy: the builders were united in wickedness, and confusing their speech broke up their purpose. The tongues of Pentecost are more praiseworthy still, because they come from one Spirit and bring many people back into harmony. Babel divides a bad unity; Pentecost creates a good one.

A Greek writer on Babylon, quoted by Eusebius. The first men, proud of their strength and size, built a huge tower where Babylon now stands, already close to heaven, until the winds came to help the gods and threw it down on the builders. The ruins were called Babylon, and from then on people spoke many languages. Alexander Polyhistor cites a similar Sibylline account.

12.overview:
The Lord tells Abram to leave his country, his kin, and his father’s house for a land he will be shown, and promises to make him a great nation, make his name great, and bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram, seventy-five, sets out from Haran with Sarai, Lot, and their household. At Shechem the Lord promises the land to his seed, and Abram builds altars there and near Bethel. Then famine drives him down to Egypt, where he has Sarai say she is his sister. Pharaoh takes her into his house, the Lord strikes Pharaoh’s house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends Abram away.

The promise is barely spoken before it is put at risk. The land cannot feed Abram, and the wife through whom the promised seed must come ends up in Pharaoh’s house. Abram does nothing to get her back. The Lord does.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined and dated much later.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Abraham 2, a first-person parallel to vv. 1–13, was published by Joseph Smith in the Times and Seasons in March 1842.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional dating puts Abraham c. 2000–1800 BC; Ussher has Abram leave Haran in 1921 BC. Genesis gives his age as 75 (v. 4); Abraham 2:14 gives 62.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Haran in upper Mesopotamia; Shechem, Bethel, and Ai in the central hills of Canaan; the Negev (“the south”); Egypt.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Abraham 2:1–25. The wife-sister story recurs in Genesis 20 (Abraham and Abimelech) and 26 (Isaac and Rebekah).

12.hermeneutics:
Going down to Egypt in a famine was ordinary. Egypt watered its fields from the Nile flood, so when the rains failed in Canaan, herders went south. A tomb painting at Beni Hasan (c. 1900 BC) shows a chief named Abisha leading a party of 37 Asiatics into Egypt, and a frontier report from the late 13th century BC (Papyrus Anastasi VI) records officials letting herders from Edom past a border fort to the pools of Pithom to keep them and their flocks alive. Abram’s trip in v. 10 follows a well-worn road, the same one Jacob’s family will take for the same reason (Genesis 42–46).

Egyptian stories assume that a beautiful woman could be taken for Pharaoh and that her husband stood in the way. In the *Tale of Two Brothers*, copied around 1200 BC, Pharaoh has the wife of Bata brought to live in the palace, and she then has the tree that holds her husband’s heart cut down, so that he dies. Abram’s fear in v. 12 is that plot told from the husband’s side. Genesis turns it around: the Egyptian king is the one wronged, and he asks the moral question, “What is this that thou hast done unto me?” (v. 18).

Pharaohs did gather foreign women into their households. The Amarna letters (14th century BC) show Amenhotep III taking princesses from Mitanni and Babylon, with gold sent to the bride’s family, while he refused to give any Egyptian princess abroad. Read against that practice, the flocks, servants, and camels of v. 16 look like gifts to the bride’s brother, which is what Pharaoh thought Abram was (v. 19).

Abram, seventy-five, leaves Haran with Sarai and Lot
At Shechem the land is promised; the first altar
An altar between Bethel and Ai; moving south
