Sarai taken into Pharaoh’s house; Abram enriched
Plagues; Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends him away

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Famine and Egypt; the promise endangered

notes: **Go, and go:** The chapter opens with the Lord’s “Get thee out” (*lekh lekha*, v. 1) and nearly closes with Pharaoh’s “go thy way” (v. 19). Both use the same Hebrew imperative. The first sends Abram into the promise; the second sends him back to it.
**Bless:** Verses 2–3 use the root “bless” five times (four verbs and one noun).
**Woman or sister:** In vv. 10–20 the word *ishah* (“woman” or “wife”) appears ten times, while “sister” appears only twice, in Abram’s request and in Pharaoh’s complaint about it (vv. 13, 19).

The Abraham story begins at 11:27 with the heading “these are the generations of Terah” (*toledot*), so chapter 12 opens a unit already under way: Terah’s family has left Ur and stopped in Haran (11:31). Chapters 12–14 follow Abram’s moves through the land until chapter 15 turns from journeys to covenant.
**Links:** The builders at Babel wanted to “make us a name” (11:4); here the Lord promises to make Abram’s name great (v. 2). The wife-sister story returns in Genesis 20 and 26.

traditions.text: The Book of Abraham tells the call in the first person and adds what Genesis leaves out. Famine in Ur kills Abram’s brother Haran, Terah follows Abram to Haran and turns back to idolatry there, and Abram is sixty-two, not seventy-five, when he leaves. The promise of v. 3 is expanded: through Abram’s priesthood and literal seed all families of the earth will be blessed “with the blessings of the Gospel.”

In Genesis, Abram himself proposes that Sarai call herself his sister (vv. 11–13). In the Book of Abraham the Lord gives the instruction as Abram nears Egypt, and Abram passes it on to Sarai in nearly the words of Genesis 12:13. Genesis 20:12 adds that Sarai was Abraham’s half-sister, the detail later readers used most often to explain the episode.

Nephi and the risen Jesus both quote the promise of v. 3 as a covenant still in force: “in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” Jesus tells the Nephites it is fulfilled as the Holy Ghost is poured out on the Gentiles through him. In D&C 124:58 the Lord repeats the same promise to Joseph Smith and his seed.

An Aramaic retelling of Genesis found in Qumran Cave 1. As Abram enters Egypt he dreams of a cedar and a date palm growing from one root; when the cedar is about to be cut down, the palm saves it by crying that the two share a single root. Abram reads the dream as Pharaoh’s plan to kill him and spare Sarai, so the sister plan comes from a dream, where Abraham 2:22–25 has it come from the Lord. The scroll adds a poem on Sarai’s beauty, a spirit sent to afflict Pharaoh’s house for two years, and Abram healing Pharaoh by prayer and by laying his hands on his head.

Before the call comes, Abram prays at night to be kept from the evil spirits that rule men’s hearts. After the call the angel opens Abram’s mouth to speak Hebrew, “the tongue of the creation,” unused since Babel. Jubilees says Abram lived in Egypt five years before Sarai was seized, and it never mentions the sister plan.

Josephus makes Abram a philosopher who argued from the irregular motions of the heavens that there is one God, and who left Chaldea when the people rose against him. He goes to Egypt partly to hear what the priests teach about the gods, ready to follow them or correct them. Pharaoh learns from his priests that the plague is God’s anger, and afterward Abram teaches the Egyptians arithmetic and astronomy, which pass from them to the Greeks.

Philo reads the call as the soul’s journey: “country” is the body, “kindred” the senses, and “father’s house” speech, three dwellings the mind must leave to be purified. In *On Abraham* he tells the Egypt episode literally: Sarah and her husband, with no other help, take refuge in God, who strikes the king and his whole household for consenting to the wrong.
traditions.cite: On the Migration of Abraham 2–3; On Abraham 92–98

traditions.text: Explains the call with a parable: a traveler sees a great building lit up and asks whether it can have no owner, and the owner looks out and says, I am the owner. Abraham asked the same of the world, and God answered by speaking to him. Another passage fills a gap in v. 14: Abram hid Sarai in a chest at the Egyptian border, the customs officers made him open it, and all Egypt shone with her beauty.

Reads *lekh lekha* as “go for yourself,” that is, for your own good: in Haran Abram would have no children, in the land he would. Since travel costs a man his family, his wealth, and his name, the three blessings of v. 2 answer those three losses.

Stephen says God first appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia “before he dwelt in Charran,” and moved him on to Canaan after his father died. Genesis records the call after Haran, while Abraham 2:3 and 2:6 have the Lord speak in both places. Hebrews makes the departure a model of faith, since Abraham went out not knowing where he was going.

Defends Abram against the Manichaeans: he called Sarai his sister “and told no lie,” since she was a close relative, just as Lot is called his brother. He kept silent about the marriage and left her protection to God, because taking no precaution at all would have been tempting God rather than trusting him. Augustine insists that the plagues kept Pharaoh from touching her.

A Greek historian at Herod’s court, quoted by Josephus. He says Abram came with an army from the land of the Chaldeans, ruled at Damascus, and later moved with his people to Canaan, and that a village near Damascus was still called “the Habitation of Abram.” Genesis says nothing of this, though Damascus appears in 14:15 and 15:2.

13.overview:
Abram comes back from Egypt rich and returns to his altar between Bethel and Ai. He and Lot now own more flocks than the land can support, and their herdsmen quarrel. Abram gives Lot first choice. Lot looks out over the Jordan plain, watered “as the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt,” and settles near Sodom, whose men are “wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly.” Then the Lord tells Abram to look in every direction: all the land he sees will belong to him and his seed, who will be as countless as the dust. Abram moves to Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.

Watch the eyes. Lot lifts up his eyes and picks what looks best (v. 10). Abram does not choose at all. Only after Lot has gone does the Lord tell him to lift up his eyes (v. 14), and what he sees is given to him.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined and dated much later.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Right after the return from Egypt (v. 1). Traditional dating puts Abraham c. 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The hill country between Bethel and Ai; the plain of the Jordan toward Sodom and Zoar near the Dead Sea; Mamre at Hebron.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jubilees 13:16–21; Genesis Apocryphon 20:33–21:22; Josephus, Antiquities 1.8.3. The Book of Abraham ends before this chapter (Abraham 2:25 reaches Genesis 12:13).

13.hermeneutics:
Large herding households lived alongside farming towns, and the two had to share the land. Letters from Mari on the middle Euphrates (18th century BC) describe tribal herders whose villages lay in the river valley while their flocks used the open steppe, and pastoral groups who camped around the walls of fortified towns. The archive records their dealings with kings and townsmen. Verse 7 says the same thing in one line: the quarrel breaks out while “the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.” Abram and Lot were not alone on empty hills. Two large camps crowding pasture already in use by others had to separate.

The same Mari letters name the two great tribal groups of the region “sons of the left” and “sons of the right,” probably meaning north and south: a person facing east, toward the sunrise, has north on the left hand and south on the right. Abram’s offer in v. 9 uses that compass. Left or right means north or south along the ridge of the hill country. Lot takes neither. He looks east, down to the Jordan plain, and “journeyed east” (v. 11), and v. 12 sets the two men apart: Abram “dwelled in the land of Canaan,” Lot in “the cities of the plain.”

Abram offers Lot his choice of the land
Lot chooses the well-watered plain toward Sodom
The Lord gives Abram all the land he can see
Abram settles at Mamre in Hebron; an altar

close.text: At Mamre, Abram builds an altar to the LORD

rows.text: Lot lifts up his eyes and chooses

rows.label: D

notes: **One verb, three times:** *nasa* means to bear or to lift. The land could not “bear” Abram and Lot (v. 6); Lot “lifted up his eyes” (v. 10); the Lord tells Abram to “lift up” his (v. 14).
**Separate:** The verb “separate” appears three times (vv. 9, 11, 14). Abram proposes it, Lot carries it out, and the Lord speaks to Abram only “after that Lot was separated from him.”
**Land:** The Hebrew *erets* (“land,” “earth”) appears nine times in eighteen verses, and in v. 16 twice in the image of “the dust of the earth.”

Chapter 13 closes the round trip that began with the famine in 12:10. Abram returns to the very spot of 12:8, the altar he had made “at the first” (v. 4). Lot’s choice sets up the next chapter, where he is captured as a man who “dwelt in Sodom” (14:12).

**Links:** The promise of seed “as the dust of the earth” (v. 16) is later joined by the stars (15:5) and the sand of the seashore (22:17). The note that the plain was well watered “before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah” (v. 10) points ahead to Genesis 19.

traditions.text: Genesis promises the land to Abram’s seed “for ever” (v. 15). The Book of Abraham, in the Lord’s word to Abram in Haran, gives the land “for an everlasting possession, when they hearken to my voice.” The added clause makes keeping the land depend on obedience.

Genesis compares Abram’s seed to dust (v. 16). In Abraham 3:14 the Lord, speaking at night among the stars, compares it to the sand. D&C 132:30 joins the images and extends the promise beyond this life: Abraham’s seed will continue “both in the world and out of the world,” as innumerable as the stars or the sand on the seashore.

The Qumran retelling adds that Lot took a wife from the daughters of Egypt before leaving, which supplies an origin for the unnamed wife of Genesis 19. Lot parts from Abram because of their shepherds’ conduct, buys a house in Sodom, and Abram says the parting grieved him. The scroll then has Abram actually walk the land as the Lord commands in v. 17, from the Gihon river to the Euphrates and back to Mamre.

Jubilees gives the reason for Abram’s grief at the parting: “for he had no children.” Lot was the nearest thing he had to an heir. Its version of the promise blends the dust of v. 16 with the sand of the sea from later chapters, and it dates the promise to the year Lot was taken captive.

Josephus says Abram let Lot choose and took for himself what Lot left, “the lower grounds at the foot of the mountains,” and settled at Hebron. He adds that Hebron was seven years older than Tanis in Egypt, the same note found in Numbers 13:22, and that Sodom was then a fine city.

Philo makes the parting a lesson in peacemaking. Lot is “an inconstant, variable, whimsical man,” and his shepherds, far from their master, kept picking fights. Abraham’s household was larger and could have won, but he stopped the quarrel rather than grieve his nephew with a defeat.

Explains the quarrel of v. 7. Abram’s animals went out muzzled so they would not graze other people’s fields, while Lot’s did not. Lot’s herdsmen argued that the land was promised to Abram, who had no son, so Lot would inherit it anyway. The verse answers them: the Canaanite and the Perizzite were still in the land, and the promise was not yet due.

Following the midrash, Rashi reads Lot’s choice against him. He chose the plain because its people were given to sexual immorality, and the words “journeyed east” (*miqqedem*) are played on as leaving “the One who was before” the world, as if Lot said he wanted neither Abram nor his God. Second Peter, by contrast, calls Lot “just” and “righteous,” vexed by what he saw in Sodom.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 13:10–11; Genesis Rabbah 41:7; 2 Peter 2:7–8

traditions.text: This Aramaic paraphrase spells out what Genesis leaves general. The men of Sodom were “depraved in their wealth,” sinned in their bodies, shed innocent blood, and practiced strange worship. On v. 7 it says Abram had told his shepherds to keep the flocks off the fields of the Canaanites and Perizzites, while Lot’s shepherds grazed there, the same explanation Genesis Rabbah gives.

Hebrews remembers Abraham as a man who lived in tents “in the land of promise, as in a strange country,” with Isaac and Jacob, heirs of the same promise. It explains the patience: he was looking for a city with foundations, whose builder and maker is God. Like Irenaeus after it, Hebrews reads the land promise of vv. 14–17 as pointing past Canaan.

Quotes vv. 14–17 and notes that Abraham never received the land, not even a foot of it (Acts 7:5), and lived there as a stranger. Since God is faithful, Irenaeus concludes, Abraham and his seed, the believers, will receive it at the resurrection of the just. JST Genesis 15:9–12 makes a similar point in the Lord’s answer to Abram: though he dies, he will still receive the land.

Says Abram and Lot parted “without breach of charity,” to keep their households from strife. He suggests that a custom of fair division comes from this scene: the greater divides, and the lesser chooses. He reads the dust of v. 16 as hyperbole and asks whether the seed means Israel alone or all who share Abraham’s faith.

14.overview:
Four kings from the east, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, crush a revolt by five cities of the Dead Sea plain, among them Sodom and Gomorrah, and carry off their goods and people, Lot included. Abram “the Hebrew” arms 318 men born in his household, pursues the raiders north to Dan, strikes them at night, chases them past Damascus, and brings everything back. Two kings meet him on his return. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of “the most high God,” brings bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth of all. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, and Abram refuses to take even a thread or a shoelatchet.

Abram answers the two kings in opposite ways. From one he accepts a blessing and to him he gives a tithe. From the other he will take nothing, so that Sodom can never say it made Abram rich.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see an older, separate source behind this chapter’s war report.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith’s revision of the Bible (JST, 1830–1833) adds a long passage on Melchizedek (JST Genesis 14:25–40).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional dating c. 2000–1800 BC. None of the four eastern kings has been securely identified in outside records.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. Older place names carry glosses: “Bela, which is Zoar” (v. 2), “En-mishpat, which is Kadesh” (v. 7).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: A campaign down the east side of the Jordan to El-paran and Kadesh; battle in the vale of Siddim at the Dead Sea; pursuit north to Dan and Hobah near Damascus; the valley of Shaveh, “the king’s dale” (v. 17).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: JST Genesis 14:25–40; Alma 13:14–19; D&C 84:14; 107:2–4; Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:1–10; Jubilees 13:22–29; Josephus, Antiquities 1.9–1.10.2.

14.hermeneutics:
Kings in Abram’s world ruled in blocs. A letter in the Mari archive (18th century BC) reports that no king is strong on his own: ten or fifteen kings follow Hammurabi of Babylon, and other great kings each have a following of their own. Lesser kings paid tribute to an overlord, and stopping payment meant revolt. Verse 4 describes that system exactly: the five cities “served” Chedorlaomer twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth, and the march of the fourteenth year (vv. 5–7) is how overlords answered. The names fit such a world. Chedorlaomer has the shape of Elamite royal names beginning *Kudur-*, and Tidal resembles the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya, though none of the four kings has been found in outside records.

Melchizedek blesses Abram by “the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth” (v. 19). Phoenician inscriptions use a close title for the high god. The Karatepe inscription (8th century BC) calls on “El, creator of the earth,” and a later Punic inscription from Leptis Magna repeats the phrase. *El* was the name of the high god across Canaan, so Melchizedek speaks the region’s religious language. In v. 22 Abram takes up the same title but puts “the LORD” in front of it: “the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth.” The God by whom Melchizedek blessed him, Abram says, is the LORD he worships.

breakdown.label: Four eastern kings; five vassal cities rebel
The eastern kings’ campaign through Transjordan and the south
Battle in the vale of Siddim; Lot taken captive
Abram pursues to Dan, routs the kings, rescues Lot
Melchizedek brings bread and wine, blesses Abram; the tithe
Abram refuses the king of Sodom’s goods

structure.summary: An inclusio in vv. 17–24: the king of Sodom frames Melchizedek. The battle report before it (vv. 1–16) moves in sequence.

open.text: The king of Sodom goes out to meet Abram

close.text: The king of Sodom speaks; Abram refuses his goods

rows.label: B
rows.text: He blesses Abram and the most high God

rows.label: C
rows.text: Abram gives him a tenth of all

notes: **The interruption:** The king of Sodom comes out to meet Abram in v. 17 but does not speak until v. 21. Melchizedek fills the gap, so Abram has received the priest-king’s blessing before he answers Sodom.
**Most High:** *El Elyon* (“the most high God”) appears four times (vv. 18, 19, 20, 22), and “possessor of heaven and earth” twice (vv. 19, 22). Abram’s oath repeats Melchizedek’s words.
**Goods and taking:** “Goods” (*rekhush*) appears five times (vv. 11, 12, 16 twice, 21), and so does “take” (vv. 11, 12, 21, 23, 24). The kings take, Abram brings back, and then he refuses to take.

Chapter 14 ends the subsection on Abram’s journeys (11:27–14:24). It reads differently from its neighbors: a war report with lists of kings and glossed place names, and the only scene where Abram leads men in battle. The next words, “After these things” (15:1), turn from battle to vision.

**Links:** Lot’s capture as one who “dwelt in Sodom” (v. 12) follows from his choice in 13:12. Elsewhere in the Bible Melchizedek appears only in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5–7, which build a priesthood “after the order of Melchizedek” on these verses.

traditions.text: Joseph Smith’s revision adds sixteen verses about Melchizedek at the end of the chapter. As a child Melchizedek feared God, shut the mouths of lions, and quenched fire; he was ordained a high priest after “the order of the covenant which God made with Enoch,” and his people sought the city of Enoch that God had taken up. He is called the Prince of peace and the keeper of God’s storehouse, and Abram pays his tithe into that storehouse for the poor.

Alma holds up Melchizedek as king of a Salem whose people “had waxed strong in iniquity and abomination” until he preached repentance and they repented. He established peace, so he was called the prince of peace, and he reigned under his father. Alma says the priesthood’s ordinances pointed the people forward to the Son of God, and that none before or after Melchizedek were greater. The picture of a wicked city turned to peace matches the JST account.

Genesis records only a blessing and a tithe. D&C 84:14 makes Melchizedek the one from whom Abraham received the priesthood, and traces Melchizedek’s own priesthood through his fathers back to Noah. D&C 107 explains that the higher priesthood was first called the Holy Priesthood after the Order of the Son of God and took Melchizedek’s name “because Melchizedek was such a great high priest.”

After reading Hebrews 7, he said that “Salem” should be “Shiloam,” a term meaning righteousness and peace. In Willard Richards’s notes, Melchizedek is a king and priest to the most high God who held keys of power and blessings and administered endless lives to the sons and daughters of Adam.
traditions.cite: Discourse, 27 August 1843, as reported by Willard Richards, Joseph Smith Papers, pp. [70]–[72]

traditions.text: Abram falls on the enemy the fifth night, near Dan, while some are asleep and others too drunk to fight. Josephus explains the name Melchizedek as “The righteous King,” says he was made priest because he was righteous, and identifies Salem with Jerusalem. Melchizedek feeds the whole army, and he accepts Abram’s tenth.

Philo reads Melchizedek as the kingly mind, “king of peace” as opposed to the tyrant mind that makes war. His bread and wine are food for the soul, and he is priest because right reason has the true God for its inheritance. In *On Abraham* he calls him “the great high priest of the most high God” and has him offer sacrifices of thanksgiving for the victory.

Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names Melchizedek as “Shem bar Noah,” the king of Jerusalem. The Talmud adds that God meant Melchizedek’s own children to be priests, but because he blessed Abram before he blessed God (vv. 19–20), God gave the priesthood to Abraham’s descendants instead, and it reads Psalm 110:4 that way. D&C 84:14 also has the priesthood pass from Melchizedek to Abraham, with no hint of a penalty.
traditions.cite: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 14:18; Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 32b

traditions.text: The same passage asks about the 318 men of v. 14. One rabbi says Eliezer alone was worth all of them; others note that the letters of Eliezer’s name add up to 318. Two sages fault Abram: one for taking Torah students to war, another for giving the captives back to Sodom, when keeping them could have brought them to God.

A Dead Sea Scroll that turns Melchizedek into a heavenly figure. At the end of the tenth jubilee, on a Day of Atonement, he proclaims release to captives, judges the holy ones of God, and rescues his people from Belial. The scroll applies Psalm 82:1 (“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty”) to him. Like Alma 13 and Hebrews 7, it treats the Melchizedek of these three verses as far greater than a local king.

Hebrews builds an argument from what Genesis leaves out. Melchizedek has no recorded father, mother, or genealogy, so he is “made like unto the Son of God.” Since the lesser is blessed by the greater, and Levi paid tithes through Abraham while still in his loins, Melchizedek’s priesthood outranks the Levitical one.

In his dialogue with a Jewish teacher, Justin points out that Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, was uncircumcised, yet Abraham, the first to be circumcised, gave him tithes and received his blessing. For Justin this shows that circumcision was never the measure of righteousness.

Cyprian sees the Lord’s Supper prefigured: Melchizedek offered bread and wine, and Christ, a priest after his order, offered “that very same thing.” Augustine says that in this scene the Christian sacrifice first appeared.
traditions.cite: Cyprian, Epistle 62.4; Augustine, City of God 16.22

15.overview:
After the war, the word of the LORD comes to Abram in a vision: “Fear not.” Abram answers that he is childless and his servant Eliezer will inherit. The Lord promises a son from his own body, shows him the stars, and says his seed will be like them. Abram believes, and the Lord counts it to him for righteousness. When Abram asks how he can know he will inherit the land, the Lord has him cut a heifer, a goat, and a ram in half. At sunset a deep sleep and great darkness fall on him, and he hears that his descendants will serve in a foreign land for four hundred years. After dark a smoking furnace and a burning lamp pass between the pieces, and the Lord covenants to give the land from Egypt to the Euphrates.

Only the fire passes between the pieces. Abram prepares the animals and watches; God alone walks the path of the oath.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined and dated much later.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith’s revision of the Bible (JST, 1830–1833) expands the vision (JST Genesis 15:9–12): Abram learns he will receive the land even after death and sees the days of the Son of Man.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Not dated; after the war of ch. 14 and before Hagar’s marriage to Abram ten years after he entered Canaan (16:3). Traditional dating c. 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Not named in the chapter. Abram’s home was then at Mamre near Hebron (14:13), where Jubilees places the sacrifice.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: JST Genesis 15:9–12; Jubilees 14:1–20; Josephus, Antiquities 1.10.3. Verse 6 is quoted in Romans 4:3, Galatians 3:6, and James 2:23.

15.hermeneutics:
“Fear not” was how a god’s word to a king began. Oracles delivered to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (7th century BC) open with “Fear not!” and continue, “I am Ishtar of Arbela,” followed by promises to cast down his enemies. Verse 1 has the same shape: a command not to fear, a divine “I,” and a promise of protection, “I am thy shield.” Abram has just defeated four kings, and the Lord speaks to him the way gods spoke to kings. Abram’s reply turns from enemies to what no victory has given him, an heir.

Hebrew speaks of “cutting” a covenant, and ancient treaty texts show why. A letter from Mari (18th century BC) reports an official going to “kill a donkey” to seal peace between two groups. The Aramaic treaty of Sefire (8th century BC) cuts up a calf and declares that the vassal who breaks the treaty will be cut up the same way. The slaughtered animal shows what will happen to the one who breaks the oath. Jeremiah 34:18–19 describes Judah’s leaders passing “between the parts of the calf” in just this way, and then breaking their word.

In Genesis 15 Abram cuts the animals, but he does not walk between them. Only the smoking furnace and the burning lamp, signs of God’s presence like the smoke and fire on Sinai (Exodus 19:18), pass through (v. 17). The party who takes the oath, and with it the curse, is God.

breakdown.label: “Fear not”: the Lord as shield and reward
Abram objects: no child, and a servant as heir
A son of his own, seed like the stars; Abram believes
The land promised; “whereby shall I know?”
Animals cut in two; Abram drives away the birds
Deep sleep: bondage, judgment, return in the fourth generation
Fire passes between the pieces; the land covenant

structure.summary: Parallel panels (A B C D / A′ B′ C′ D′): a scene about the heir and a scene about the land, built the same way.

right.label: A′
right.text: God speaks: “I am the LORD that brought thee out”

left.label: B
left.text: “Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me?”

right.label: C′
right.text: Sign: the cut animals and the fire

right.label: D′
right.text: The Lord cuts a covenant for the land

notes: Each panel opens with God saying “I am” (vv. 1, 7), and Abram answers both with the rare address “Lord GOD” (*Adonai Yahweh*, vv. 2, 8). The first panel settles the heir, the second the land.
**Inherit:** The root *yarash* (“be heir,” “inherit”) appears five times (vv. 3, 4 twice, 7, 8), and “seed” four times (vv. 3, 5, 13, 18).

**Bring out:** One verb runs through the chapter four times: the heir will “come forth” from Abram’s body (v. 4), God “brought him forth” to see the stars (v. 5) and “brought thee out” of Ur (v. 7), and Abram’s seed will “come out” of bondage (v. 14).

“After these things” (v. 1) turns the story from journeys to covenant. The subsection (15:1–17:27) runs from this covenant for the land through Hagar and Ishmael (ch. 16) to the covenant of circumcision and the promise of a son by Sarah (ch. 17).
**Links:** The four hundred years of v. 13 are counted again at the Exodus, where Exodus 12:40–41 gives 430 years, and Galatians 3:17 counts 430 years from the promise to the law.

traditions.text: Joseph Smith’s revision has Abram ask how he can receive the land as an everlasting inheritance, and the Lord answers that even if Abram dies he will still possess it, because the Son of Man lives and must first be quickened. Abram then sees “the days of the Son of Man,” is glad, and his soul finds rest; only then is his belief counted for righteousness. Jesus says the same in John 8:56, and Helaman 8:17 says Abraham saw Christ’s coming and was filled with gladness.

In the Book of Abraham the stars are shown in a vision: the Lord puts his hand on Abraham’s eyes, names the great lights, and, in the night, says, “I will multiply thee, and thy seed after thee, like unto these.” D&C 132:29–31 says Abraham’s seed would continue as innumerable as the stars both in and out of the world, and tells Joseph Smith that the promise is his too.

Jubilees dates the vision to the new moon of the third month and the sacrifice to the middle of that month, the season of the Feast of Weeks. It says the covenant with Abram was made “according as we had covenanted with Noah in this month,” and that Abram renewed the festival for ever. It also has him pour the blood on an altar and burn the pieces, turning the scene into a sacrifice.

A Jewish apocalypse written after the fall of Jerusalem. God says the true Jerusalem is a city prepared with him, distinct from the one that was destroyed, shown to Adam before he sinned, to Moses on Sinai, and to Abraham “by night among the portions of the victims.” Like the JST, it reads the night among the pieces as a vision of far more than the land.

Josephus ties the vision to the battle: God commends Abram’s virtue and tells him he will not lose the reward for such deeds, and Abram asks what good rewards are with no one to inherit them. In his telling Abram is offering a sacrifice, and birds of prey circle “as desirous of blood” before the divine voice warns of four hundred years of affliction in Egypt. The promise he hears ends with conquering the Canaanites and taking their cities.

Philo wrote a whole treatise, *Who Is the Heir of Divine Things*, on vv. 2–18. On the dividing of the animals (v. 10) he notes that the text does not say who divided them, and takes it to be God, whose Word is “the divider of all things,” splitting the universe into matched halves.

Reads the animals as the kingdoms that would rule Israel: Babylon, Media, Greece, and, in the young pigeon, Rome. The furnace and the torch showed Abraham four things: Gehenna, the kingdoms, the giving of the Torah, and the Temple. One rabbi adds that on that day God told Abraham about both this world and the world to come.

Explains the ritual by the custom of covenant partners cutting an animal and passing between the parts, citing Jeremiah 34:19, with the fire standing for God’s presence. The birds are not divided because Israel, likened to a dove, will endure. He counts the four hundred years of v. 13 from Isaac’s birth, with only 210 of them spent in Egypt.

Asks why Abraham’s descendants were enslaved in Egypt, and one answer, Shmuel’s, points to v. 8: Abraham pressed God too hard by asking “whereby shall I know?” Augustine, below, defends the same question.

Paul builds his case for justification by faith on v. 6. Abraham’s faith was counted for righteousness while he was still uncircumcised (Genesis 17 comes later), so he is father of all who believe. Galatians adds that Scripture “preached before the gospel unto Abraham.” James quotes the same verse and adds that Abraham was called the Friend of God.
Argues to Trypho that Abraham, while uncircumcised, “was justified and blessed by reason of the faith” he placed in God. Circumcision came afterward as a sign, not as the source of his righteousness.

Defends Abram’s question in v. 8: he asks by what sign he will know, in the way Mary asked “How shall this be?” He reads the undivided birds as the spiritual, the descending birds of prey as evil spirits, and the darkness at sunset as tribulation near the world’s end. He takes the four hundred years as a round number within the 430 of Galatians 3:17.

16.overview:
Ten years after entering Canaan, Sarai is still childless, so she gives her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram as a wife, hoping to “obtain children by her.” Hagar conceives and begins to look down on her mistress. Sarai blames Abram, he leaves Hagar in Sarai’s hands, and Sarai treats her so harshly that Hagar runs away. The angel of the LORD finds her at a spring on the road to Shur. He tells her to go back and submit, promises her descendants beyond counting, and tells her to name her son Ishmael, because the LORD has heard her affliction. Hagar calls the Lord “Thou God seest me,” and the well is named Beer-lahai-roi. She bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.

The one person here who meets God is the Egyptian slave, alone in the wilderness. Abram and Sarai talk about her; God talks to her, by name, and she is the one who names him (v. 13).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined and dated much later.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: A revelation recorded July 12, 1843, says God commanded Abraham and Sarah gave Hagar to him “because this was the law” (D&C 132:34–35, 65).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Ten years after Abram entered Canaan (v. 3); Abram is 86 at Ishmael’s birth (v. 16). Traditional dating c. 2000–1800 BC; on Ussher’s reckoning, 1910 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Abram’s household in Canaan; a spring in the wilderness on the road to Shur, toward Egypt, between Kadesh and Bered (vv. 7, 14).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jubilees 14:21–24; Josephus, Antiquities 1.10.4. Hagar flees again in Genesis 21:9–21; Paul reads the story as allegory in Galatians 4:21–31.

16.hermeneutics:
Sarai’s plan was a recognized legal arrangement. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) deal with a wife who gives her husband a slave woman to bear children (§§144–147). If the slave bears children and then claims equality with her mistress, she may not be sold, but she may be put back among the slave women; if she bore no children, she may be sold (§§146–147). Verses 4–6 follow the same plot: Hagar conceives, her mistress becomes small in her eyes, and Abram puts Hagar back under Sarai’s hand. The law expected the quarrel. Genesis shows what it cost the woman caught in it.

A marriage contract from Nuzi (15th–14th century BC) writes the same arrangement in advance: if the wife, Gilimninu, bears no children, she must obtain a slave woman from the Lullu country as a wife for her husband, Shennima, and Gilimninu will have authority over the children. The children were the wife’s to govern, not the slave’s. That is Sarai’s hope in v. 2, literally “it may be that I shall be built up from her,” and it helps explain why Hagar’s contempt stung so sharply.

Hagar runs toward home. Shur lay “before Egypt” (25:18), on the desert road to Egypt’s eastern border, which the pharaohs had guarded with forts since the reign of Amenemhat I (c. 1990–1960 BC). In the Story of Sinuhe, the hero, fleeing the other way, hides from the watchmen on the “Walls of the Ruler,” built to repel the Asiatics. An Egyptian slave woman on that road is going back to her own people, and the angel meets her before she reaches the border.

Hagar conceives and despises Sarai; Sarai afflicts her; Hagar flees
The angel finds Hagar at a spring: return and submit
Countless seed; a son named Ishmael, a wild man
Hagar names the God who sees; Beer-lahai-roi
Ishmael born when Abram is eighty-six

structure.summary: Inclusio: Sarai bears Abram no children (v. 1); Hagar bears him a son (vv. 15–16).

rows.label: A
rows.text: In Abram’s house: Sarai’s plan, Hagar’s contempt, the flight

rows.label: B
rows.text: In the wilderness: the angel’s command and promise

rows.label: C
rows.text: Hagar names the God who sees her

notes: **Her name:** “Hagar” appears seven times, but only the angel speaks to her by it (v. 8). To Sarai and Abram she is “my maid” and “thy maid” (vv. 2, 5, 6).

**Eyes:** The Hebrew *ayin* appears five times in vv. 4–7: Sarai is despised “in her eyes” (vv. 4, 5), Abram says do what is good “in thine eyes” (v. 6), and the angel finds Hagar by a “fountain” (*ayin*, twice in v. 7). Then Hagar names the God who sees (v. 13).

**Hearing and affliction:** Abram “hearkened” to Sarai (v. 2), and the son is named because the LORD “hath heard” Hagar (v. 11); both are *shama*. Sarai “dealt hardly” with Hagar (v. 6), the angel says “submit” (v. 9), and God hears her “affliction” (v. 11): one Hebrew root.

Chapter 16 sits between two promises of an heir. Chapter 15 promised Abram a son from his own body; chapter 17 will name Sarah as the mother. In between, Sarai tries to secure the promise by the means her world offered.

**Links:** Hagar’s story continues in 21:9–21, where she is sent away and God again meets her in the wilderness. Ishmael receives his own *toledot* heading at 25:12, where Hagar is named as his mother.

traditions.text: Genesis presents the plan as Sarai’s idea (v. 2). The revelation says God commanded Abraham, and Sarah gave Hagar to him “because this was the law,” so that from Hagar many people would spring, in fulfillment of the promises. It asks whether Abraham was therefore under condemnation and answers no, since the Lord commanded it. Josephus, below, also has Sarai act at God’s command.

The same revelation speaks of the law of Sarah, saying Sarah administered unto Abraham according to the law when the Lord commanded him to take Hagar. It also says Abraham received concubines and “it was accounted unto him for righteousness,” the phrase Genesis 15:6 uses of his faith.

Jubilees places Sarai’s plan right after the covenant: Abram rejoiced and told Sarai, and “he believed that he would have seed, but she did not bear.” It then tells the marriage and Ishmael’s birth in Abram’s eighty-sixth year, and leaves out Hagar’s contempt, Sarai’s harshness, the flight, and the angel entirely.

Josephus has Sarai bring Hagar to Abram “at God’s command.” Hagar affronts Sarai as though the rule of the house would pass to her son. The angel tells Hagar her trouble came from ingratitude and arrogance toward her mistress, but promises a son who would reign over that country, and Josephus explains Ishmael as “Heard of God.”

Philo reads Sarah as wisdom and Hagar as the general studies that prepare for it: grammar, geometry, astronomy, rhetoric, music. A student must first join with the handmaid before he can father virtue’s offspring. Hagar is Egyptian because such learning works through the bodily senses, and he takes her name to mean “sojourning.”
traditions.cite: On Mating with the Preliminary Studies 9–12, 20

traditions.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai says Hagar was Pharaoh’s daughter. After seeing the wonders done for Sarai in his palace (12:17), Pharaoh gave her to the household, reasoning that his daughter was better off a maid in that house than a mistress in another. The midrash reads her name as “here is your reward” (*ha agrikh*).

Uses v. 3 as the scriptural hint for a rule: a man whose wife has borne no children after ten years of marriage should take another wife. Since the ten years are counted from Abram’s arrival in Canaan, the rabbis conclude that years spent outside the land of Israel do not count toward the ten.

Following the midrash, Rashi has Sarai charge Abram with praying only for himself in 15:2 (“seeing I go childless”), when he should have prayed for both of them. On v. 13 he says Hagar was not frightened by the angel because she had seen angels often in Abraham’s house.

A Spanish rabbi who does not excuse the patriarchs here. He says Sarai sinned by afflicting Hagar and Abraham sinned by allowing it, and that God heard Hagar’s affliction by giving her a son whose descendants would afflict the seed of Abraham and Sarah.

Turns Hagar’s words in v. 13 into thanksgiving to the Lord, whom she calls the living and eternal One “who seest, but art not seen.” It adds that the glory of the Shekinah of the Lord had been revealed to her there, so that her naming of God becomes a confession of what she saw.

Paul reads the two mothers as two covenants: Hagar, the bondwoman, answers to Mount Sinai and the earthly Jerusalem in bondage, and the free woman to the Jerusalem above. The son “born after the flesh” is Ishmael, the son “by promise” Isaac, and believers are children of the free woman.

Clement takes up Philo’s reading by name: Hagar stands for the secular learning a believer may use, and Sarah for true wisdom. When Abraham says “do to her as it pleaseth thee” (v. 6), Clement hears him saying that he embraces secular culture as a handmaid but honors Sarah’s knowledge as his true wife.

Clears Abraham of blame: he took Hagar to have children, not from desire, and to obey his wife, who by the right of 1 Corinthians 7:4 could use his body for childbearing through another. Abraham’s handing Hagar back to Sarai in v. 6 shows, Augustine says, that he was no slave to the handmaid. D&C 132:35 reaches the same verdict, no condemnation, on other grounds.

17.overview:
Thirteen years after Ishmael's birth, the LORD appears to Abram at ninety-nine and sets out the covenant in full. Abram becomes Abraham, “a father of many nations,” and Sarai becomes Sarah, the mother of kings. The covenant takes a sign in the flesh: every male in the household, born there or bought, is to be circumcised, and from then on every boy at eight days old. Abraham laughs at the promise of a son at a hundred and pleads for Ishmael. God blesses Ishmael but names Isaac, not yet conceived, as the heir of the covenant. That same day Abraham circumcises himself, Ishmael, and every man of his house.

Watch how the sign and the line split. Ishmael receives the sign, and a promise of twelve princes, before Isaac exists. The mark goes on everyone in the household; the covenant line runs through one child who has not been born.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign this chapter to the priestly writer.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith's revision of Genesis 1–24 (June 1830–March 1831) rewrote vv. 3–12 and 17–18 (JST Genesis 17:3–12, 23–24).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Abraham's ninety-ninth year, Ishmael's thirteenth (vv. 1, 25). Traditional dating places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: The covenant of Genesis 15; Abraham 2:9–11 (the promise of seed and priesthood); Jubilees 15 (a retelling).

17.hermeneutics:
Neo-Assyrian kings rewarded loyal servants with royal grants: land and privileges that passed to the servant's descendants. The grant documents praise the servant who “walked before” his king in truth and with a whole heart. Moshe Weinfeld set the Abraham covenants beside these grants. Heard that way, “walk before me, and be thou perfect” (v. 1) is a king's word to a trusted servant, and what follows reads like a grant: land “for an everlasting possession” and a royal line (vv. 6, 8, 16).

Israel was not the only people that circumcised. A tomb relief at Saqqara in Egypt (tomb of Ankhmahor, about 2300 BC) shows the operation on young men, Herodotus reports it among Egyptians and the peoples of Syria-Palestine (2.104), and Jeremiah counts Egypt, Edom, Ammon and Moab among the circumcised (Jeremiah 9:25–26). Where an age shows, it is youths. Genesis moves the rite to the eighth day and extends it to slaves bought from foreigners (v. 12). A rite of growing up becomes a mark of belonging to a household from birth; Ishmael, at thirteen, receives it at the older age (v. 25).

Overlords renamed the people they took under their authority. Pharaoh Necho renamed Eliakim as Jehoiakim when he put him on Judah's throne, and Nebuchadnezzar renamed Mattaniah as Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:34; 24:17); Joseph and Daniel received court names (Genesis 41:45; Daniel 1:7). When God renames Abram and Sarai in the same speech that sets up the covenant, the new names mark a new standing under him, and each name carries part of the promise (vv. 5, 16).

breakdown.label: God Almighty appears: walk before me, and be perfect
Abram becomes Abraham; nations, kings, and the land promised
Circumcision: the covenant's sign in the flesh
Sarai becomes Sarah, mother of nations and kings
Abraham laughs and pleads for Ishmael; Isaac named heir
That same day Abraham circumcises his whole household

structure.summary: Inclusio: Abraham's age and God's coming and going frame five divine speeches. No chiasm is claimed.

open.text: Abram is ninety-nine; the LORD appears

close.text: God goes up; Abraham, ninety-nine, is circumcised

rows.text: “I am the Almighty God; walk before me”
“As for me”: nations, kings, land, everlasting covenant
“As for Sarai”: a new name and a son
“As for Ishmael”: blessed, but the covenant goes to Isaac

notes: **Whose part:** the speeches turn from God's side (“As for me,” v. 4) to Abraham's (“thou,” v. 9), then to Sarah (v. 15) and Ishmael (v. 20). In Hebrew each opens with the pronoun or name placed first for emphasis.
**Counts:** “circumcise” 10 times, “seed” 7 times, “everlasting” 4 times (vv. 7, 8, 13, 19). On the count of “covenant,” see Traditions (Mishnah).
**Falling on his face:** Abraham falls on his face twice (vv. 3, 17). The first time he listens; the second time he laughs, the first play on Isaac's name.

Chapter 17 closes the covenant section that opens at 15:1, inside Terah's *toledot* (11:27), which carries the Abraham story to Ishmael's line at 25:12. Chapter 15 makes the covenant with land and seed; chapter 17 adds a sign, new names, and a named heir due “at this set time in the next year” (v. 21). The next unit repeats that date at Mamre (18:10, 14).

**Links:** Isaac's circumcision on the eighth day (21:4) carries out v. 12, and Stephen sums up the two together (Acts 7:8). Moses' near death over his son's circumcision (Exodus 4:24–26) and the mass circumcision at Gilgal (Joshua 5:2–9) show the sign held binding.

traditions.text: Before the covenant speech the JST adds a complaint from God: his people have strayed from the ordinances given to their fathers, neglected baptism, taken up “the washing of children,” and claimed that Abel's blood was shed for sins. The covenant of circumcision is then given so Abraham may know that children are not accountable before God until they are eight years old. The eighth day of v. 12 becomes a pointer to baptism at eight, the age set in D&C 68 and defended in Moroni 8.

Where Genesis has Abraham fall on his face and laugh (v. 17), the JST has him rejoice, and his question becomes a statement that a son will be born to a man of a hundred. His plea for Ishmael becomes a prayer that the boy might live “uprightly” before God. Jubilees also reads “rejoiced” at this point, and Augustine took Abraham's laughter as wondering delight.
traditions.cite: JST Genesis 17:23–24; Jubilees 15:17; City of God 16.31

traditions.text: The Book of Abraham gives the promise of seed a priesthood shape: Abraham's descendants will bear “this ministry and Priesthood unto all nations,” and all who receive the gospel will be counted his seed and rise up to call him father. D&C 132 says the promises about his seed continue beyond this world, extends them to Joseph Smith's generation, and tells them to do the works of Abraham. Both read the many nations of v. 5 as reaching past Abraham's physical descendants.

Retells the chapter almost word for word but sets it at the feast of the first fruits of the grain harvest in the third month. It makes the eighth day absolute: the law is written on the heavenly tablets, and a boy not circumcised on that day does not belong to the children of the covenant. It adds that the highest angels, those of the presence and of sanctification, were created circumcised, and that Ishmael and Esau, though sons of Abraham, were not chosen.

Philo reports hearing a scoffer mock the idea that God's great gift to Abraham and Sarah was an extra letter in each name, and adds that the man soon hanged himself over a trifle. His own reading treats the new names as new natures. Abram turns from studying the world to knowing its Maker, and Sarah's name moves from “my authority,” one person's virtue, to “princess,” virtue itself.

Josephus says circumcision was commanded to keep Abraham's descendants from mixing with other peoples, and promises to explain its reason in another work. He adds a custom of his own day: the Arabs circumcised at thirteen because Ishmael, the founder of their nation, was circumcised at that age (v. 25).

Rabbi Ishmael said circumcision is so great that thirteen covenants were made over it, because the word “covenant” appears thirteen times in Genesis 17, a count the Hebrew text bears out. Rabbi Judah the Prince added that for all Abraham's obedience he was not called “perfect” (v. 1) until he was circumcised.

Rabbi Levi tells of a king who said a noblewoman's one flaw was an overlong fingernail: trim it and she is perfect. The foreskin was Abraham's one flaw. The midrash also hears *dai*, “enough,” in *Shaddai* (v. 1): if Abraham refused the sign, God's world had lasted long enough. Bar Kappara ruled that anyone who still calls Abraham “Abram” breaks a commandment, since v. 5 retires the old name.

Paul points to the order of events: Abraham was counted righteous (15:6) before he was circumcised, and received circumcision as “a seal of the righteousness of the faith” he already had. That makes him father of believers whether circumcised or not. Paul also reads v. 5 as God calling into being what did not yet exist, believed by a man whose body was as good as dead.

Barnabas joins this chapter's circumcision of Abraham's household to the 318 men of 14:14. In Greek numerals 18 is written IH, the first letters of Jesus' name, and 300 is T, the shape of the cross, so the rite pointed ahead to both. He also notes that Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians and idol priests circumcise, so the cut alone cannot mark the covenant.

Arguing with a Jewish teacher, Justin says Abraham was justified while uncircumcised and received circumcision “for a sign, and not for righteousness.” His proof is that women cannot receive the rite yet can be fully righteous, so the mark in the flesh cannot itself be righteousness. It is Paul's argument from Romans 4 with a new example.

Asks how an infant could be “cut off” for breaking the covenant (v. 14) when the failure is his parents'. His answer is that every infant broke God's first covenant in Adam, so circumcision was a sign of regeneration and the uncircumcised child was lost through original sin. JST 17:11 and Moroni 8 take up the same question about children and answer that they are not accountable.

18.overview:
In the heat of the day the LORD appears to Abraham at Mamre as three men standing near his tent. Abraham runs to meet them, bows, and hurries Sarah and a servant into baking bread and dressing a calf, then stands by while they eat. The guests ask for Sarah, and the speaker promises she will have a son by this time next year. Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughs to herself and then denies it. As the men set out toward Sodom, the LORD decides not to hide his plan, and Abraham bargains for the city from fifty righteous down to ten.

Watch the word “righteous.” It comes seven times as Abraham presses his case (vv. 23–28). The LORD has just said he chose Abraham so his household would do “justice and judgment” (v. 19), and Abraham turns that standard back on its giver: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?”

18.hermeneutics:
The Ugaritic tale of Aqhat (about 1300 BC) has a scene close to this one. Danel, a ruler who had begged the gods for a son, sits at the gate judging the cause of the widow and the orphan. He sees the craftsman god Kothar coming, tells his wife Danatiy to prepare a lamb, and serves the divine guest, who eats and drinks. Hospitality to gods who arrive as travelers, and a son granted to a childless man, were familiar story material in Canaan. Genesis tells it about Israel's God: the host runs, bows, and stands while the visitors eat, and the speaker turns out to be the LORD himself (vv. 2, 8, 13).

“Cry” in v. 20 is the cry of someone wronged who appeals to a judge. Israel's law has God hear the cry of the widow and orphan (Exodus 22:22–23), and a woman “cried unto the king” to get back her house and land (2 Kings 8:3–5). Hammurabi's law stela invites the oppressed man with a case at law to stand before the king's image and have the inscription read to him. So when the LORD says he will “go down now, and see” whether the deeds match the cry (v. 21), he speaks like a judge checking a complaint before sentence. Abraham answers in the same court language, appealing to the Judge of all the earth not to sweep away the righteous with the wicked (v. 25).

breakdown.label: Three men at the tent door; Abraham begs them to stay
Cakes, a tender calf, butter and milk under the tree
A son promised to Sarah; she laughs, then denies it
The LORD decides to tell Abraham about Sodom
Abraham draws near: fifty righteous, and the Judge of all
Forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten; the LORD goes his way

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. The bargaining runs in six steps.

rows.text: Thirty: “let not the Lord be angry”
Twenty: “I have taken upon me to speak”

notes: **The asks:** Abraham drops by five once, then by tens. His apologies come in pairs: “I have taken upon me to speak” (vv. 27, 31) and “let not the Lord be angry” (vv. 30, 32). Each time the LORD repeats the number back and agrees.
**Haste:** in vv. 2–7 Abraham runs twice and “hastens” three times (vv. 6, 7), a ninety-nine-year-old host in a hurry in the heat of the day.
**Laughter:** Sarah's laugh is named four times in vv. 12–15, twice in her denial and its answer, another play on the coming child's name, Isaac.

Chapters 18–21 run from the promise of a son “at the time appointed” (18:14) to his birth “at the set time” (21:2), with Sodom's fall and the Gerar episode between. Chapter 18 has no new heading. Its first line says the LORD appeared “unto him,” reaching back to Abraham at the end of chapter 17, and Mamre ties back to 13:18.

**Links:** Abraham's question in v. 25 returns in Jeremiah 5:1, where Jerusalem could be pardoned if one just man were found. The promise “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” (v. 14) is echoed to Mary in Luke 1:37.

traditions.text: Abraham greets his guests as “brethren” rather than “My Lord,” and when the party turns toward Sodom the JST calls them angels “which were holy men,” sent forth after the order of God. In the JST of chapter 19 the same visitors are again holy men whom Lot shelters, and three of them, not two, arrive in Sodom. The JST keeps the visitors as men commissioned by God, distinct from the LORD with whom Abraham stays behind to plead.

A retelling of Genesis narrated by an angel to Moses on Sinai, so this scene is told by the visitors themselves: “we appeared unto Abraham” at the oak of Mamre on the new moon of the fourth month. Sarah laughs, is rebuked, and is told her son's name, Isaac, which Jubilees says was already written on the heavenly tablets. Genesis 18 never names the child; Jubilees moves the name from 17:19 into this scene.

A Jewish philosopher in Alexandria. Philo praises Abraham's household, where women and men, slaves and free, all hurry to serve strangers, and suggests Abraham only gradually realized his guests were prophets or angels. He finds it a wonder that beings without bodies seemed to eat and drink. In his allegory the three are one vision: God in the middle, flanked by his creative power and his royal power, seen as one by a purified soul and as three by a soul still learning.

The guests “made a shew of eating,” then revealed that they were angels: one sent about the child, two to overthrow Sodom. In his version Abraham stops bargaining when God tells him there is not one good man in Sodom, though ten would have saved it. The Talmud and Philo also say the angels only seemed to eat.

Reads “the heat of the day” as the third day after Abraham's circumcision: God came to visit the sick and made the sun hot so travelers would not trouble him, but Abraham went out looking for guests anyway. The three men are Michael, who came to announce Isaac; Raphael, to heal Abraham; and Gabriel, to overturn Sodom. Since angels do not eat, they only appeared to.

This Aramaic paraphrase has Abraham sitting at the door “ill from the pain of circumcision.” It explains why there are three angels: no angel is sent on more than one errand, so one came to announce Sarah's son, one to deliver Lot, and one to overthrow Sodom. The Talmud gives the third angel a different errand, healing Abraham.

God gives the good news about Sarah before the bad news about Sodom, a lesson in how to deliver hard news. The “cry” of v. 20 is the cry of Peletith, Lot's daughter, burned by Sodom for secretly feeding a poor man; her cry reached the throne, and God said, “I will go down now, and see.” Ezekiel 16:49 supplies the charge: Sodom had plenty and did not help the poor.

Rashi notes that the Hebrew for “sat” in v. 1 can be read as “he was sitting down”: Abraham tried to rise for God, and God told him to sit while he himself stood. Rashi takes it as a pattern for Israel's judges, who sit while God stands in their assembly (Psalm 82:1). He also says Abraham sat at the tent door to watch for passers-by he could invite in.

Hebrews draws a rule from this scene: do not forget to entertain strangers, for some have “entertained angels unawares.” Clement of Rome, writing to the church at Corinth, says Abraham was given a son in his old age because of his faith and his hospitality, and goes on to say Lot was saved for the same reasons. Both make the meal under the tree an example for believers rather than only a story about Abraham.

Uses the chapter against a Jewish teacher to argue that one of the three at Mamre was God, distinct from the Father who never leaves heaven, sent with two angels to judge Sodom. For Justin this visitor was the Son before his birth. Philo had already seen God among the three, but as the Father with his two powers.

Takes the three as angels and notes that some read one of them as Christ, appearing before he took flesh. He answers that Abraham speaks to three as one Lord, and Lot later speaks to the two as one Lord too, so the singular proves only that both men recognized the Lord present in his messengers. God, he argues, can show himself to mortals through creatures subject to him without changing his own nature.

19.overview:
Two angels reach Sodom at evening, and Lot, sitting in the gate, presses them to stay at his house. The men of the city, young and old, surround the house and demand the guests. Lot goes out, offers his daughters instead, and is pulled back inside as the attackers are struck blind. At dawn the angels take Lot, his wife and daughters by the hand and lead them out. Lot bargains to flee to little Zoar; fire and brimstone fall, and his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Later, in a cave, his daughters make him drunk and conceive Moab and Ammon.

Notice whose rescue this is. Lot lingers and has to be led out by the hand, yet the narrator credits his escape to Abraham, who had stood before the LORD pleading for the city: “God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out” (v. 29).

19.hermeneutics:
City gates were where business was done and disputes were judged. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, Danel sits at the gate to decide the cases of widows and orphans, and Israel's elders do the same (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2). Lot “sat in the gate” (v. 1), a sign that he has become a man of standing in Sodom. The mob's sneer in v. 9, that this newcomer “will needs be a judge,” shows they still count him an outsider.

The Dead Sea basin is a country of salt, bitumen and sulfur. Genesis already mentions its bitumen pits (14:10). Strabo describes asphalt rising from the lake, scorched rocks and ashy soil on its shore, and Tacitus speaks of a burnt plain that once held great cities. At the southwest end the salt ridge of Jebel Usdum, “Mount Sodom,” weathers into upright columns. First hearers knew a dead, smoking landscape, and a story like v. 26 explains a landmark they could picture.

Moab and Ammon were real kingdoms east of the Jordan in Israel's time; the Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) speaks for a king of Moab and his god Chemosh. Peoples told origin stories about their neighbors, and this one does two things at once. It makes Moab and Ammon Israel's kin through Abraham's nephew, and it gives them a shameful birth. Deuteronomy uses both: Israel may not take their land, given to “the children of Lot” (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19), yet they are barred from the assembly (23:3).

The warning; Lot's sons-in-law think he is joking
Led out at dawn; Lot pleads for Zoar
Fire and brimstone; Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt
Abraham sees the smoke; God remembered Abraham
In the cave: Moab and Ammon are born

notes: **Where the panels break:** Abraham's guests leave him with a promise; Lot's guests are besieged, and the guests end up rescuing their host (v. 10).
**Key words:** “overthrow” comes three times (vv. 21, 25, 29), and “the cry” of the city (v. 13) picks up 18:20–21.
**Looking:** Lot is told not to look behind him (v. 17); his wife looks back (v. 26); next morning Abraham looks toward Sodom from the place where he had stood before the LORD (vv. 27–28).

The Sodom story runs from 18:16 to 19:29, and the cave scene (vv. 30–38) closes Lot's part in Genesis; he is not mentioned again. The wording of v. 29 echoes the Flood's “God remembered Noah” (8:1), and Abraham's view of the smoke (v. 28) closes the scene that opened with him looking toward Sodom (18:16).
**Links:** Sodom becomes the Bible's byword for judgment (Isaiah 1:9–10; Matthew 10:15). Moab returns through Ruth, great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:13–17).

traditions.text: In the JST the mob is angry with Lot and demands his daughters as well as the guests. Lot does not offer the girls; he pleads with the crowd not to take them, saying “God will not justify his servant in this thing,” and asks them to let the strangers have peace in his house. The angels of God who pull him inside are described as holy men.

Other JST readings run through the chapter. Three angels, not two, come to Sodom, matching the three at Mamre, and Lot's guests are “these holy men.” At the end the JST passes judgment where Genesis is silent: the firstborn “dealt wickedly,” and both daughters “did wickedly.”

The prophet names Sodom's sins as Jerusalem's sister: “pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness,” and failing to strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. Then she grew haughty and “committed abomination.” Later Jewish writers built on this verse, and Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer quotes it directly.

Lists Lot among the righteous whom Wisdom saved, the man who fled the fire that fell on “the five cities.” The smoking waste land, plants whose fruit never ripens, and “a standing pillar of salt” remain as witnesses. The pillar, it says, is a monument of an unbelieving soul.

Says the cities were burned for their uncleanness and fornication, and warns that God will judge any place that acts like Sodom. It calls the sin of Lot and his daughters one that had not been on the earth since Adam, and says the heavenly tablets decree a like judgment on his descendants.

Sodom grew proud from its wealth, unjust to men and impious to God, and “hated strangers.” Lot's wife kept turning back, too curious about the city's fate, and became a pillar of salt. Josephus adds his own testimony: “For I have seen it, and it remains at this day.”

Why salt? Genesis Rabbah says Lot's wife sinned through salt: she went to the neighbors asking for salt for her guests, so the town would learn they were there. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says she was a daughter of Sodom who looked back to see what would become of her father's house, and was punished by the salt she sinned with.
traditions.cite: Genesis Rabbah 51:5; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 19:26

traditions.text: Describes Sodom as a city that grew rich and made cruelty to travelers its law. Guests were laid on a bed and stretched or cut to fit it; beggars were given marked coins that no one would take for bread. A young woman who smuggled bread to the poor was smeared with honey and left on the wall for the bees, and that, Rav says, is the “great” cry of 18:20.

Jesus compares his coming to Lot's day, when people ate, bought, planted and built until fire fell, and adds, “Remember Lot's wife.” Second Peter calls Lot a just man vexed day after day by what he saw and heard in Sodom, making him a model of God's rescue of the godly.

Clement of Rome says Lot was saved because of his hospitality and godliness. His wife, of a different mind, became a pillar of salt “unto this day,” a sign that the double-minded who doubt God's power bring judgment on themselves. Josephus, writing about the same years, also says the pillar could still be seen.

Passes on a teaching from an older presbyter: where Scripture records a patriarch's deed without blaming it, readers should not condemn it. Lot's daughters, thinking all mankind had perished, acted to preserve the race and are to be excused. The pillar of salt that still stands becomes a figure of the Church, the salt of the earth.

Treats the fire on Sodom as a preview of the last judgment. The command not to look back, he says, means that those reborn by grace must not turn back in heart to the life they left. Lot's wife, turned to salt, became a seasoning for believers, a warning to savor.

A Greek geographer describing the Dead Sea region. Near Masada he notes scorched rocks, ashy soil and dripping pitch, and repeats the local report that thirteen cities once stood there with Sodom as their capital. Earthquakes, eruptions of fire, and hot waters full of asphalt and sulfur destroyed them, some swallowed and some abandoned.

The Roman historian reports a plain near the lake that was once fertile and held great cities, later burned by lightning, where the ground still looks scorched and plants wither. He grants that cities may have been destroyed by fire from heaven, but blames the lake's fumes for the barren soil.

20.overview:
Abraham moves south to Gerar and again says of Sarah, “She is my sister.” King Abimelech takes her into his house, but God comes to him in a dream: he is a dead man, for she is married. Abimelech protests that he acted with a clean heart, and God agrees, saying he himself kept the king from touching her. In the morning the king confronts Abraham, who says he feared for his life and that Sarah really is his father's daughter. Abimelech returns her with flocks, servants, a thousand pieces of silver and the run of his land. Abraham prays, and God heals the king's household, whose wombs had been closed.

The outsider comes off better than the patriarch. Abraham assumed “the fear of God is not in this place” (v. 11), yet the king obeys at once and his servants are “sore afraid” (v. 8). Still, God calls Abraham a prophet whose prayer the king needs (v. 7).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Between the promise of a son (18:10) and Isaac's birth (21:1–2), when Sarah was about ninety (17:17). Traditional dating places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Gerar in the western Negev, between Kadesh and Shur (v. 1), near Gaza on Canaan's southern border (10:19).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 12:10–20 (Abram, Sarai and Pharaoh) and 26:1–11 (Isaac, Rebekah and Abimelech). Abraham 2:22–25 has the Lord himself tell Abraham to call Sarai his sister in Egypt.

20.hermeneutics:
Abimelech says Abraham nearly brought on him “a great sin” (v. 9). In the ancient Near East that phrase was a set term for adultery. Egyptian marriage contracts speak of “the great sin” a wife might commit, and texts from Ugarit use it of a queen's offense against her husband the king. Hearers would take the king's words as a precise legal charge. A foreign king knows the gravity of the act, and God accepts his plea of a clean heart and clean hands (vv. 5–6).

Kings across the region expected the gods to speak to them in dreams. Gudea of Lagash built his temple after a dream described at length on his clay cylinders, and letters from Mari pass on dreams with divine warnings to King Zimri-Lim. Genesis has the God of Abraham use the same channel with a king of Gerar, as he later does with Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. The dream works: Abimelech rises early and acts on it (v. 8).

Marriage to a half-sister on the father's side was possible in Abraham's world, and Tamar could still tell Amnon that King David would let him marry her (2 Samuel 13:13). Israel's law later forbade it (Leviticus 18:9; 20:17). Abraham's defense in v. 12 rests on a custom his first hearers knew had once been allowed and was no longer.
