God warns Abimelech in a dream; the king pleads innocence
The servants fear; Abimelech confronts Abraham
Abraham explains: his fear, and a half-sister wife
Sarah restored with flocks, servants and silver
Abraham prays; God heals Abimelech's house

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, mostly as dialogue.

rows.text: God: “thou art but a dead man”
Abimelech: integrity of heart, innocency of hands
God: I withheld thee; restore her, or die
Abimelech: “What hast thou done unto us?”
Abraham: fear for his life; she is my sister

notes: **Death to life:** “die” threatens three times (vv. 3, 7 twice) and the chapter ends in healing and births (v. 17). “Restore” brackets the action: God's command (v. 7, twice) and the king's obedience (v. 14).
**Three tellings:** the wife-sister story also appears at 12:10–20 and 26:1–11. Only here does God speak to the foreign king, and only here does the patriarch explain himself at length.

Chapter 20 sits between the promise of a son “at the time appointed” (18:14) and its fulfillment (21:1–2), and it puts the mother of that child in a foreign king's house just before the birth. It is the second of three wife-sister stories, and the only one inside the Isaac birth unit. Abimelech and Gerar return at 21:22–34 and in Isaac's story (26:1–33).
**Link:** Psalm 105:14–15 sums up these episodes: God “reproved kings for their sakes,” saying, “Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”

traditions.text: In the Book of Abraham the plan to call Sarai his sister comes from the Lord, who warns Abraham that the Egyptians will kill him for his beautiful wife. Abraham then passes the instruction to Sarai. That casts light on 20:13, where Abraham tells Abimelech the arrangement went back to the time God caused him to wander from his father's house.

Jubilees moves Abraham from Hebron to Gerar and then to the Well of the Oath with no mention of Abimelech or Sarah's capture. Since it follows Genesis closely through the surrounding chapters, the silence stands out: the episode simply drops out of its retelling, perhaps because it reflects badly on the patriarch. Its list of Abraham's trials elsewhere still includes his wife being taken from him.

Abimelech falls in love with Sarah but is struck by a dangerous illness, and only after his physicians despair does the warning dream come. The king tells Abraham he would never have touched her had he known she was his wife, and offers him land and money to stay. Josephus has Abraham explain that calling Sarah his sister was no lie, because she was his brother's daughter. He merges the end of the story with the oath at Beersheba in the next chapter.

Notes that God speaks to this king only in a dream at night and draws a rule: God appears to the prophets of the nations only at the hour people part from each other, as if through a curtain, but to Israel's prophets openly. On Abraham's prayer in v. 17 Rabbi Hama says this is the first time in the book that anyone prays for another, and with it the knot was untied.

A Mishnah rules that paying damages does not bring forgiveness until the injured party is asked, and cites God's words to Abimelech: restore the wife, and Abraham will pray for you. The Gemara also faults the king: when a guest comes to town, does one ask about his food and drink, or about his wife? Rava finds here the rule that whoever prays for another while needing the same thing is answered first: Abraham prayed for wombs in Gerar to open, and the next verse reads, “the LORD visited Sarah.”

Counts Sarah's capture among Abraham's ten trials. Abimelech becomes impotent and his household barren down to the smallest insect; the angel Michael comes with drawn sword, and the king asks whether it is just to slay him when he did not know. Abraham then prays that the God who made the world to increase and multiply would let Abimelech's house multiply. The midrash contrasts the two kings: whatever Pharaoh gave, he gave to Sarah, but Abimelech gave his gifts to Abraham.

This Aramaic paraphrase softens Abraham's claim in v. 12: Sarah is his sister as “the daughter of my father's brother,” a cousin, matching Josephus. It also explains the wandering of v. 13 as the time people tried to turn Abraham to idolatry and he left his father's house.

Explains the hard phrase of v. 16, a “covering of the eyes.” Abimelech's lavish gifts protect Sarah's name: had he sent her back empty-handed, people would say he had abused her and then dismissed her, but a costly settlement shows she was returned against his will. Genesis Rabbah reads the king more sharply, as telling Abraham he had now profited from Sarah twice and should keep her out of sight.

The Manichean Faustus accused Abraham of selling his wife twice, to Pharaoh and to Abimelech. Augustine answers that Abraham hid part of the truth but said nothing false, guarded his life by ordinary means rather than tempt God, and trusted God with Sarah's chastity. He then reads Sarah, kept undefiled among foreign kings who bring her gifts, as a figure of the Church.

In his survey of Abraham's life, Augustine notes that the patriarch did at Gerar what he had done in Egypt and again received his wife back untouched. He takes v. 12 at face value: Sarah was his sister through his father, and so close kin. Her beauty, he adds, was so great that even at her advanced age a foreign king could desire her.

21.overview:
The LORD does for Sarah what he promised: she bears Abraham a son in his hundredth year, at the set time. Abraham names him Isaac and circumcises him on the eighth day, and Sarah says God has made her laugh. At the feast for Isaac's weaning, Sarah sees Hagar's son mocking and demands that mother and son be cast out. God tells the grieving Abraham to listen to her, and promises Ishmael a nation too. In the wilderness of Beersheba the water runs out, Hagar leaves the boy under a shrub, and God hears him and shows her a well. Then Abimelech asks Abraham for an oath, they settle a dispute over a well, and Abraham calls on the everlasting God at Beersheba.

Notice the laughter around Isaac's name. Sarah's laugh of joy (v. 6) is followed at once by Ishmael's “mocking” (v. 9), the same Hebrew verb, and that laugh sets the expulsion in motion.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: Joseph Smith's revision of Genesis (June 1830–March 1831) changes vv. 32–34 (JST Genesis 21:31–32).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Isaac born in Abraham's hundredth year (v. 5), the weaning some years later (v. 8). Traditional dating places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Abraham's camp in the Negev near Gerar and Beersheba; the wilderness of Beersheba and of Paran to the south (vv. 14, 21, 31–34).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jubilees 16:12–14 and 17:1–14; Josephus, Antiquities 1.12.2–3; Isaac's own oath with Abimelech at Beersheba (26:26–33).

21.hermeneutics:
Babylonian law spoke directly to a household like Abraham's. In the Code of Hammurabi, a wife may give her husband a slave woman to bear children; if that slave then claims equality with her mistress, she may not be sold but may be counted among the slaves again (§146). The slave's sons inherit with the wife's sons only if the father, in his lifetime, has called them “my sons”; if not, the slave woman and her sons go free and share nothing (§§170–171). Against that background Sarah's demand is about inheritance, as she says (v. 10), and sending Hagar and Ishmael away is something like a release from the household without a share. Abraham's grief (v. 11) shows he had treated Ishmael as his son.

Ancient mothers nursed for a long time. The Egyptian Instruction of Any reminds a son that his mother's breast was in his mouth for three years, and the mother in 2 Maccabees says she gave her son suck three years (2 Maccabees 7:27). A weaning feast (v. 8) marks a child who has survived infancy, perhaps two or three years old. By Genesis's own numbers Ishmael would then be sixteen or more (16:16; 21:5), a point that changes how readers picture v. 14, where Hagar carries the provisions and “the child.”

breakdown.label: Isaac born, named and circumcised; Sarah's laughter
Weaning feast; Sarah demands Hagar and Ishmael go
Sent into the wilderness; the water runs out
God hears the boy; a well; Ishmael grows in Paran
Abimelech and Phichol ask Abraham for an oath
A disputed well, seven ewe lambs, a covenant at Beersheba
Abraham plants a grove and calls on the everlasting God

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three scenes, each tied to a name.

rows.text: Isaac, “he laughs”: the promised son is born
Ishmael, “God hears”: sent away and saved
Beer-sheba, “well of the oath”: a treaty with Abimelech

notes: **Laughter:** the verb “laugh” runs through the whole unit (17:17; 18:12, 13, 15 twice; 19:14, KJV “mocked”; 21:6, 9, KJV “mocking”), with the noun once more in 21:6. Each time it plays on Isaac's name.
**God hears:** in vv. 12–17 “voice” comes four times (Sarah's, Hagar's, the lad's twice), and in v. 17 God “heard” the lad twice, acting out Ishmael's name.
**Seven and swear:** “swear” comes three times (vv. 23, 24, 31) and “seven” three times (vv. 28–30). The two Hebrew words sound alike, and v. 31 builds the name Beer-sheba on them.

Chapter 21 closes the unit that began at Mamre: Isaac arrives “at the set time of which God had spoken” (v. 2), answering 17:21 and 18:14. The next verse, “after these things” (22:1), opens the testing of Abraham.

**Links:** Ishmael's rescue and Isaac's binding are told in matching terms: Abraham rises early (21:14; 22:3), a son is near death, an angel calls from heaven (21:17; 22:11), and a well or a ram comes into view (21:19; 22:13). Isaac later reopens the Beersheba treaty with another Abimelech (26:26–33).

traditions.text: In Genesis Abraham plants the grove and calls on the LORD (v. 33). In the JST it is Abimelech and Phichol who plant the grove at Beersheba and call on the name of the Lord before returning home, and Abraham worships the everlasting God. The Philistine king who swore by God in v. 23 ends the chapter as a worshiper.

Says Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife because God commanded it and “this was the law,” and that from Hagar sprang many people as part of the promises. That matches God's promise here that the son of the bondwoman will also become a nation because he is Abraham's seed (vv. 13, 18).

Isaac is born at the feast of first fruits, the same feast at which Jubilees set the covenant of circumcision, and he is the first child circumcised on the eighth day under that covenant. At the weaning feast Abraham rejoices to see both his sons before him; Sarah sees Ishmael “playing and dancing” and grows jealous. Hagar lays the boy under an olive tree, and Jubilees later lists the sending away of Hagar and Ishmael among Abraham's trials.

Sarah at first loved Ishmael like her own son, but after Isaac's birth feared the older boy could harm him once Abraham died. Abraham thought it barbarous to send away a child and a woman without supplies, and agreed only because God approved. Hagar lays the dying child under a fir tree, and shepherds help her after the angel shows her the spring.

Reads Sarah's “all that hear will laugh with me” (v. 6) as a wider blessing: when Sarah conceived, many barren women conceived with her, the deaf heard and the blind saw. On v. 2 the rabbis also answer gossip left over from chapter 20. Isaac's face looked like Abraham's, and he was born at the full time, so no one could say he came from Abimelech's palace.

What was Ishmael doing when Sarah saw him “mocking”? Rabbi Akiva said immorality; Rabbi Ishmael, idolatry; another sage, bloodshed, Ishmael shooting arrows at Isaac and calling it play. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai read it more kindly as a quarrel over inheritance: Ishmael boasted that as firstborn he would take a double share, which is why Sarah answers about inheritance (v. 10). Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer keeps the arrow.

This Aramaic paraphrase has Ishmael mocking with “strange worship,” and Abraham dismissing Hagar with a bill of divorce. It names Ishmael's wives, Adisha, whom he put away, and Fatima from Egypt. The grove of v. 33 becomes a garden where Abraham fed passing travelers and taught them to confess the name of the everlasting God, extending his hospitality of chapter 18.

Counts the expulsion as Abraham's ninth trial. Ishmael, aged seventeen, shoots an arrow at Isaac; Abraham writes Hagar a bill of divorce and ties a veil around her waist to mark her a servant. In the wilderness Hagar strays toward her father's idols and the water fails. Later Abraham twice rides out to visit Ishmael, sworn to Sarah not to dismount, and blesses the house where Ishmael's second wife gives him bread and water.

Paul reads the two mothers as an allegory of two covenants: Hagar, the bondwoman, stands for Sinai and the earthly Jerusalem; Sarah, the free woman, for the Jerusalem above. Believers are children of promise like Isaac. He quotes Sarah's words in v. 10 as scripture's verdict, and sees Ishmael's mocking as persecution of the one born by the Spirit.

Explains that Isaac means laughter, a name drawn from both parents: Abraham's laugh of wondering delight and Sarah's laugh of joy mixed with doubt, for which the angel rebuked her. At the birth her laughter turns into open praise (v. 6). Like Paul, he then reads the casting out of the bondwoman as the passing of the old covenant before the new, Sarah standing for the Jerusalem above.

Credits Isaac's birth to Sarah's own faith: she received strength to conceive past the age for it because she judged him faithful who had promised. From one man as good as dead came descendants as many as the stars. The same chapter then turns to Abraham's offering of Isaac, the story that follows this one.

22.overview:
God tells Abraham to take Isaac, his only son by Sarah, to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering. Abraham sets out early, travels three days, and climbs the mountain with Isaac, who carries the wood and asks where the lamb is. Abraham binds him on the altar and takes the knife, but the angel of the LORD stops him, and a ram caught by its horns is offered instead. God then swears by himself to bless Abraham's seed. The chapter closes with news from Haran about Nahor's children, a list that ends with Rebekah.

The reader is told in v. 1 that this is a test; Abraham is never told. From where he stands, the command undoes the promise of 21:12 that his seed would be called through Isaac. Everything in the scene turns on how he holds both at once.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC. Isaac's age is not given; he is old enough to carry the wood up the mountain (v. 6).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Beer-sheba (v. 19) to “the land of Moriah,” a three-day journey (v. 4). 2 Chronicles 3:1 places Solomon's temple on “mount Moriah” in Jerusalem.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: No other scripture retells the scene. Jacob 4:5 and D&C 132:36 comment on it, and Abraham 1:7–15 tells of Abraham himself bound on an altar in Chaldea.

22.hermeneutics:
Child sacrifice was a real practice in Israel's world. 2 Kings 3:27 reports that Mesha, king of Moab, offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall during a siege. Greek writers say the Carthaginians, colonists from Phoenicia, burned children to their god in times of crisis (Diodorus Siculus 20.14), and the sacrificial precinct excavated at Carthage held thousands of urns of infant bones. Israel's law forbids the practice outright (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). A first hearer would know the command of v. 2 as something the neighbors did, which puts the weight of the story on the stopped knife.

Israel's law also claimed every firstborn for God and then required that firstborn sons be redeemed, with an animal given in their place (Exodus 13:13; 34:20). Micah 6:7 asks whether God wants “my firstborn for my transgression” and answers no. Genesis 22 plays out that pattern as a story: the son is claimed, then released, and a ram is offered “in the stead of his son” (v. 13).

A burnt offering (*olah*) was burned whole on the altar; nothing came back to the worshiper. The name Moriah appears only once more in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 3:1, as the hill of Solomon's temple. Israelite hearers would connect “in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” (v. 14) with Jerusalem, where a lamb went up as a burnt offering every morning and every evening (Numbers 28:3–4).

breakdown.label: The test: take thine only son to Moriah
Three days' journey; the young men left behind
Father and son climb: “where is the lamb?”
Isaac bound on the altar; the knife taken
The angel stops him; the ram; Jehovah-jireh
God swears by himself; return to Beer-sheba
Nahor's twelve children, with Rebekah in the line

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. Its hinges are three calls, each answered “Here am I.”

rows.text: Isaac calls “My father”: “Here am I, my son”
The angel calls “Abraham, Abraham”: “Here am I”

notes: **Three calls:** Abraham gives the same answer to God who commands, to the son who asks about the lamb, and to the angel who stops the knife.

**Repetition to watch:** “thine only son” (vv. 2, 12, 16); “they went both of them together” (vv. 6, 8), echoed when Abraham and the young men go “together” to Beer-sheba (v. 19). The Hebrew word for “son” comes 10 times in vv. 1–19.

**Seeing:** the verb *ra'ah* (“see”) occurs five times. Abraham sees the place (v. 4), says God will “provide,” literally “see” (v. 8), sees the ram (v. 13), and names the place for it, using the verb twice (v. 14).

The test opens the last stretch of Abraham's story (22:1–25:18), still under the *toledot* of Terah that began at 11:27. The stretch closes with the deaths of Sarah and Abraham and the list of Ishmael's sons (25:12–18), before Isaac's heading at 25:19. Verses 20–24 look ahead: a genealogy ending in Rebekah prepares for the search for Isaac's wife in ch. 24.
**Back to the call:** the Hebrew “get thee” (*lekh lekha*) occurs in Genesis only at 12:1 and 22:2. The first time, Abraham leaves his father's house; the last time, he is asked to give up his son.

traditions.text: Jacob, Nephi's brother, says the Nephites kept the law of Moses because it pointed to Christ, and that this obedience was counted for righteousness just as Abraham's obedience was in offering Isaac. He then calls that offering “a similitude of God and his Only Begotten Son.” It is the plainest statement in scripture that the father in Genesis 22 stands for the Father, and Irenaeus and Melito draw the same likeness from the scene (below).

Abraham's own record opens with Abraham as the intended victim. Priests in Chaldea offered men, women, and children to idols, and they laid hands on Abraham to offer him up, with his father's consent, until the angel of the Lord's presence loosed his bands. Read with Genesis 22, Abraham stood on both sides of the altar: once rescued from it, later asked to bind his own son on one. Philo says the opposite about Chaldea (below).

D&C 132 sets the command beside the written law against killing and says that because Abraham did not refuse, it was accounted to him for righteousness, the phrase Jacob 4:5 also uses. D&C 101, given to Saints driven out of Jackson County, says they must be “chastened and tried, even as Abraham.” Both treat the story as the model of a trial that cuts against ordinary rules.

The risen Jesus quotes the oath of v. 18 to the Nephites in the form “in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.” He explains its fulfillment as his own coming to them first, and then the Holy Ghost poured out on the Gentiles. Paul likewise reads the promised seed as Christ (Galatians 3:16).

Jubilees gives the test a backstory like Job's. Prince Mastema, an accusing spirit, tells God that Abraham loves Isaac above everything and should be told to offer him; the angel narrating the story says Mastema was “put to shame” when the knife was stopped. The command comes on the twelfth day of the first month, which brings the third day close to Passover, and Abraham keeps a seven-day festival every year afterward. Jubilees names the mountain as Mount Zion.

Philo answers critics who said Abraham did nothing unusual, since Greeks and barbarians had sacrificed children before him. Others, he replies, acted from custom, fear, or love of glory, and Abraham had none of these motives; Babylon and Chaldea, where he grew up, did not sacrifice children, so the act was not a habit of his homeland. On that point Abraham 1 says the reverse.

Josephus makes Isaac 25 years old and has him help build the altar. Abraham explains the command in a speech, and Isaac answers that he would not deserve to have been born if he refused God and his father, then goes straight to the altar. Josephus adds that Abraham hid the command from Sarah, and has God say he did not desire human blood.

Here Isaac is 37 (one reading has 26), far too strong to be bound against his will, so he asks his father to tie him tightly in case he flinches and spoils the offering. Abraham's tears fall into Isaac's eyes. When Abraham protests that God's commands contradict each other, God answers that he said to bring Isaac up, not to slaughter him, and the midrash applies to Isaac the words of Jeremiah 19:5, “neither came it into my mind.”

Counts the binding as Abraham's tenth trial and also makes Isaac 37. When the blade touched Isaac's neck his soul left him and returned at the voice from heaven, and Isaac learned that the dead will be raised, blessing God “who quickeneth the dead.” The ram, it says, was made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath. The resurrection reading runs parallel to Hebrews 11:19.

On public fast days for rain, the first added blessing ends by asking that he who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah answer the congregation. The Talmud explains the ram's-horn shofar of the New Year the same way: God tells Israel to sound it so that he will remember the binding of Isaac and count it as if they had bound themselves before him.

Hebrews says Abraham offered his “only begotten son” reasoning that God was able to raise him from the dead, and so received him back “in a figure.” James uses the same scene to argue that faith is made complete by works. The two letters draw different lessons from one story, and Jacob 4:5 holds both: obedience counted for righteousness, and a figure of the Son.

A bishop in Asia Minor, best known for a Passover sermon. In fragments kept in a Greek chain-commentary on Genesis, he reads the ram as the Lord, the thicket as the cross, and the place as Jerusalem, and says Christ carried the cross to the hill as Isaac carried the wood. He also marks where the likeness stops: “Christ suffered, and Isaac did not suffer.”

Writes that Abraham readily gave up his only-begotten and beloved son so that God might be pleased to offer his own beloved and only-begotten Son for all Abraham's seed. Christians follow, he says, by “taking up the cross as Isaac did the wood.” It is the same Father-and-Son reading that Jacob 4:5 gives.

In his treatise against the Jews, Tertullian reads Isaac carrying his own wood as an early sign of Christ's death. Later in the same work he pairs the details: Isaac was spared and a ram caught by its horns in the thicket was offered, while Christ carried his wood on his shoulders and wore a crown of thorns. Augustine repeats the thorn reading two centuries later.
traditions.cite: Against the Jews 10, 13; Augustine, City of God 16.32

23.overview:
Sarah dies at 127 in Hebron, and Abraham, who has lived in Canaan for decades without owning any of it, asks the Hittites of the town for a place to bury her. They offer him the pick of their own tombs. He asks instead to buy the cave of Machpelah from Ephron, who offers it as a gift, then names a price of 400 shekels as if it hardly mattered. Abraham weighs out the silver in front of everyone at the city gate, the field and cave become his, and he buries Sarah there.

Nineteen of the twenty verses are about a sale, not a death. The first piece of the promised land that Abraham owns is a grave, and the text records the purchase with the care of a legal deed: parties, price, witnesses, boundaries, even the trees.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC. Sarah dies at 127 (v. 1), when Abraham is 137 and Isaac 37 (17:17; 21:5).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Kirjath-arba, later called Hebron, in the hills of southern Canaan; the field of Machpelah faces Mamre (v. 17). Tradition places the cave beneath the Herodian enclosure in Hebron.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 25:9–10, 49:29–32 and 50:13 look back on the purchase; Acts 7:16 speaks of a tomb Abraham bought at Shechem.

23.hermeneutics:
In 1953 Manfred Lehmann argued that the bargaining reflects Hittite law. Hittite Laws §§46–47 tie feudal service to land: a buyer who takes over a whole holding takes on its duties, while one who buys only part may not. On this reading Abraham wanted only the cave “in the end of his field” (v. 9), and Ephron pressed the whole field on him (v. 11) to be rid of the obligations. Later scholars doubted it, since Genesis never mentions such service and Hittite law belonged to Anatolia. Gene Tucker (1966) pointed instead to Neo-Babylonian sale records written as dialogues, with offer, counteroffer, payment, and a closing description of the property. Either way, the first hearers would recognize a formal sale.

Sales were public. Deals were struck at the city gate before the elders and townsmen (Ruth 4:1, 9), and vv. 10 and 18 stress that all who went in at Ephron's gate heard this one. Silver was weighed, not counted, since coins came centuries later; “current money with the merchant” (v. 16) means silver of the trading standard. Against other biblical prices 400 shekels is steep: Jeremiah pays 17 shekels for a field (Jeremiah 32:9) and David 50 for a threshing floor (2 Samuel 24:24). Ephron's “what is that betwixt me and thee?” is polite bargaining that names a high price.

A “stranger and a sojourner” (v. 4) was a resident alien, someone who lived among a people without a member's right to land. Israel's law later uses the same pair of words for Israel's own standing before God: “the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). A sojourner could not simply take a grave; it had to be granted or sold to him.

breakdown.label: Sarah dies at Hebron; Abraham mourns
First exchange: the Hittites offer their best tomb
Second exchange: Abraham names Machpelah; Ephron offers it free
Third exchange: Abraham insists; 400 shekels weighed out
Field, cave, and trees made sure before witnesses
Sarah buried; the purchase confirmed

structure.summary: Inclusio: three rounds of bargaining framed by Sarah's death and burial, both set at “Hebron in the land of Canaan.”

open.text: Sarah dies in Kirjath-arba, Hebron in the land of Canaan

close.text: Sarah buried before Mamre, Hebron in the land of Canaan

rows.text: Abraham stands up and asks; “bury thy dead” in our tombs
Abraham bows and names the cave; “bury thy dead,” it is a gift
Abraham bows and offers payment; “bury therefore thy dead,” for 400 shekels

notes: **Three rounds:** each opens with Abraham rising or bowing (vv. 3, 7, 12) and ends with the other side telling him to bury his dead (vv. 6, 11, 15). The courtesy never changes; only the terms do.
**Counted words (Hebrew):** “bury” 8 times, “sons of Heth” 8 times, and “give” 7 times, all in vv. 4–13, where the question is whether the land will be given or sold.
**Deed language:** vv. 17–18 and v. 20 repeat that the field and cave were “made sure” to Abraham “for a possession,” the formula of a property record.

Sarah's death begins the closing movement of Abraham's life: a burial ground (ch. 23), a wife for Isaac (ch. 24), and Abraham's own death and burial in the same cave (25:7–10). The unit ends at 25:18, before Isaac's *toledot* at 25:19.

**Forward:** Machpelah becomes the family tomb. Isaac and Rebekah, Leah, and finally Jacob are buried there, and Jacob's dying charge to be laid in “the field of Ephron the Hittite” brings his body back from Egypt (49:29–32; 50:13).

traditions.text: Speaking after news that the missionary Lorenzo Barnes had died in England, Joseph Smith said he wanted an honorable burial beside his father, so that he could greet him at the resurrection. He tied this to the patriarchs: it was on this principle that the ancients were “so particular to have an honorable burial with their fathers,” and he cited Joseph's charge that his bones be carried to Canaan. Abraham's insistence on owning a family grave is the first instance of that concern in Genesis.
traditions.cite: Discourse, 16 April 1843, as reported by Wilford Woodruff, [25]–[26] (Joseph Smith Papers)

traditions.text: In Abraham's account the Lord promises, while Abraham is still in Haran, to give the land to his seed “for an everlasting possession.” Genesis 23 shows how far that is from fulfillment at Sarah's death: the only ground Abraham holds is a cave bought for silver. Stephen draws the same contrast in Acts 7 (below).

Counts Sarah's death and burial as the tenth and last of Abraham's trials, a test of whether he would stay patient and not complain. He bargains “in patience of spirit,” refuses the land as a gift, and says nothing of the promise that the whole land would be his, for which he is written on the heavenly tablets as the friend of God. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer makes the binding of Isaac the tenth trial instead.

Retells the chapter in two sentences: Sarah dies at 127, the Canaanites publicly grant a burying place, and Abraham pays Ephron 400 shekels, after which he and his descendants build their tombs there. In the *Jewish War* he adds what visitors were shown in his own day: monuments of Abraham's family at Hebron, made of very fine marble and finely worked.

Notices that v. 1 gives Sarah's age in three parts, each with its own “years,” and reads them one by one: at a hundred she was as free of sin as at twenty, and at twenty as beautiful as at seven. In “a stranger and a sojourner” (v. 4) it hears a double claim. If the Hittites will sell, Abraham pays as a stranger; if not, he will take the land as a resident, by right of God's promise in 12:7. Rashi passes on both readings.

Explains why Sarah's death follows the binding of Isaac: when she heard that her son had been readied for slaughter and nearly killed, her soul left her and she died. He gives two readings of Kirjath-arba, “city of the four”: four giants lived there, or four couples were buried there, Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 23:2 (from Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 32; Genesis Rabbah 58:4)

traditions.text: The rabbis make Ephron the example of a man who says much and does little. He spoke as if 400 shekels were nothing, then took the full-weight shekels of v. 16, which the Talmud reads as large standard coins (*centenaria*). Rashi notes that Ephron's name is spelled in v. 16 without one of its letters, a sign that something was lacking in him.

Names three places the nations cannot call stolen, because scripture records that they were paid for: the cave of Machpelah (v. 16), the Temple site that David bought from Ornan (1 Chronicles 21:25), and Joseph's tomb at Shechem, bought by Jacob (33:19). The public weighing of the silver becomes a title deed for later generations.

In Stephen's speech God gave Abraham no inheritance in the land, “not so much as to set his foot on,” though he promised it to his seed. Stephen also says the patriarchs were laid in a tomb Abraham bought from the sons of Emmor in Sychem, which merges Machpelah with Jacob's purchase at Shechem (33:19; Joshua 24:32). Augustine follows Stephen in dating Abraham's real possession of the land from this purchase.

Takes up Abraham's description of himself in v. 4. The patriarchs lived in the land of promise as in a strange country and died in faith, confessing that they were “strangers and pilgrims on the earth” and seeking a heavenly country. A grave bought at full price becomes a sign of faith in a promise not yet received.

Describing his friend Paula's pilgrimage, Jerome explains Kirjath-arba as the city of the four men: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and “the great Adam,” whom the Hebrews held, on the strength of Joshua 14:15, to be buried there. Others, he adds, made Caleb the fourth. It is the same tradition Rashi records, with Adam among those buried at Hebron.

24.overview:
Abraham, now old, makes his chief servant swear to find Isaac a wife among his own kin in Mesopotamia and never to take Isaac back there. The servant travels with ten camels to the city of Nahor, stops at the well at evening, and asks God for a sign: the girl who offers water to him and to his camels. Rebekah does just that, and she turns out to be Abraham's great-niece. Her brother Laban welcomes the servant, who tells the whole story over again. The family agrees, Rebekah says “I will go,” and Isaac brings her into Sarah's tent.

At 67 verses this is the longest chapter in Genesis, and much of the length is repetition: the servant retells to Rebekah's family nearly everything the reader has just watched. The small changes in his version show a careful negotiator at work.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC. Isaac is 40 when he marries Rebekah (25:20), three years after Sarah's death.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Abraham's home in Canaan to “Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor” (v. 10), in the Haran region, then back to Isaac in the south country near the well Lahai-roi (v. 62).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: The servant's own retelling (vv. 34–49). Abraham 2:2–5 places Nahor, Milcah, and Terah's household in Haran.

24.hermeneutics:
Israel's storytellers had a stock scene for finding a wife, which Robert Alter calls the betrothal type-scene: a man travels to a foreign land and meets a young woman at a well, water is drawn, she runs home with the news, and a meal and a marriage follow. Jacob meets Rachel this way (29:1–14), and Moses meets Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21). Hearers who knew the pattern would notice what is different here. The groom stays home and a servant stands in for him, and the woman is the one who draws the water, runs, and acts. That fits the Rebekah who later steers Jacob's blessing (ch. 27).

The “city of Nahor” (v. 10) may be a real place as well as a family name. Letters from Mari (18th century BC) and later Assyrian texts name a town called Nahur in the upper Euphrates region near Haran, and nearby towns carry names like Serug's (11:20–23). The servant's long trip north is a trip back to the family's home country, the land Abraham was called to leave.

Marriage in the ancient Near East was a contract between households. Old Babylonian law speaks of a betrothal payment (*terhatum*) brought by the groom's side to the bride's family, and the Laws of Hammurabi (§§159–161) settle what happens if either side backs out after gifts are given. The servant's gold for Rebekah and his “precious things” for her brother and mother (v. 53) fit that pattern. So does Laban's leading role with the mother: Bethuel, the father, speaks only once (v. 50).

At the well of Nahor: the servant asks for a sign
Rebekah waters the camels; gifts and worship
Laban runs out and brings the servant home
The servant retells his mission
The family consents; Rebekah says “I will go”
Isaac meets Rebekah and brings her into Sarah's tent

structure.summary: Parallel panels: the servant's speech (vv. 34–49) retells the first half of the chapter point by point.

left.text: Prayer for a sign at the well

left.label: C
left.text: Rebekah gives water to him and the camels

left.label: D
left.text: Gifts first, then “Whose daughter art thou?”

right.label: D′

left.label: E
left.text: The servant bows and blesses the LORD

notes: **Changes in the retelling:** in the event he gives the gifts before asking her family (vv. 22–23); telling it, he asks first (v. 47), so the family hears of a properly conducted approach. He leaves out Abraham's warning never to take Isaac back (vv. 6, 8) and opens with Abraham's wealth and Isaac as sole heir (vv. 35–36).

**The LORD at every step:** the divine name occurs 19 times in the Hebrew. Prayer (v. 12), praise (v. 27), and worship (vv. 26, 52) mark each stage, and the family's answer is “The thing proceedeth from the LORD” (v. 50).
**A nameless servant:** he is called “servant” 15 times in Hebrew but never named, while the people he serves and meets all are.

The search for Rebekah closes Abraham's active part in the story; his charge to the servant (vv. 2–8) is the last thing he says in Genesis. Isaac meets Rebekah coming from Lahai-roi (v. 62), the well where the angel found Hagar (16:14), and the unit ends with Abraham's death and Ishmael's line (25:1–18).

**Forward:** Jacob also finds his wife at a well in the same family's country (29:1–14). Rebekah's family blesses her that her seed may “possess the gate of those which hate them” (v. 60), close to God's oath to Abraham in 22:17.

traditions.text: Abraham's account says Nahor married Milcah, the daughter of Haran, and that Terah stayed behind in Haran and “turned again unto his idolatry.” That background explains both halves of Abraham's charge: the bride should come from his own kin, but Isaac must not go back to the land and household Abraham was called out of. Abraham 2:6 also records the promise of the land to his seed, which Abraham repeats to the servant in v. 7.

Reads Rebekah at the well as the model teacher. She goes down to the spring of God's wisdom and comes up filled; she carries a pitcher where Hagar carried a bulky skin; she lowers it onto her arm so the learner gets what he can take; and she gives more than the little he asked for. Watering the camels means training memory, since the camel chews its food over again.

Explains the oath under the thigh as both men placing a hand under each other's thigh and calling on God as witness. At the well the other girls refuse the stranger water, saying they need it all at home, and Rebekah rebukes them. She also tells him that her father Bethuel is dead, so Laban and her mother run the household, which would explain why Bethuel hardly appears.

Asks the same question about Bethuel and answers it differently: he tried to block the match and died that night, so the “few days” the family asks for in v. 55 are the week of mourning. From “we will inquire at her mouth” (v. 57) it draws the rule that an orphan girl may be married only with her consent. Josephus has Bethuel dead before the servant arrives; the midrash has him die during the visit.

Notices the chapter's length. The ordinary talk of the patriarchs' servants, it says, is dearer to God than the Torah of their descendants: the story of Abraham's servant fills two or three columns and is told twice, while some laws of purity are learned only from a single extra letter.

With the rabbis, Rashi takes the servant to be Eliezer of Damascus (15:2). In v. 39 the word for “peradventure” is spelled so that it can be read “to me,” and the midrash hears Eliezer hoping Abraham would turn to him and take his own daughter for Isaac. Abraham refuses: his son is blessed, he answers, and Eliezer is under a curse, and the two cannot be joined.

Collects midrashic details the text leaves out. The servant ran to Rebekah because he saw the water rise in the well to meet her; he came “this day” (v. 42) because the road shrank for him and he arrived the day he set out. Isaac was coming from Lahai-roi (v. 62) because he had gone to bring Hagar back to Abraham as a wife, a reading that sets up Rashi's view of Keturah in ch. 25.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 24:17, 42, 62 (from Genesis Rabbah 60:5, 14; Sanhedrin 95a)

traditions.text: Lists Abraham's servant with Saul and Jephthah as three men who asked improperly. His sign at the well could have been met by a lame or blind girl, and he had bound himself to take her for Isaac. God answered him better than he asked, the Talmud says, and sent Rebekah.

Reads Isaac's going out “to meditate in the field at the eventide” (v. 63) as prayer, since the same Hebrew word is used of pouring out a complaint before the LORD in Psalm 102:1. On this basis it credits Isaac with instituting the afternoon prayer, as Abraham did the morning prayer and Jacob the evening prayer.

Fills in why Isaac brings Rebekah into his mother's tent. While Sarah lived, a cloud hung over the tent, its doors stood open to guests, a blessing rested on her dough, and a lamp burned from one Sabbath eve to the next; all four stopped at her death and returned when Rebekah came. Only then, seeing she was like his mother, did Isaac take her in.

Works out the dates: Isaac marries at 40, in Abraham's 140th year, three years after Sarah's death. He then reads the oath with the servant's hand under Abraham's thigh as a sign that the God of heaven and earth would come in the flesh descended from that thigh. For Augustine the custom of the oath becomes a small prophecy of Christ.

25.overview:
Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, and sends her six sons away east with gifts, while everything he owns goes to Isaac. He dies at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah. A short list of Ishmael's twelve sons and his death follows. Then the story turns to Isaac. Rebekah, childless for twenty years, conceives twins who fight inside her, and the LORD tells her that the elder will serve the younger. Esau, red and hairy, grows into a hunter; Jacob, born gripping his heel, stays among the tents. One day Esau comes in starving and sells Jacob his birthright for bread and red lentil stew.

A new heading at v. 19, “these are the generations of Isaac,” splits the chapter in two. Abraham's story ends with v. 18, and Jacob's begins at once, with the brothers' rivalry set before either is born.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places Abraham about 2000–1800 BC. The twins are born when Isaac is 60 (v. 26), so they are 15 when Abraham dies at 175 (21:5; v. 7).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The cave of Machpelah at Hebron (vv. 9–10); Beer-lahai-roi in the south (v. 11); Ishmael's tribes “from Havilah unto Shur,” across northern Arabia toward Egypt (v. 18).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 1:28–34 repeats the lines of Ishmael and Keturah and calls Keturah Abraham's concubine. D&C 132:37 speaks of Abraham's concubines and their children.

25.hermeneutics:
Clay tablets from Nuzi, a 15th–14th century BC town in northern Mesopotamia, were once read as proof that a birthright could be sold. One much-cited contract (JEN 204) has a man hand over his inheritance share in a grove to his brother in exchange for three sheep. Later study pointed out that the tablet never says the seller was the eldest son, and that sales of inheritance shares turn up in other cuneiform texts too. What it does show is that an heir's share was property that could pass between brothers by contract, sealed here, as in v. 33, by a formal act. The stakes were real: Israel's law gives the firstborn a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17), and Esau trades a double share for one meal.

Ishmael's twelve sons (vv. 13–15) are not invented names. Several appear in Assyrian and Babylonian records as north Arabian tribes and oases. Kedar is the Qedarite confederation that fought Assyrian kings in the 8th–7th centuries BC; Tema is the oasis of Tayma, where the Babylonian king Nabonidus later lived for ten years; Dumah is the oasis of Adummatu; Massa and Adbeel appear among Arab groups in the annals of Tiglath-pileser III. Keturah's sons Midian, Sheba, and Dedan likewise belong to the incense routes of Arabia. A first hearer would recognize the desert peoples on Israel's eastern and southern edges, all counted here as Abraham's kin and all sent away from the land.

breakdown.label: Keturah's sons sent east; everything given to Isaac
Abraham dies at 175 and is buried at Machpelah
The generations of Ishmael: twelve princes
The generations of Isaac: twins struggle and are born
Hunter and tent-dweller; each parent's favorite
Esau sells his birthright for red stew

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, cut into three blocks by two *toledot* headings.

rows.text: Abraham's last sons, death, and burial

notes: **Two death notices:** Abraham (v. 8) and Ishmael (v. 17) die in the same words: he “gave up the ghost,” died, and was gathered to his people.
**Twelve again:** Ishmael's sons are twelve “princes” (v. 16), as promised in 17:20. Nahor also had twelve sons (22:20–24), and Jacob will have twelve.

**Red and birthright:** Esau is born “red” (*admoni*, v. 25) and asks for “that same red” stew, the Hebrew word *adom* doubled in v. 30, which gives him the name Edom. “Birthright” (*bekorah*) then comes four times in the closing scene (vv. 31–34).

Verses 1–18 close Abraham's section: his death and burial, then the short *toledot* of Ishmael (25:12), the line set aside, before the chosen line. The *toledot* of Isaac at 25:19 opens the Jacob cycle, which runs to 35:29, where Esau and Jacob bury Isaac together.

**Forward:** the sale of the birthright prepares for the stolen blessing of ch. 27, and the oracle of v. 23 echoes through Israel's history with Edom, down to Malachi 1:2–3. Esau gets his own *toledot* at 36:1.

traditions.text: The revelation on eternal marriage says Abraham received concubines who bore him children, and that this was accounted to him for righteousness because they were given to him; Genesis 25:6 is the passage that speaks of those concubines and their sons. The same verse says that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, having done only what they were commanded, “have entered into their exaltation,” a Restoration word on where Abraham was “gathered” at his death (v. 8).

Abraham calls what he sought “the right of the firstborn,” handed down from Adam through the fathers, and ties it to the priesthood and to the blessings of the fathers. Read beside Genesis 25, it gives the birthright Esau sells a priestly as well as a property meaning. Hebrews 12 makes a similar judgment about what Esau gave away (below).

Makes Keturah a third wife taken from the household servants, after Hagar had died. It adds that Jacob learned to write while Esau learned war, and that Abraham himself loved Jacob, told Rebekah to watch over him, and blessed him as heir of all the promises. Genesis never shows Abraham with the twins; Jubilees makes him the first to choose Jacob.

Sets Abraham's death with Jacob asleep in his arms; the boy wakes, finds his grandfather “cold as ice,” and runs to tell Rebekah. Isaac and Ishmael bury him and the household mourns forty days. Jubilees then asks why a man it calls perfect lived only 175 years when the forefathers lived close to a thousand, and blames the growing wickedness of the generations for shrinking lifespans.

Reads “gathered to his people” (v. 8) as Abraham leaving mortal things to join the people of God, the angels, having received immortality. He calls Rebekah Perseverance and the oracle of v. 23 a picture of the soul pregnant with good and evil, whose cure is that the two be separated.
traditions.cite: On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain 4–5

traditions.text: Says Abraham settled Keturah's sons and grandsons as colonies in Troglodytis and Arabia Felix, and that one grandson conquered Libya, which was later called Africa after him. His retelling of the twins goes straight from their birth to Isaac at Gerar and leaves out the sale of the birthright altogether.

A writer on Jewish history known only through Alexander Polyhistor, as quoted by Josephus. He says three of Keturah's sons gave their names to Assyria and Africa, that two of them fought beside Heracles against Antaeus in Libya, and that Heracles married one son's daughter. Like the Assyrian annals in Hermeneutics, he places Keturah's line among real peoples, though far more freely.

Identifies Keturah with Hagar, renamed because her deeds were sweet as incense and because she kept herself for Abraham after they parted. Jubilees, which has Hagar dead before Sarah, rules this out, so the two traditions give opposite answers to the same question. On v. 22 the midrash explains the struggle in the womb: Jacob strained toward the doors of houses of study, Esau toward the gates of idol temples.

Dates the stew to the day Abraham died: Jacob was cooking lentils, the customary first meal for mourners, for his father Isaac. On that day, Rabbi Yohanan says, Esau committed five sins, the last that he despised the birthright. Rashi adds that God took five years from Abraham's life so he would not see Esau go astray, which is why Abraham dies at 175 and Isaac at 180 (35:28).

Warns readers not to be a “profane person, as Esau,” who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat and afterward could not inherit the blessing though he sought it with tears. The letter joins the sale in ch. 25 to the lost blessing of ch. 27 as one story of trading the future for the present.

Paul cites v. 23 to show that God chose Jacob before either twin had done good or evil. Irenaeus builds on Paul, reading the twins as two peoples and Jacob as a figure of Christ: grasping the heel means victory, and taking the firstborn's rights that his brother despised pictures the younger people receiving Christ when the elder rejected him.

Asks why Abraham married again so late, and suggests Keturah's sons, like Hagar's, stand for those who receive gifts but not the inheritance (v. 6); the marriage also shows, he adds, that a second marriage is no sin. On v. 23 he notes that Christian writers almost all read “the elder shall serve the younger” as the Jews and the Christians, while granting it was also fulfilled when Edom became subject to Israel.

26.overview:
A famine drives Isaac to Gerar, where the LORD tells him not to go down to Egypt and renews to him the oath sworn to Abraham. Afraid of the local men, Isaac says Rebekah is his sister, until King Abimelech sees them together and orders that no one touch them. Isaac's crops yield a hundredfold, and he grows so rich that the Philistines push him out. He reopens his father's wells, which they had stopped, and digs new ones, naming them for the quarrels, until one, Rehoboth, brings no strife. At Beer-sheba the LORD appears again, Abimelech comes to make a treaty, and Isaac's servants strike water. Esau marries two Hittite women.

Almost everything Isaac does here, Abraham did first: famine, a wife passed off as a sister, Abimelech and Phichol, wells, an oath at Beer-sheba. The chapter says outright that Isaac is blessed for Abraham's sake (vv. 5, 24).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Genesis.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Traditional chronology places the patriarchs about 2000–1800 BC. Esau is 40 at the chapter's close (v. 34), so Isaac is about 100 (25:26).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Gerar, in the western Negev between Gaza and Beer-sheba, with its valley and wells (vv. 1, 17); then Beer-sheba (vv. 23, 33).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 12:10–20 and 20:1–18 (Abraham's wife-sister stories) and 21:22–34 (his treaty with Abimelech at Beer-sheba). In Abraham 2:22–25 the Lord himself directs Abraham's version in Egypt.

26.hermeneutics:
Abimelech's alarm in v. 10 matches how Israel's neighbors spoke of adultery. Egyptian marriage documents and texts from Ugarit call it “the great sin,” the phrase Abimelech uses in the parallel story (20:9), and treat it as an offense against the gods as well as the husband. A king who took another man's wife, even unknowingly, could expect the guilt to fall on his whole people, which is exactly his complaint: “thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.”

In the Negev, with little rain and no rivers, a dug well was wealth. Digging and naming a well claimed its water, and stopping a rival's wells with earth (v. 15) was an act of hostility, the same tactic Israel's armies used on enemy land (2 Kings 3:19, 25). Isaac's names for the wells, Esek (“contention”) and Sitnah (“enmity”), then Rehoboth (“room”), record each dispute and its end. The treaty that follows is sealed the way many ancient covenants were, with a shared meal and oaths sworn the next morning (vv. 30–31).

The Philistines known from Egyptian records arrived on the coast in the early 12th century BC: reliefs of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu show him fighting the Peleset among the Sea Peoples, and they settled Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ashdod. Calling Abimelech “king of the Philistines” centuries earlier either uses the name later hearers knew for the people of that coast, or refers to an earlier Aegean group in the region. Either way, Israelite hearers would hear Isaac's quarrels at Gerar as the first round of a long rivalry.

A hundredfold harvest; envy; Isaac sent away

At Beer-sheba the LORD appears; altar and well

Esau's Hittite wives grieve his parents

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, with two appearances of the LORD bracketing Isaac's conflicts at Gerar.

rows.text: The LORD appears at Gerar: the oath renewed, “because that Abraham obeyed”
Trouble with the Philistines: the wife, the harvest, the wells
The LORD appears at Beer-sheba: “for my servant Abraham's sake”

notes: **Wells:** “well” occurs eight times in the Hebrew, not counting the name Beer-sheba, and “dig” seven times. Each new well moves Isaac further from Gerar, from strife to room (v. 22) to the well of the oath (v. 33).
**Abraham everywhere:** Abraham is named eight times in a chapter about Isaac, and both divine speeches ground the blessing in him (vv. 5, 24).

**The third wife-sister story** (after 12:10–20 and 20:1–18). Only here is the wife never taken. Abimelech learns the truth by seeing Isaac “sporting” with Rebekah (v. 8), a play on Isaac's own name, which means “he laughs.”

Chapter 26 is the one chapter given wholly to Isaac, and it sits inside Jacob's story, between the sale of the birthright (25:29–34) and the stolen blessing (ch. 27). Michael Fishbane's reading of the Jacob cycle as a chiasm pairs it with ch. 34, both interludes about dealings with the people of the land.

**Forward:** Esau's Hittite marriages (vv. 34–35) prepare for Rebekah's complaint in 27:46 and Isaac's charge to Jacob not to marry a Canaanite (28:1). Esau's later marriage to Ishmael's daughter (28:8–9) answers the same grief.

traditions.text: In Abraham's account the Lord himself tells Abraham, before he enters Egypt, that the Egyptians will kill him for Sarai's beauty and that she should say she is his sister. Genesis 12 and 20 report no such instruction, and in Genesis 26 Isaac adopts the plan on his own, out of fear (v. 7). The Restoration text changes how the family's practice began, though not how Isaac uses it.

The promise repeated to Isaac in v. 4, that in his seed all nations will be blessed, is explained in Abraham 2 as a priesthood and gospel blessing. Those who receive the gospel are counted as Abraham's seed, and through his seed and priesthood all families receive the blessings of salvation. Genesis 26 shows that promise passing from Abraham to Isaac.

Follows the chapter closely but drops the wife-sister scene; Abimelech simply orders that no one touch Isaac or anything of his. Jubilees adds that Isaac knew he had sworn peace with the Philistines under pressure, and has him curse them “unto the day of wrath and indignation,” a curse that looks ahead to Israel's later wars with the coastal peoples.

Philo read the Greek Bible, where Isaac's servants report at v. 32 that they did not find water. He takes the four wells as the four regions men search, earth, water, air, and heaven: in three they find something they can name, but heaven, the fourth well, stays beyond their reach. Critics who call the account of the wells needless wordiness, he says, miss the point. Jubilees also has one well come up dry, so both follow a text that differs here from the Hebrew.

Also leaves out the wife-sister episode. He makes Abimelech an old friend of Abraham whose kindness turns to envy, explains the well names as strife, enmity, and a large space, and has Isaac keep retreating rather than fight, buying safety by prudence. When Abimelech later fears revenge, it is Isaac's good nature, preferring the old friendship to the recent anger, that makes the treaty possible. Esau's wives become daughters of great Canaanite lords, and Isaac, who disliked the marriages, keeps silent.

The Mishnah closes its tractate on betrothal by saying Abraham kept the whole Torah before it was given, citing v. 5's list of charge, commandments, statutes, and laws. Rashi takes each term in turn and makes the plural “laws” include the Oral Law as well as the written. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer uses the same verse to say Abraham kept every precept.
traditions.cite: Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14; Rashi on Genesis 26:5; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 31

traditions.text: Explains why God forbids Isaac to go to Egypt (v. 2) when Abraham had gone there in his famine: Isaac had been offered on the altar as an unblemished burnt offering, and such an offering may not leave the holy land. The midrash reads the binding of ch. 22 as having changed Isaac's standing for good.

Stresses how unlikely the hundredfold harvest was: the soil of Gerar was hard and it was a famine year, and the yield was counted against an estimate made for tithing. On Esau's marriage at forty, it compares him to the boar of Psalm 80:13, which lies down showing its split hooves as if it were clean: he married at forty to look like his father, who had done the same (25:20). The wives were a grief to Isaac and Rebekah, it adds, because they served idols.

Notes that Isaac, unlike his father, had one wife and no concubine, and that he repeated his father's ruse of calling his wife his sister, and that Rebekah, like Sarah, stayed untouched once the strangers knew she was a wife. He warns against ranking Isaac above Abraham for his single marriage, since God says twice here that he blesses Isaac for Abraham's sake (vv. 5, 24).

The pagan critic Celsus had mocked Genesis for saying God gave wells to the righteous. Origen replies that scripture often uses real events to point to deeper truths, the wells and marriages among them. As proof that the righteous did dig wells in the land of the Philistines, he points to the remarkable wells still shown at Ascalon in his own day. Philo had already answered the same kind of scoffing at these wells (above).

27.overview:
Isaac, old and nearly blind, sends Esau to hunt game so he can eat and bless him before he dies. Rebekah overhears, cooks two kids from the flock, dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes, and covers his arms and neck with goatskin. Isaac is suspicious of the voice but trusts the hands, and blesses Jacob with plenty, rule over nations, and lordship over his brothers. Esau returns too late, weeps for a blessing, and receives a lesser word. He resolves to kill Jacob after Isaac dies, and Rebekah arranges Jacob's escape to Laban.

Isaac does not take the blessing back. Once spoken, it stands: “yea, and he shall be blessed” (v. 33). The whole chapter turns on a word that cannot be recalled, and Esau's question, “Hast thou but one blessing?” (v. 38), is left with only a partial answer.
