historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly proposals run as late as the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC. Counting back from 47:9 (with 41:46, 45:6, 31:41), Jacob is about 77 when he reaches Laban; Rashi, adding fourteen years of study, makes him 63 at the blessing.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Isaac's household in the south, at Beer-sheba (26:23–33; 28:10). Esau has already married two Hittite women, a grief to both parents (26:34–35).

27.hermeneutics:
Speech by the head of a household carried legal force in the ancient Near East. E. A. Speiser compared Genesis 27 with tablets from Nuzi (15th–14th century BC) in which a father's spoken statement was upheld in court, and in one case (AASOR 16 56) the father grasped his son's hand as he spoke. Later study has trimmed Speiser's claims: none of these texts is a paternal blessing, and the point of contact is narrower. Oral declarations counted when made with recognized gestures and before witnesses. Read that way, Isaac's checks are not idle. He asks Jacob to come near so he can feel him, then to kiss him, and only then blesses (vv. 21–27). The procedure is complete, so when Esau arrives Isaac can only confirm what he has done.

The blessings are also about nations. Israel's first hearers knew Edom as Esau's people (36:1), a neighbor that David brought under garrison so that “all they of Edom became David's servants” (2 Samuel 8:14). Under Joram of Judah, Edom revolted and set up its own king, and the writer of Kings adds that it stayed free “unto this day” (2 Kings 8:20–22). Isaac's words to Esau, that he will serve his brother and one day break his yoke from his neck (v. 40), would have sounded to them like that history told in advance. The family quarrel and the later border wars between Judah and Edom are read together.

breakdown.label: Isaac sends Esau to hunt before the blessing
Rebekah's plan: kids, Esau's clothes, goatskins
Jacob before Isaac: the voice, the hands, the blessing
Esau returns: Isaac trembles; a lesser blessing
Esau plans murder; Rebekah sends Jacob to Laban
Rebekah to Isaac: the daughters of Heth
Isaac blesses Jacob knowingly and sends him away

structure.summary: A run of two-person scenes. No strong pattern beyond that; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: Each scene puts two characters on stage. Jacob and Esau never appear together; they nearly cross in v. 30, as Jacob is “yet scarce gone out.” Rendsburg notes this and counts 28:1–5 (Isaac and Jacob) as a seventh scene.

**Repetition to watch:** the root “bless” (*barak*) occurs 23 times in the chapter, 17 as a verb and 6 as the noun “blessing.” “Come near” (*nagash*) occurs 6 times in vv. 21–27 as Isaac tests his son. Rebekah says “obey my voice” three times (vv. 8, 13, 43).
**Wordplay:** Esau's complaint in v. 36 sets “my birthright” (*bekorati*) beside “my blessing” (*birkati*), two words that differ by the order of their letters.

The Jacob story opens with “the generations of Isaac” (25:19) and runs to Esau's own *toledot* heading at 36:1. Within it, 27:1–28:9 is one unit: the blessing is stolen, Isaac knowingly repeats it (28:1–5), and Esau's marriage closes the episode (28:6–9). Rendsburg pairs this unit with ch. 33, where Jacob, returning, bows to Esau and presses on him a “blessing” (33:11).
**Echoes:** Jacob deceives his father with a goat and his brother's garment; years later his sons deceive him with a kid of the goats and Joseph's coat (37:31–33).

traditions.text: Retells the scene closely but trims Jacob's lie: he says only that he is Isaac's son, never that he is Esau. Isaac fails to recognize him because it was “a dispensation from heaven to remove his power of perception.” Esau's blessing turns harsher: his dwelling will be far from the dew of heaven, and if he throws off his brother's yoke he will sin unto death and his seed will be rooted out.

Fills in the end of the chapter. Rebekah learns of Esau's threat in a dream. Jacob at first refuses to run, boasting that if Esau tries to kill him he will kill Esau, and then refuses to leave his blind father without being sent. Rebekah answers with the line from v. 45, that she will not be bereft of both sons in one day, and goes to Isaac herself, as in v. 46.

Treats the blessing as a prayer. Isaac wants a meal so that he may then pray for his son, and Josephus composes the prayer, addressed to the “Lord of all ages, and Creator of all substance.” When Esau arrives Isaac falls silent, because his prayers have been spent on Jacob. Esau is promised excellence in hunting, strength, and arms, and glory for his descendants, though he will still serve his brother.

An Aramaic paraphrase that dates the scene to the night of 14 Nisan, the eve of Passover, when “the treasures of the dew are opened,” which suits a blessing that begins with dew (v. 28). The fine garments Rebekah puts on Jacob had once been Adam's; Genesis Rabbah, cited by Rashi, says instead that Esau had coveted them from the hunter Nimrod. In v. 41 Esau decides not to repeat Cain's mistake of killing his brother while their father still lived.
traditions.cite: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 27:1, 15, 41; Rashi on 27:15

traditions.text: Shares the Targum's setting: Passover night, when the treasuries of dew open. Rebekah's two kids are explained as one for the Passover offering and one for Isaac's meal. Isaac's words in v. 22 become a motto: the voice of Jacob is the study of Torah and the confession of one God, the hands of Esau are bloodshed. Rabbi Judah counts ten blessings in vv. 28–29, matching the ten sayings of creation.

Asks why Isaac's eyes were dim and gives several answers. God dimmed them so that Isaac would not hear people in the market call him the father of the wicked Esau. Or, when Abraham bound Isaac on the altar, the angels wept and their tears fell into his eyes. Or Isaac looked up at the Divine Presence from the altar; the Targum gives this last answer, saying he saw the Throne of Glory.

Reads later history as repayment. Jacob made Esau cry out “with a great and exceeding bitter cry” (v. 34), and the same words return when Mordecai cries out in Shushan (Esther 4:1). Rabbi Yohanan reads Isaac's “with subtilty” (*mirmah*, v. 35) in Jacob's favor, as the wisdom of his Torah.

Repunctuates Jacob's answer in v. 19 so it is not a lie: “I am” the one bringing you food, and “Esau is thy firstborn.” On v. 27 he notes that washed goatskins smell foul, so the fragrance Isaac smelled must have been the Garden of Eden entering with Jacob. Jubilees, by a different route, also keeps Jacob from saying he is Esau.

Uses Esau as a warning: he sold his birthright for one meal, and afterward, when he wanted the blessing, he was rejected and “found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” The same letter lists Isaac's blessing of both sons, about things still to come, among the acts of faith.

Reads Jacob's life as a pattern of Christ and the church. As Jacob took away Esau's blessing, the later people took the blessings of the former, and as Esau plotted against his brother, the church suffers the same from its opponents.

Denies that Jacob's guile was fraud, pointing to 25:27, where Jacob is a “plain” man, a word some Latin writers rendered “without guile.” He reads the blessing as Christ's: the field's fragrance is the odor of Christ's name, and the grain and wine are the sacrament. He also notes that Isaac, though startled, does not complain of being deceived but confirms the blessing at once.

28.overview:
Isaac blesses Jacob a second time, now knowingly, passing on “the blessing of Abraham” and sending him to his mother's family in Paddan-aram for a wife. Esau sees it and takes a daughter of Ishmael as a further wife. On the road north Jacob sleeps in the open with a stone at his head and dreams of a stairway reaching heaven, with God's messengers going up and down on it. The LORD stands above it and repeats the promises of land, offspring, and blessing to all families, and adds his own: “I am with thee.” Jacob wakes afraid, sets the stone up as a pillar, anoints it, names the place Bethel, “house of God,” and vows a tenth.

The promise comes to Jacob at his lowest point, alone and on the run, before he has done anything to earn it. His vow, by contrast, is conditional: “If God will be with me” (v. 20).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC, on Jacob's way to the twenty years he spends with Laban (31:41).

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Beer-sheba toward Haran (v. 10). Bethel, earlier called Luz (v. 19), lies in the hill country where Abraham had built an altar (12:8).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: God appears again at Bethel in 35:1–15, with a second pillar and the name Israel; Hosea 12:4 recalls it. Esau's wives: 26:34–35; 36:2–3, where Ishmael's daughter is called Bashemath.

28.hermeneutics:
The word for Jacob's “ladder,” *sullam*, appears only here in the Hebrew Bible. Its likely Akkadian cognate, *simmiltu*, means a stair or ladder, and it shows up in the myth of Nergal and Ereshkigal as the long stairway that the messenger Namtar climbs from the underworld to the gate of the high gods. A ziggurat at Sippar carried a name about a stairway to heaven. Against that background Jacob sees a stair, not a ladder for him to climb, with messengers (*mal'akhim*) going about their business between heaven and earth. His waking words fit the same world: this is a “house of God” and a “gate of heaven” (v. 17). The difference is that the stair is not built by human hands, and the LORD speaks from it to a sleeping man.

Standing stones (*matsevot*) marked holy places across Canaan, and Jacob's anointed pillar is one of them. Later law tells Israel to break down the Canaanites' pillars and forbids setting one up (Exodus 23:24; Deuteronomy 16:22, where KJV has “image”). Bethel itself became the royal shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam set up a golden calf, and Amos was told not to prophesy there because it was “the king's chapel” (1 Kings 12:29; Amos 7:13). Israelite hearers would have known Bethel both as Jacob's holy place and as a center of worship the prophets condemned. The story gives the place its first meaning: here God met Jacob, and the stone is a witness to a vow.

breakdown.label: Isaac blesses Jacob with Abraham's blessing; sends him away
Esau marries Mahalath, Ishmael's daughter
Night on the road: a stone at his head
The dream: stairway, messengers, and the LORD's promise
Jacob wakes: house of God, gate of heaven
The stone anointed as a pillar; Luz renamed Bethel
Jacob's vow and promised tenth

structure.summary: Two short episodes, then the Bethel dream. No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: **Key word:** “place” (*maqom*) occurs 6 times in vv. 10–22, 3 of them in v. 11 alone. An unnamed spot becomes a named one (v. 19).
**The dream report** uses “behold” (*hinneh*) 4 times (twice in v. 12, then vv. 13, 15): a stair, messengers, the LORD, and “I am with thee.”

**The stone:** it is put at Jacob's head (*mera'ashotav*, v. 11), set up as a pillar with oil on its “top” (*rosh*, v. 18), and promised as God's house (v. 22). The same word *rosh* names the stair's top that reaches heaven (v. 12).

Verses 1–9 close the blessing story that began in 27:1: Isaac's second blessing undoes nothing of the first, and Esau's marriage ends the scene. Verse 10 starts the journey out. God meets Jacob at Bethel on the way out and at Peniel on the way back (32:30), and messengers of God appear at both ends of the journey (28:12; 32:1–2).
**Echoes:** God sends Jacob back to Bethel to build an altar (35:1–15). Jesus tells Nathanael he will see the angels of God “ascending and descending upon the Son of man” (John 1:51).

traditions.source: Joseph Smith, as recorded in his History
traditions.text: In a Nauvoo sermon he tied Jacob's ladder to Paul's ascent into the third heaven, saying Paul “could understand the three principal rounds of Jacob's Ladder,” which he named the telestial, terrestrial, and celestial glories. The wording comes from the compiled History; Willard Richards's notes taken that day record only “Ladder and rainbow.” The reading joins Genesis 28 to the three kingdoms of D&C 76.
traditions.cite: History, 1838–1856, vol. D-1, p. 1556; 2 Corinthians 12:2; D&C 76

traditions.text: An apostle writing on temples, he read Bethel as a temple scene: Jacob saw himself at the foot of a ladder reaching to the Lord, and the covenants he made there were the rungs he himself would have to climb to reach the promised blessings. He concluded that temples are to Latter-day Saints what Bethel was to Jacob.

Adds a scene before the journey: Rebekah weeps after Jacob, and Isaac, calling her “my sister,” comforts her that Jacob is an upright and perfect man who will return in peace. Jubilees dates Jacob's arrival at Luz to the new moon of the first month and has him sleep under a tree. His pillar is set up “for a sign.”

Jacob hates the Canaanites and will not lodge with them, so he sleeps outdoors on a heap of stones. Josephus has the figures on the ladder only descending, “more excellent than human,” and gives God a long, encouraging speech. He translates Bethel for Greek readers as *Theia Hestia*, “the divine hearth.”

Offers readings side by side. The ladder is the altar ramp, with the high priests going up and down. Or it is Sinai, since *sullam* and *Sinai* have the same numerical value (130), with Moses and Aaron as the messengers. One rabbi reads “on it” as “on him”: the angels went up to see Jacob's likeness engraved on high, then came down to find him asleep.

Names the ascending angels: the two who had visited Sodom, banished for revealing divine secrets, had walked with Jacob to Bethel. They went up and called the others to come see “Jakob the pious, whose likeness is inlaid in the throne of glory,” and the rest came down to look. It shares Genesis Rabbah's idea of Jacob's image on high.

Sees the angels as the guardian princes of empires. Babylon's climbs seventy rungs and comes down, Media's fifty-two, Greece's one hundred eighty, and Edom's keeps climbing until God promises to bring it down. In another version Jacob is invited to climb, fears he too will fall, and does not go up.

Explains why v. 11 has “stones” and v. 18 “the stone”: the stones quarreled over which would hold the righteous man's head, and merged into one. It also says the sun set early so Jacob would stay the night, and the road shrank for him. Rashi adds that the ladder's midpoint stood over the future Temple.

Works out Jacob's age from Ishmael's death, which he reads into 28:9: Jacob was 63 when he left home. Since the numbers in 31:41 and 47:9 require him to be 77 on arrival at Laban's, Rashi concludes that Jacob spent fourteen years studying at the school of Eber on the way.

Jesus meets Nathanael, whom he calls an Israelite without guile, and promises that he will see heaven open and God's angels ascending and descending “upon the Son of man.” Jesus takes the place of the ladder, or of Jacob himself, as Genesis Rabbah's “on him” reading would have it. The guileless Israelite is a pointed contrast with Jacob the deceiver.

In his debate with Trypho, Justin puts the ladder in a list of Old Testament figures of the wooden cross, beside Moses' rod and the tree of life. He argues that the God who stood above the ladder was not the Father, and he reads the anointed stone as a sign of Christ, the Anointed, citing Psalm 45:7, “God, thy God, hath anointed thee.”

Insists Jacob was not worshiping the stone when he poured oil on it. Since “Christ” comes from chrism, anointing, the act points to Christ, and Augustine links it to Jesus' words to Nathanael in John 1. He makes the same argument against the Manichaeans, calling the stone at Jacob's head Christ the head of man.

29.overview:
Jacob reaches a well near Haran where shepherds wait for all the flocks before rolling away its heavy stone. When Rachel arrives with her father's sheep, Jacob rolls the stone away alone, waters her flock, kisses her, and weeps. Laban welcomes him and asks his wages; Jacob offers seven years for Rachel. On the wedding night Laban brings Leah instead. In the morning Jacob protests, and Laban answers that the younger is not given before the firstborn. Jacob finishes Leah's wedding week, receives Rachel, and serves seven more years. The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and gives her four sons.

The deceiver is deceived. Jacob, who passed himself off as the firstborn to a father who could not see, is fooled in the dark with a firstborn daughter. His protest, “wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?” (v. 25), uses the same root as Isaac's word for what Jacob did to Esau, “subtilty” (27:35).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC. The chapter spans Jacob's first fourteen years with Laban (vv. 20, 30; 31:41).

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Haran in Paddan-aram, “the land of the people of the east” (v. 1), home of Abraham's brother Nahor's family (v. 5; 24:10).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Hosea 12:12 recalls that Israel “served for a wife.” D&C 132:1, 37 names Jacob among the patriarchs whose plural marriages the Lord justified.

29.hermeneutics:
Marriage in the ancient Near East was a contract between families. In Hammurabi's laws the groom pays a bride-price to the bride's father (King translates it “purchase price”), and the bride brings a dowry; the laws settle the two together if a wife dies childless (§§163–164). Jacob arrives with nothing to pay, so his labor stands in for the price: seven years, then seven more. Old Babylonian marriage contracts also list a slave woman among the bride's dowry goods, as Rebekah left home with her nurse and maids (24:59, 61). Laban's gifts of Zilpah to Leah and Bilhah to Rachel (vv. 24, 29) are that dowry, and they matter in the next chapter, where both maids bear Jacob's sons. Later, Leah and Rachel will accuse their father of having “sold” them and used up what was paid (31:15).

Israel's own law later forbade a man to take his wife's sister as a rival wife while the first was alive (Leviticus 18:18). Hearers who knew that law would hear the trouble in this marriage from the start: two sisters married to one man, one loved and one “hated” (v. 31), each counting sons against the other. The text does not comment, and Jacob's family does not follow a law that has not yet been given, but the rivalry it describes is exactly what that law aimed to prevent.

Seven years' service for Rachel
The wedding night: Leah given instead

structure.summary: A well scene, a contract, a deception, then the first births. No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: **Key words:** “serve” (*'abad*) occurs 6 times in vv. 15–30, from Laban's question about wages to the second seven years. In vv. 1–14 the “well” appears 7 times, the “stone” 5 times.
**Reversal:** Laban's excuse in v. 26 sets the “younger” beside the “firstborn” (*bekirah*), the very order Jacob had overturned with Esau.
**Naming:** each of Leah's sons gets a short speech that plays on his name and calls on “the LORD” (vv. 32, 33, 35); her hopes move from being loved, to being joined, to praise.
Rendsburg's outline of the Jacob cycle labels 29:1–30 “arrival at Haran” and pairs it with Jacob's flight from Haran in ch. 31.

The Haran years run from Jacob's arrival (29:1) to his parting from Laban (31:55), inside the larger journey from Bethel to Peniel (28:10–32:32). Verses 31–35 begin the birth account that runs to 30:24.

**Echoes:** a stranger meets a future wife at a well in 24:11–20 (Rebekah) and Exodus 2:15–21 (Zipporah). Leah, the unloved wife, becomes the mother of Levi and Judah, the lines of Israel's priests and kings. At Ruth's wedding the elders bless the bride to be like Rachel and Leah, “which two did build the house of Israel” (Ruth 4:11).

traditions.text: The revelation opens by answering Joseph Smith's question about how the Lord justified Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, with Moses, David, and Solomon, in having many wives and concubines. It says Isaac and Jacob “did none other things than that which they were commanded,” and have entered into their exaltation. Genesis frames Jacob's two marriages as Laban's trick; the revelation treats them as within the law.

Has Jacob tell Laban to take his daughter back, and then turns Laban's excuse into law. It is written on the heavenly tablets that no one should give a younger daughter before the elder, and Moses is told to command Israel accordingly. Jubilees describes Leah's eyes as weak but her form very handsome, and dates Reuben's birth to the fourteenth day of the ninth month.

Rachel arrives at the well as the shepherds are wondering why she is late, and Jacob explains their kinship at length. Josephus explains the switch plainly: Jacob was “in drink and in the dark.” Laban apologizes, pleading necessity. Josephus adds that Laban had promised to make Jacob head shepherd and wanted to keep his daughter from marrying among the Canaanites.

Builds a pattern from wells: whoever meets young women coming out of a town will prosper, as with Abraham's servant, Moses, Saul, and Jacob. Jacob rolls the stone away alone, and the water rises to meet him. It explains why Rachel was tending the sheep: God had sent a plague on Laban's flocks before Jacob came, so that Jacob's arrival would bring increase.

Jacob rolls the stone away “with one of his arms,” and the well rises to its brim and keeps rising for twenty years, the length of his stay. At the feast Laban reminds the townsmen that the wells have not failed since Jacob came and asks for “cunning counsel” to keep him; the plan is Leah. Leah's eyes are moist from weeping and praying not to be given to Esau.

Asks why Jacob wept at the well and why Laban ran to kiss him. Jacob wept because he came empty-handed, unlike Abraham's servant with his ten camels; Esau's son Eliphaz had overtaken him on the road and taken everything. Laban ran out expecting gold, embraced him to feel for coins, and kissed him in case he carried pearls in his mouth.

Leah's eyes were “tender” from weeping. People said the elder daughter would go to the elder son and the younger to the younger, and Leah prayed not to fall to the wicked Esau. Rav Huna concludes that prayer overturned the decree, and she even married before her sister. Rashi repeats the explanation.

Turns the wedding into a town conspiracy. Laban tells his neighbors the water has been blessed since Jacob came, and they agree to trick him into staying seven more years. At the feast they sing “ha laya,” a pun on “she is Leah,” and cover the lamps. In the morning Jacob calls Leah a deceiver, daughter of a deceiver, and she answers that his father called him Esau and he answered too.

Explains how Jacob was fooled. He had agreed on secret signs with Rachel, but when she saw Leah being led in, she gave the signs to her sister so Leah would not be shamed, and for that modesty she was rewarded with King Saul among her descendants. Rashi later says that God “remembered Rachel” (30:22) for this same act, while Genesis Rabbah 70:19 tells the night differently, with Leah answering to Rachel's name.

Answers Jewish teachers who cited Jacob to allow several wives. Justin says Jacob's marriages were types, not models: Leah is the synagogue and Rachel the church, and Christ serves for both as Jacob served for both. Leah's weak eyes stand for weak spiritual sight. He also states that it was not lawful for Jacob to marry two sisters at once.

Defends Jacob against the Manichaeans: having several wives was no crime when it was the custom and no law forbade it. In the City of God he adds that Jacob kept Leah, though she was given to him by fraud, so as not to put her to shame. Elsewhere he reads Leah's name as “suffering” and her weak eyes as the labor of the active life.

30.overview:
Rachel, still childless, gives Jacob her maid Bilhah, who bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah answers with her maid Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Reuben finds mandrakes, and Rachel buys them from Leah with a night with Jacob; Leah conceives Issachar, then Zebulun, then a daughter, Dinah. At last God remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph. Jacob then asks to go home. Laban asks him to name his wages, and Jacob asks only for the speckled, spotted, and dark animals born from now on. Laban removes all such animals, but Jacob's peeled rods and selective breeding make the marked young many and strong, and Jacob grows rich.

Every son gets a name with a reason, spoken by his mother. The names record the sisters' rivalry as it happens: “With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister” (v. 8). The chapter turns at Joseph's birth (v. 25), when the story shifts from wives to wages.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC. Joseph's birth ends Jacob's fourteen years of service for his wives; the flock bargain covers the last six years (31:41).

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. The naming speeches play on the Hebrew sound of each name.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Laban's household and pastures near Haran in Paddan-aram.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jacob's sons listed by mother in 35:23–26 and 46:8–27. D&C 132:34, 37 compares Sarah's giving Hagar to Abraham and counts Jacob's marriages as commanded.

30.hermeneutics:
A barren wife could give her husband a slave woman to bear children for her, and the practice appears in law and contract. Hammurabi's laws assume it and protect the wife's rank: the slave who has borne children may not claim equality with her mistress (§§144–147). A Nuzi adoption contract (HSS 5 67) requires a childless wife to provide a slave woman and gives the wife authority over the children. Rachel's words fit this world. Bilhah will bear “upon my knees,” and Rachel says, literally, “I shall be built up” from her (v. 3), the same phrase Sarah used of Hagar (16:2). The sons count as Rachel's and Leah's, which is why the mothers, not the maids, name them.

Mandrakes were famous in the ancient world as a love charm. Theophrastus (4th century BC) reports that the root was used for love potions and that those who dug it were told to speak of love while cutting. The Hebrew *duda'im* sounds like *dodim*, “love,” and the Song of Songs pairs mandrakes with lovers' gifts (Song 7:13). Rachel wants them as a fertility aid. The story's answer is pointed: Leah, who gave the mandrakes away, conceives, and Rachel conceives only when “God remembered Rachel” (v. 22).

In the Levant most sheep were white and most goats dark; the Song of Songs pictures hair like a flock of goats and teeth like newly washed sheep (Song 4:1–2). Jacob's request for only the speckled and dark-marked animals sounded like a tiny wage, which is why Laban agrees at once (v. 34).

rows.text: Oracle fulfilled, struggle in childbirth, Jacob becomes Israel

notes: **Naming formula:** “called his name” occurs 12 times from 29:32 to 30:24, for eleven sons and Dinah. Leah's first speeches call on “the LORD” (YHWH); from 30:2 to 30:23 the narrative says “God” (*Elohim*) nine times, and “the LORD” returns only in Joseph's name (v. 24).

**Hire:** the root *s-k-r* (“hire,” “wages”) occurs 6 times: Leah has “hired” Jacob with the mandrakes (v. 16, twice) and names Issachar for her “hire” (v. 18); then Jacob bargains for his own “hire” (vv. 28, 32, 33).
**Wordplay:** Laban's name is the Hebrew for “white,” and Jacob beats him by peeling white streaks (*lavan*) in rods of poplar (*livneh*, v. 37).

The birth account runs from 29:31 to 30:24; the wage story starts at v. 25 and carries into ch. 31, where Laban's sons complain that Jacob has taken their father's wealth (31:1). Benjamin, the twelfth son, is born only after the return, on the road near Bethlehem (35:16–19).

**Echoes:** the sons named here become the tribes of Israel (49:1–28). Rachel, who cried “Give me children, or else I die” (v. 1), dies giving birth to Benjamin (35:16–19); Jeremiah 31:15 hears her weeping for her children.

traditions.text: Explains Sarah's giving Hagar to Abraham as obedience to God's law and says Abraham was not under condemnation for it. It goes on to say that Isaac and Jacob “did none other things than that which they were commanded,” which places Rachel's and Leah's gifts of their maids in the same light. Genesis itself only reports the rivalry.

Dates every birth to the day and year, so that the sons' births overlap across the four mothers; Reuben comes first, and Joseph's birth falls in the same year as Zebulun's. It makes Zebulun and Dinah twins and says Leah gave Issachar to a nurse. Jacob's wage is the lambs and kids born black, spotted, and white, and Laban and his sons, envious, take back the sheep and watch Jacob with evil intent.

Gives each name a meaning for Greek readers: Dan is “divine judgment,” Naphtali “unconquerable in stratagems,” since Rachel outwitted her sister's fruitfulness, Gad “fortune,” and Issachar one “born by hire.” Reuben brings “apples of mandrakes,” Rachel longs to eat them, and she yields Jacob for the night to soften her sister's anger. Josephus also insists the maids were by no means slaves, though subject to their mistresses.

Issachar tells his own birth story. Rachel did not eat the mandrakes but offered them in the house of the Lord, and God gave her two sons because she wanted Jacob for the sake of children, not pleasure. Leah's six sons and Rachel's two are thus both explained by the mandrakes. Augustine, centuries later, also doubted the fruit had any power.

Records disagreement over what *duda'im* were: mandrakes, barley, or the fruit of a tree. All agree Reuben picked only from ownerless land, since it was harvest and he would not take another's grain, and that he brought them to his mother before tasting them. Rashi identifies the plant as violets, called jasmine in Arabic.

Explains the rods as working through sight: the ewe saw the peeled rods at the trough, startled, and bore young that looked like them. The rabbis illustrate with a story of an Ethiopian couple who had a white son, explained by white portraits in their house. Rabbi Huna offers another cause, reading 31:12 to mean that angels carried rams from Laban's flock into Jacob's.

Reads Dinah's name, from *din* “judgment,” as Leah's verdict on herself. Knowing twelve tribes would come from Jacob and that she and the maids had already borne ten, she reasoned that another son would leave Rachel with fewer than a maid. Her unborn child was changed to a daughter. Rashi adds that Rachel, naming Joseph, asked for just one more son for the same reason.

Dates the mandrakes to the month of Sivan, at wheat harvest. Its version of Dinah's birth goes further than the Talmud's: after Leah's prayer the unborn children were exchanged, Joseph given to Rachel's womb and Dinah to Leah's. When Joseph is born, Jacob says by the Holy Spirit that the house of Joseph will be a flame to consume the house of Esau, an echo of Obadiah 18, and so he no longer fears Esau.

Reads the two flocks as two kinds of mind. Laban's flock “devoid of all distinctive marks” is matter without quality, and the uneducated soul that takes such matter for its gods. Jacob presides over the marked and many-colored flock, the mind that has been shaped by learning and knows that a Creator stamped every species with its form.

Reads the many-colored sheep as Christ's wages: people of every nation gathered into one company of faith, as the Father promised the Son the nations for his inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Jacob's sons by two sisters and two maids show that Christ raises up children of God from free and slave alike, giving all the same Spirit. Justin had already made the speckled-sheep comparison.

Reports that he once saw a mandrake and examined it by sight, smell, and taste: a nice-looking, sweet-smelling, but insipid fruit. He doubts it makes barren women fruitful, since Leah, not Rachel, conceived after the trade, and Leah bore two more children before God opened Rachel's womb. He then reads the fruit as good reputation, which the scholar must earn by taking up active work.

31.overview:
Laban's sons resent Jacob's wealth, Laban turns cold, and the LORD tells Jacob to go home. Jacob tells Rachel and Leah how God gave him their father's flocks, and they agree to leave. While Laban is away shearing, Jacob slips off with family and herds, and Rachel steals her father's household gods. Laban catches up in the hills of Gilead, warned by God in a dream not to harm Jacob. He accuses Jacob of theft; Jacob, not knowing, invites a search, and Rachel hides the gods in her camel saddle and sits on them. Jacob lays out twenty years of hard service. The two men raise a pillar and a heap of stones as witness, swear not to cross it to do harm, eat together, and part.

Theft runs through the chapter, and the closing covenant is a boundary between two men who no longer trust each other: “The LORD watch between me and thee” (v. 49).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC, at the end of Jacob's twenty years with Laban (vv. 38, 41).

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. Laban's name for the heap, Jegar-sahadutha (v. 47), is Aramaic, the first Aramaic words in the Bible; Jacob's Galeed means the same, “heap of witness.”

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Laban's pastures near Haran across “the river” (the Euphrates) to the hill country of Gilead east of the Jordan, after a seven days' pursuit (vv. 21–23).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jacob's own account of the flock years (vv. 7–12) credits God and a dream, where 30:31–43 describes his rods. Hosea 12:12 recalls his flight and service.

31.hermeneutics:
Rachel's theft of the *teraphim*, her father's household gods (v. 30), was once explained from the Nuzi tablets. Sidney Smith in 1926, followed by Cyrus Gordon and E. A. Speiser, argued that possessing the family gods secured a claim to a father's estate, so Rachel was grabbing an inheritance for Jacob. Moshe Greenberg (1962) and M. J. Selman, in his 1974 Tyndale lecture, undercut the theory. In the Nuzi wills the gods usually go to the eldest son as part of a property already assigned, and holding them gave no claim by itself; Jacob, moreover, wants distance from Laban, not his estate. The theory is now widely doubted, and the text itself gives Rachel no motive.

Herding had its own law. Hammurabi's code sets a hired shepherd's duties: if an animal is killed by a lion or by an act of god, the shepherd swears his innocence and the owner bears the loss (§266). Exodus 22:13 is the same: bring the torn remains as evidence and owe nothing. Jacob claims he did more than the law required. What beasts tore he never brought to Laban: “I bare the loss of it” (v. 39).

The covenant terms also follow known forms. Laban's demand that Jacob take no other wives besides his daughters (v. 50) matches a clause found in marriage contracts from the Old Assyrian period on, including Nuzi, protecting a wife's position. Each man swears by his family's god: Laban by the God of Abraham and of Nahor, Jacob by “the fear of his father Isaac” (v. 53).

breakdown.label: Laban's sons complain; the LORD says return
Jacob's case to Rachel and Leah; they agree
Flight; Rachel steals the household gods
Laban pursues; God warns him in a dream
Laban's accusation; the search; Rachel sits on the gods
Jacob's defense: twenty years of service
Covenant: pillar, heap, Galeed and Mizpah
Boundary oath, sacrifice, meal; Laban goes home

structure.summary: Flight, pursuit, dispute, treaty. No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: **Key word:** “steal” (*ganab*) occurs 8 times: Rachel steals the gods (v. 19), Jacob “stole away unawares,” literally stole Laban's heart (vv. 20, 26, 27), Laban asks who stole his gods (vv. 30, 32), and Jacob says he made good what was stolen by day or night (v. 39).
**The gods** (*teraphim*) are named 3 times (vv. 19, 34, 35); Laban also calls them “my gods” (v. 30). Jacob's oath that the thief “let him not live” (v. 32) hangs over the rest of Rachel's story.
**The treaty** repeats “heap” (*gal*) 7 times and “witness” (*'ed*) 4 times in vv. 44–52. Jacob sets up a second pillar (*matsevah*, v. 45), as at Bethel (28:18).

The chapter ends the Haran years that began at the well in 29:1; Laban leaves the story at v. 55, and in 32:1–2 God's messengers meet Jacob as they did at Bethel. Rendsburg pairs this flight from Haran with the arrival in ch. 29. God speaks as “the God of Beth-el” (v. 13), tying the return to the vow of 28:20–22.
**Echoes:** at Shechem Jacob has his household give up their foreign gods and buries them (35:2–4). Gilead and Mizpah reappear as Jephthah's home and meeting place (Judges 11:11).

traditions.text: Tells the flight briefly and leaves out Rachel's theft entirely. Jacob speaks kindly to his wives, and they answer that they will go with him to every place he goes. Laban overtakes Jacob, Jacob makes a feast, and each swears not to cross the mountain of Gilead to harm the other. Jubilees adds that Gilead had earlier been the land of the Rephaim, giants seven to ten cubits tall whom the Lord destroyed for their wickedness.

Says Jacob had taught Rachel to despise such gods, so she took them for another reason: if her father caught them, she could use the images to win his pardon. Laban searches, and gives up because he does not suppose his daughter in that condition would go near the images. The men swear on a hill and set up a pillar “in the form of an altar.”

Describes what the teraphim were: the head of a slain firstborn, salted and spiced, with incantations written on a gold plate under its tongue, set in a wall where it spoke, and Laban bowed to it. The well that had overflowed for twenty years stopped when Jacob left, which is how the shepherds knew he had fled (v. 22). Jacob heads for Gilead because he foresees that deliverance will come from there in the days of Jephthah, and he names the heap Galeed “in the holy tongue.”

Gives the same grim description of the teraphim and adds a reason for the theft: Rachel took them so they could not tell Laban that Jacob had fled. Jacob's curse on the thief was the word of a righteous man, so Rachel died early, in childbirth (35:18). It also reads the heap as a boundary that later bound David until he broke the pillar.

Credits Rachel with good intentions: she would not leave the old man in his corruption, so she took his idols to wean him from them. Rashi repeats this reading. Josephus, by contrast, has Rachel keep the images as a bargaining piece.

Asks why Rachel died before Leah. One rabbi blames her for speaking before her elder sister in v. 14. Rabbi Yosei answers that Jacob had called Rachel first, and traces her death to Jacob's own curse in v. 32, “an error which proceedeth from the ruler” (Ecclesiastes 10:5). Rashi adopts the curse explanation.

On “ten times” (v. 7) he says the Hebrew word means counts of ten, so Laban changed the terms a hundred times; Genesis Rabbah has Laban reneging ten times on each agreement. On v. 47 he notes that Jegar-sahadutha is simply the Aramaic for Galeed, “heap of witness.”

Prefers the patriarchs' anger to the humility of their descendants. Jacob's angry speech in vv. 36–37 is really mild: he only asks why Laban pursued him, and invites him to show anything found. Rabbi Simon notes that a son-in-law living in his father-in-law's house would normally use at least a knife of his, yet Laban found not even a needle. David, by contrast, brings up bloodshed when he pleads with Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:1).

Explains why Jacob says “the fear of Isaac” (v. 42) instead of naming the God of Isaac: God does not attach his name to the righteous while they live. God had said “God of Isaac” at Bethel (28:13) only because Isaac, blind, was as good as dead. On v. 52, following Genesis Rabbah, Rashi notes that the oath forbids crossing the heap “for harm,” so crossing it to trade was allowed.

Opens his treatise on flight with this chapter: Jacob fled Laban out of hatred, as he had fled Esau out of fear. Laban stands for the soul that worships shapeless matter. When Laban searches the tent and does not find the images (v. 33), Philo reads it as the empty-handedness of anyone who looks for vain fancies in a house full of real things.

Includes the theft in his reading of Jacob's household as a type of the church. Rachel, the church, stole Laban's gods and has hid them to this day, and so, Justin tells Trypho, Christians have lost their ancestral gods. It is the same chapter of his Dialogue that makes Leah the synagogue.

32.overview:
Jacob, heading home from Haran, meets angels at a place he names Mahanaim. He sends messengers to Esau and learns that his brother is coming with four hundred men. Afraid, he splits his household into two camps, prays for rescue, and sends ahead a gift of more than five hundred animals in separate droves. That night he takes his family across the Jabbok and stays behind alone. A man wrestles him until dawn and puts his hip out of joint, and when Jacob will not let go without a blessing, renames him Israel. Jacob calls the place Peniel, “face of God.”

Watch the word “face.” In v. 20 Jacob plans to appease Esau’s face with the gift that goes before his face, then see Esau’s face and hope Esau will lift up his face: four times in Hebrew, though the KJV shows one. Before he sees his brother’s face, he sees God “face to face” (v. 30).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars date the book’s final form much later.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals run from the monarchy to the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal period, early 2nd millennium BC by traditional reckoning. Ussher dates Jacob’s return to Canaan 1739 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. Hebrew verse numbers here run one ahead of the KJV (KJV 32:1 is Hebrew 32:2).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: East of the Jordan in Gilead: Mahanaim, then the ford of the Jabbok, a tributary of the Jordan, and Peniel (also spelled Penuel) beside it.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 35:9–10 (the name Israel given again at Bethel); Hosea 12:3–4.

32.hermeneutics:
Jacob’s message to Esau follows the standard opening of an ancient letter. Letters from the archives of Mari and Amarna begin with a fixed formula: “to my lord say,” then “thus says your servant,” the way a vassal wrote to his overlord. Jacob’s instructions run the same way: “Thus shall ye speak unto my lord Esau; Thy servant Jacob saith” (v. 4). Isaac’s blessing had made Jacob “lord over thy brethren” (27:29). Now Jacob writes as Esau’s servant, and the droves he sends ahead (vv. 13–20) read like a vassal’s tribute.

In the ancient Near East a name gave power over its bearer. In the Egyptian tale of Isis and Ra (Turin papyrus, c. 13th–12th century BC), the goddess forces the aging sun god to tell her his secret name, and through it she gains power over him. Read against that belief, the exchange at the Jabbok is a contest over names. The stranger makes Jacob say his own name, the name of the heel-grabber of 25:26 whom Esau called a supplanter (27:36). Then he gives Jacob a new name but refuses to give his own (v. 29). Jacob wins a blessing but gains no hold over the one who blesses him.

breakdown.label: Angels meet Jacob; Mahanaim, “two camps”
Messengers to Esau; four hundred men are coming
Jacob, afraid, divides his people into two bands
Jacob’s prayer: deliver me from Esau
A present for Esau sent ahead in droves
Night crossing of the Jabbok
A man wrestles Jacob until dawn; renamed Israel
Peniel; Jacob limps; the sinew not eaten

structure.summary: A loose frame: two meetings with God open and close the chapter, with the preparations for Esau between them. Not a chiasm.

open.text: Angels of God meet Jacob: “God’s host”

close.text: A man wrestles Jacob: “I have seen God face to face”

rows.text: Gift sent ahead; family across the Jabbok

rows.label: B
rows.text: Interlude: Rebekah in a foreign palace; pact with foreigners

rows.label: D′
rows.text: Messengers of God at Mahanaim and Peniel

rows.label: B′
rows.text: Interlude: Dinah in a foreign palace; pact with foreigners

rows.label: A′
rows.text: Oracle fulfilled; struggle at birth; Jacob becomes Israel

notes: **One word, two roles:** the “angels” of v. 1 and the “messengers” of vv. 3 and 6 are the same Hebrew word, *mal’akhim*. God’s messengers come to Jacob; then Jacob sends his own to Esau.
**Camps:** Mahanaim means “two camps” (v. 2), and Jacob then makes himself two camps (vv. 7, 10). The word *mahaneh* comes six times (vv. 2, 7, 8 twice, 10, 21).

**In the Jacob cycle:** this chapter (D′) answers Bethel (D). Both are night meetings with God at the edge of the land, one on the way out and one on the way back, and both end with Jacob naming the place.

Chapter 32 closes the Haran section of the Jacob story (28:10–32:32). It began with a vision at Bethel as Jacob left the land and ends with a struggle at the Jabbok as he comes back. The *toledot* heading for Isaac (25:19) still governs; the next heading is Esau’s at 36:1.
**Links:** Hosea 12:3–4 recalls the struggle as Jacob’s power “over the angel” at which he wept and pleaded. God confirms the name Israel at Bethel in 35:10.

traditions.text: Enos opens his short record with “the wrestle which I had before God,” then tells of praying all day and into the night until a voice tells him his sins are forgiven. He had gone to hunt in the forest, and the words of his father Jacob about eternal life sank into his heart. His struggle is prayer, not a fight, but it has the shape of Genesis 32: a long night that ends only in a blessing. Alma 8:10 uses the same image for Alma’s prayer over the city of Ammonihah.

Jacob marvels that he saw God face to face and lived (v. 30), though Exodus 33:20 says no one can. Restoration scripture names the conditions. Moses sees God face to face because God’s glory rests on him and he is transfigured, and D&C 84 ties the same experience to priesthood ordinances: without them no one can “see the face of God” and live.

The earliest reading of the story, from a prophet of the northern kingdom. Hosea says Jacob “had power over the angel, and prevailed,” and adds what Genesis lacks: Jacob wept and begged for favor. Hosea joins the wrestling to the birth story and to Bethel, and uses all three to call Israel back to its God.

Josephus calls the wrestler an angel who started the fight and lost, and glosses Israel as “one that struggled with the divine angel.” Peniel, he says, means the face of God. He has Jacob ask the angel to tell him his future, and says Jacob himself stopped eating the sinew after his injury, which is why Jews still do not eat it.

Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says the wrestler was Esau’s guardian angel, and reads Jacob’s words to Esau in 33:10, that seeing him was like seeing the face of God, as a hint that he had already met Esau’s angel. Rabbi Berekhyah takes the rare verb for “wrestled” from the word for dust: the stranger ended up in the dust, so Jacob won. Rabbi Hanina bar Yitzhak adds that the angel could not prevail because Jacob came with five amulets: his own merit and that of his father, mother, grandfather, and grandmother.

When the stranger asks to go because day is breaking, Jacob asks if he is a thief or a gambler, afraid of daylight. The angel answers that he must go up to sing God’s praise, because his turn has come for the first time since he was created. The same page explains why the sun rose “upon him” (v. 31): it had set early for Jacob at Bethel (28:11) and now rose early for him alone.

Turns the closing note of v. 32 into law. The sinew may not be eaten in the land of Israel or outside it, with or without the temple, from domestic or wild animals, and from either thigh. Birds are exempt, the Mishnah says, because a bird has no “hollow” of the thigh.

A lost Jewish work known from a few lines Origen quotes. In it Jacob speaks as a heavenly being: “I am Israel, an angel of God, and a ruling spirit,” firstborn of every living creature, and the angel Uriel fights him out of jealousy over rank. The idea of Jacob as a chief spirit before his earthly birth resembles Abraham 3:22–23, where Abraham is shown the “noble and great” spirits chosen before the world.

Justin tells the Jewish teacher Trypho that the one who wrestled Jacob was Christ, who appeared to the patriarchs before his birth. The touch that made Jacob’s thigh shrink foretold Christ’s suffering. Israel, which Justin explains as “a man who overcomes power,” was Christ’s own name, given to Jacob when he blessed him. Justin also cites Jacob’s words at Peniel as Moses’ own witness that the one who appeared to the patriarchs was God, the same figure who visited Abraham at Mamre.

Augustine also sees the angel as a type of Christ, who lets himself be overcome, as in the Passion, and still blesses the one who prevails. Jacob leaves both blessed and lame, which Augustine applies to Israel’s descendants: blessed in those who believed in Christ, lame in those who did not. He takes Israel to mean “seeing God,” the meaning the Prayer of Joseph also gives.

33.overview:
Esau arrives with four hundred men. Jacob lines up his family with the handmaids in front and Rachel and Joseph last, goes ahead of them, and bows to the ground seven times. Esau runs to meet him, embraces and kisses him, and the brothers weep. Esau at first refuses the gift of herds, then accepts it, and offers to travel together. Jacob declines, promising to follow him to Seir, but turns instead to Succoth and then to Shechem, where he buys land and builds an altar he calls El-elohe-Israel.

Jacob presses the gift on Esau as “my blessing” (v. 11). It is the same Hebrew word, *berakah*, as the blessing he took from Esau in chapter 27, and the word has not appeared since 28:4. Twenty years after taking his brother’s blessing, Jacob hands one back.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals run from the monarchy to the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Immediately after ch. 32. Ussher dates Jacob’s return to Canaan 1739 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Near the Jabbok, then Succoth east of the Jordan, then Shechem in the central hill country of Canaan, in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.

33.hermeneutics:
Letters from vassal rulers in the Amarna archive (14th century BC) open with the writer falling at the king’s feet “seven times and seven times.” Jacob acts the formula out. He bows to the ground seven times as he approaches (v. 3), calls Esau “my lord” throughout, and has his wives and children bow in turn (vv. 6–7). The blessing Jacob took had promised that his mother’s sons would bow down to him (27:29). Here the one who carries that blessing bows, and Esau, the one who was to serve, does not bow at all.

Shechem was an old, powerful town long before Jacob camped there. An Egyptian stela of the officer Khu-Sebek records a campaign of Senusret III (19th century BC) against “Sekmem,” and in the Amarna letters Shechem’s ruler Lab’ayu troubles his neighbors and is accused of handing Shechem’s land to the Habiru, landless outsiders (EA 289). Jacob pitches his tent “before the city” and buys a plot from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money (vv. 18–19), much as Abraham bought Machpelah at Hebron from the Hittites (23:16–18). Both are newcomers getting a legal foothold beside an established city with its own rulers and customs. Chapter 34 shows how exposed that position was.

breakdown.label: Jacob orders his family and bows seven times
Esau embraces Jacob; the family bows
The gift: Esau refuses, then takes “my blessing”
Esau offers escort; Jacob declines; Esau returns to Seir
Jacob builds a house and booths at Succoth
At Shechem: land bought, altar El-elohe-Israel

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: **Bowing:** the verb comes four times (vv. 3, 6, 7 twice). Jacob and every group in his household bow; Esau never does.
**Grace:** Jacob asks to “find grace” in Esau’s sight three times (vv. 8, 10, 15), and in v. 11 says God has “dealt graciously” with him, from the same Hebrew root.

**In the Jacob cycle:** this chapter (C′) answers 27:1–28:9 (C). Jacob fled fearing Esau and comes back fearing him; Isaac’s kiss (27:27) is matched by Esau’s (v. 4). The word “neck” appears in the cycle only at 27:16, 27:40, and v. 4, where Esau falls on Jacob’s neck.

Chapter 33 opens the last part of the Jacob story (33:1–36:43): the return to Canaan, the trouble at Shechem, Bethel, the deaths of Rachel and Isaac, and Esau’s genealogy. The meeting with Esau resolves the threat that drove Jacob away in 27:41–45.
**Links:** The field Jacob bought at Shechem becomes Joseph’s burial place (Joshua 24:32), and John 4:5–6 sets Jesus’ talk with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well beside it.

traditions.text: Jubilees gives the reconciliation a single verse, dated to the day: Jacob crossed the Jabbok, Esau came, was reconciled, and went home to Seir, and Jacob lived in tents. It adds that Jacob then sent food and clothing to Isaac and Rebekah four times a year, while Esau had left his father alone. It has Jacob go up “to Salem, to the east of Shechem, in peace,” which keeps both readings of *shalem* in v. 18: a place name, as in the KJV, and “safe and whole.”

Josephus has Jacob send his wives ahead separately so they could watch how the men fought if Esau attacked, and says plainly that Esau came with no evil design. In his telling Esau had been glad at Jacob’s message from the start, and after the meeting he invited Jacob to come with him to their father; Jacob pleaded that the cattle were tired. He also explains the name Seir: Esau called his home “roughness” after his own hairy roughness, a play on Hebrew *se’ir*, “hairy” (25:25).

The midrash asks why Jacob walked ahead of his family (v. 3). Rabbi Levi answers that Jacob was the most compassionate of the patriarchs: better that Esau harm him than them. It also asks why he bowed seven times and links the number to Proverbs 24:16, where a just man falls seven times and rises again.

Rashi reads Jacob’s words in v. 10, that seeing Esau was like seeing the face of God, as a calculated hint: he had seen Esau’s angel and survived, so Esau should think twice before attacking. On v. 17 he works out from the house and the two mentions of booths that Jacob stayed at Succoth eighteen months, through a summer, a winter, and another summer.

In Hebrew scrolls the word “and kissed him” in v. 4 carries scribal dots over its letters, and the rabbis debated why. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said the dots show that Esau, for once, kissed Jacob with his whole heart. Rabbi Yannai said Esau meant to bite him, Jacob’s neck turned to marble, and they wept, one for his neck and one for his teeth. Rashi, citing Sifre, gives the first view to Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai: Esau hated Jacob, but at that moment his pity was real.

Jacob promises to come to Esau at Seir (v. 14) but goes to Succoth instead. Rabbi Abbahu says he searched all of scripture and never found Jacob going to Seir. Since Jacob was a truthful man, the promise must look to the future: Obadiah 1:21 says saviors will come up on Mount Zion “to judge the mount of Esau.”

Rav reads *shalem* in v. 18 as “whole”: Jacob came whole in body, whole in wealth, and whole in his learning. The same verse says he camped before the face of the city, which the rabbis read as gracing the city with benefits, and they disagree on which: Rav says Jacob set up coinage, Samuel says markets, and Rabbi Yohanan says bathhouses. Targum Onkelos likewise renders the verse “Jacob arrived safely.”

The Hebrew of v. 20 can be read two ways: Jacob named the altar El-elohe-Israel, or the God of Israel named Jacob himself El. Rabbi Elazar takes the second reading, that God called Jacob “God.” Rashi gives the plain sense first: the altar’s name praised the God who had rescued Jacob, as the name of Moses’ altar Jehovah-nissi did in Exodus 17:15.

John sets Jesus’ conversation with the Samaritan woman at Sychar, near the ground “that Jacob gave to his son Joseph,” beside Jacob’s well. The woman asks whether Jesus is greater than “our father Jacob,” who gave the well. Genesis does not mention the well; John knows it as a landmark at the field of this chapter.

Stephen says Jacob and “our fathers” were carried to Shechem and laid in the tomb “Abraham bought” from the sons of Emmor (Hamor). Genesis has Jacob buying land at Shechem (v. 19) and Abraham buying Machpelah at Hebron (ch. 23), so the speech merges the two purchases. Genesis 50:13 adds that Jacob himself was buried at Machpelah, not Shechem; Joshua 24:32 places only Joseph’s bones there.

34.overview:
Dinah, Jacob’s daughter by Leah, goes out to visit the women of the land. Shechem, son of the local ruler Hamor, seizes and rapes her, then wants to marry her. Hamor proposes intermarriage and trade, and Shechem offers any bride-price they name. Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully that every male in the city must be circumcised. The men agree, and on the third day, while they are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill them all and take Dinah from Shechem’s house. The other brothers plunder the city. Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi for endangering the family, and they answer with a question.

Dinah never speaks. Shechem, Hamor, the brothers, the townsmen, and Jacob all do, but the narrator never reports what she wanted or felt. The chapter ends on the brothers’ question about how their sister was treated (v. 31), and no one answers it.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals run from the monarchy to the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Some time after Jacob settled at Shechem (33:18); Ussher dates the return to Canaan 1739 BC. Dinah, born after Leah’s sixth son (30:21), is now a young woman.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Shechem, a walled Canaanite city ruled by Hamor “the Hivite” (v. 2), whose men hold council at the city gate (v. 20).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: None elsewhere in scripture; Genesis 49:5–7 looks back on it.

34.hermeneutics:
The Middle Assyrian Laws (tablets copied c. 11th century BC) include a case like this one. A man who seizes an unbetrothed virgin must, if her father agrees, marry her, pay three times a virgin’s value in silver, and never divorce her; or the father may take the silver and give her to someone else (Tablet A, §55). Exodus 22:16–17 and Deuteronomy 22:28–29 run along the same lines. By those standards Shechem’s offer of marriage with “never so much dowry and gift” (v. 12) is the settlement the region’s law expected. The brothers refuse a remedy the codes treated as adequate, and the narrator sides with their outrage: it was a thing that “ought not to be done” (v. 7).

Circumcision was not unique to Israel. Herodotus (2.104) says the Egyptians practiced it from the earliest times and that the Phoenicians and the “Syrians of Palestine” learned it from them, and an Old Kingdom relief in the tomb of Ankhmahor at Saqqara shows it performed on grown men. Jeremiah 9:25–26 lists Egypt, Edom, Ammon, and Moab among the circumcised. So the brothers ask for a known rite, and adults would expect to be sore for days (v. 25). They take the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (17:10–11) and use it to disable a city.

Public business was done at the city gate. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, King Danel sits at the gate judging the widow’s case and the orphan’s. Hamor takes the proposal to “the gate of their city” (v. 20), and those who are circumcised are described as everyone “that went out of the gate” (v. 24). The agreement is a civic act binding the whole town, which is why the whole town pays for it.

breakdown.label: Dinah goes out; Shechem seizes her, then wants her
Jacob waits in silence; the brothers come home angry
Hamor and Shechem propose marriage and alliance
The brothers’ deceitful condition: circumcision
Hamor and Shechem persuade the city at the gate
Simeon and Levi kill the men; the brothers plunder
Jacob’s rebuke and the brothers’ reply

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.
notes: **Defiled:** the narrator says three times that Shechem “defiled” Dinah (vv. 5, 13, 27), once at each turn: the news, the deceit, and the plunder.
**Circumcised** comes five times (vv. 15, 17, 22 twice, 24), all in the negotiation and persuasion scenes. The ruse depends on it.

**Sister:** in Hebrew, “our sister” is the chapter’s last word (v. 31). The narrator calls her Jacob’s daughter (vv. 3, 5, 7, 19), but the brothers’ side of the story speaks of her as their sister (vv. 13, 14, 27, 31).
**In the Jacob cycle:** this chapter (B′) answers ch. 26 (B): each is an interlude in which a woman of the family is at risk among foreigners and a pact is made with a foreign ruler.

Part of the return section (33:1–36:43). Chapter 34 sits between two altars, at Shechem (33:20) and Bethel (35:7), and its aftermath drives the move: the “terror of God” on the cities keeps anyone from pursuing Jacob’s sons (35:5).

**Links:** On his deathbed Jacob curses Simeon and Levi’s anger and scatters them in Israel (49:5–7). Shechem returns as a place of covenant under Joshua (Joshua 24) and of slaughter under Abimelech (Judges 9:45).

traditions.text: Jubilees makes Dinah a child of twelve and says the Shechemites’ destruction was decreed in heaven, so that no daughter of Israel would be defiled again. It turns the episode into law, ruling that an Israelite who gives his daughter or sister to a Gentile is to be stoned, and says the killings were written on the heavenly tablets as righteousness, and Levi’s descendants were chosen for the priesthood because of his zeal. Like Josephus, Jubilees never says the men of Shechem were circumcised: the brothers simply deceived them and came on them unexpectedly. Jacob still reproaches his sons for fear of the Canaanites and Perizzites, and the dread of the Lord keeps the nearby cities from pursuing.

Levi, about twenty years old, has a vision of the heavens, and an angel gives him a shield and sword with the command to take vengeance on Shechem for Dinah. Levi says he killed Shechem first and Simeon killed Hamor. He admits Jacob was angry and grieved that men who had accepted circumcision were then killed, and calls it a sin done against his father’s will, yet still holds that God’s sentence was against Shechem.

Before she goes out to Holofernes, Judith prays to the “Lord God of my father Simeon,” who gave him a sword to punish the strangers who defiled a virgin. She praises the killing of the Shechemite rulers and the taking of their wives and goods, before asking God to break the strength of the Assyrians. Where Genesis 49 curses Simeon’s anger, Judith celebrates it.

A Jewish poet who retold the story in Greek epic verse, preserved in fragments by Eusebius. Jacob refuses the marriage unless the Shechemites are circumcised and adopt Jewish ways, and Simeon cites God’s word to give ten nations to Abraham’s descendants (see 15:19–21). The poet says God put the plan in the brothers’ minds because the Shechemites were impious and mistreated their guests.

In Josephus Dinah goes into the city during a festival to see the women’s finery. Jacob, unwilling to give his daughter to a foreigner but afraid to refuse a king, asks for time. Simeon and Levi attack while the city is feasting and the watch is asleep; Josephus leaves out the circumcision ruse and says they spared the women. Afterward God tells the alarmed Jacob to take courage and purify his tents.

Why is Dinah called “the daughter of Leah” rather than of Jacob (v. 1)? The midrash applies Ezekiel’s proverb about mother and daughter (16:44), and Rashi spells out the link: Leah too “went out,” to meet Jacob in 30:16. The reading places some blame on Dinah’s going out, a view many later readers have rejected.

The midrash weighs both sides of v. 25. Simeon and Levi are called “sons of Jacob,” yet they acted like any two strangers, because they did not consult their father. They are also called “Dinah’s brethren,” because they risked their lives for her. Rashi passes on both comments.

This Aramaic paraphrase expands the brothers’ one-line answer in v. 31 into a speech. It would not be fit, they say, for Israel’s congregations to hear that idol worshipers defiled Jacob’s daughter; better that they hear the idolaters were killed for her sake. Otherwise Shechem would have treated their sister like an outcast with no one to avenge her.

The two great medieval scholars disagree over the killings. Maimonides argues that the men of Shechem deserved death under the laws given to all humankind, because they saw Shechem’s crime and did not bring him to judgment. Nachmanides rejects that: no one dies for failing to judge his ruler. He thinks Jacob was right to be angry, since the townsmen had trusted the brothers’ promise, might have turned to God, and had done them no harm.
traditions.cite: Mishneh Torah, Kings 9:14; Ramban on Genesis 34:13

traditions.text: In his handbook for pastors, Gregory reads the story as a figure of the soul. Dinah going out to see the women of a foreign land is a soul that neglects its own state to watch other people’s doings. Shechem, prince of the country, is the devil, who seizes it while it is busy with outward cares and holds it as his own, then soothes it with false hopes so it will not grieve over its sin.

35.overview:
God sends Jacob up to Bethel. Jacob has his household give up their foreign gods and earrings, buries them under the oak at Shechem, and travels unharmed because a terror from God falls on the cities around. At Bethel he builds an altar, Rebekah’s nurse Deborah dies, and God appears again, confirms the name Israel, and renews the promises of nations, kings, and land. Near Ephrath Rachel dies giving birth to a son she names Ben-oni; Jacob calls him Benjamin. Reuben lies with his father’s concubine Bilhah. The twelve sons are listed, and Isaac dies at 180, buried by Esau and Jacob.

Isaac’s death is told here, but by Genesis’s own numbers he lived another twelve years. Jacob was 130 before Pharaoh (47:9) and Joseph then 39 (41:46; 45:6), so Jacob was 108 when Joseph was sold at 17 (37:2), and Isaac, 60 years older (25:26), was 168. Genesis closes Isaac’s story before opening Joseph’s.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Shechem south to Bethel (once called Luz), then toward Ephrath (Bethlehem), past the tower of Edar, to Mamre at Hebron.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 28:10–22 (first visit to Bethel); 32:28 (first naming as Israel); 48:7 (Rachel’s burial recalled).

35.hermeneutics:
Standing stones marked holy places and graves across Canaan and Syria. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, the first duty of a good son is to set up a stela for his family’s god in the sanctuary. Jacob raises two of them. Where God spoke with him he sets up a stone pillar and pours a drink offering and oil on it (v. 14), and on Rachel’s grave he sets a pillar that the narrator says stands “unto this day” (v. 20). Later law forbids such pillars (Deuteronomy 16:22, KJV “image”), but in Genesis they are acts of worship and of mourning.

Rachel names her son Ben-oni, “son of my sorrow,” and Jacob renames him Benjamin, “son of the right hand.” Letters from Mari (18th century BC) know a tribal group called the Binu-yamina, “sons of the right,” beside the Binu-sim’al, “sons of the left.” For someone facing east, the right hand is the south, so the names also meant southerners and northerners. Benjamin is the only son of Jacob born in Canaan, and his tribe would hold the southern edge of the northern tribes’ land, bordering Judah.

Taking a ruler’s concubine was a claim to his place. Absalom goes in to David’s concubines in the sight of all Israel (2 Samuel 16:22), and Solomon hears Adonijah’s request for David’s companion Abishag as a bid for the throne (1 Kings 2:22). Read that way, Reuben’s act just after Rachel’s death (v. 22) looks like the firstborn moving early to take his father’s place. Here Jacob only hears of it. He answers on his deathbed, when Reuben loses the firstborn’s rank (49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).
