Safe journey; altar at El-beth-el; Deborah dies
God appears: Israel named, promises renewed, pillar anointed
Rachel dies bearing Benjamin; the pillar on her grave
Beyond the tower of Edar; Reuben lies with Bilhah
The twelve sons of Jacob listed by mother
Jacob reaches Isaac at Mamre; Isaac dies at 180

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: The road: Rachel’s death; Reuben’s act

notes: **Bethel again:** Jacob sets up a pillar and pours oil on it (v. 14) and names the place Bethel (v. 15), as he did on the way out (28:18–19).
**Three burials:** Deborah under an oak (v. 8), Rachel by the road (vv. 19–20), and Isaac at Mamre (v. 29). The chapter closes a generation.
**Born in Padan-aram:** the list says all twelve were “born to him in Padan-aram” (v. 26), though Benjamin has just been born near Ephrath. The summary counts the twelve as one set.
**In the Jacob cycle:** vv. 1–22 (A′) answer 25:19–34 (A): an oracle at the start is fulfilled at the end, and each has a hard childbirth.

Chapter 35 ends the story told under Isaac’s *toledot* heading (25:19). Isaac is buried by both his sons (v. 29), as Abraham was by Isaac and Ishmael (25:9), and the next headings belong to Esau (36:1) and Jacob (37:2).

**Links:** Joshua 24:23 repeats at Shechem the call to put away “the strange gods.” Jeremiah 31:15 hears Rachel weeping for her children, and Matthew 2:18 applies the verse to Herod’s killings at Bethlehem.

traditions.text: The revelation on eternal marriage names Jacob with Abraham and Isaac as men who “did none other things than that which they were commanded” in taking wives and concubines. It says the three have already entered their exaltation and sit on thrones. It reads the household listed in vv. 23–26, two wives and two handmaids, as within God’s law.

Jubilees fills in what Genesis leaves out. Before Bethel, Jacob visits Isaac with Levi and Judah, and Isaac, at 165, blesses Levi with the priesthood and Judah with rule. Rebekah then goes with Jacob to Bethel, bringing Deborah, which explains why Rebekah’s nurse dies there. Deborah is buried under “the oak of the mourning of Deborah.”

At Bethel Levi dreams that he is made priest of the Most High. Jacob tithes everything he has, and counting his sons from Benjamin upward, Levi falls tenth, the Lord’s portion. Jacob plans to build a lasting sanctuary at Bethel, but an angel shows him seven heavenly tablets and tells him this is not the place, a nod to the later temple at Jerusalem. Jacob’s extra day of sacrifice there becomes, in Jubilees, the origin of the eighth day added to the seven-day feast of the seventh month, the feast of Tabernacles.

Genesis gives Reuben’s act one sentence; Jubilees tells it at length. Reuben sees Bilhah bathing, comes to her at night, and she tells Jacob, who never approaches her again. Jubilees then lays down a law of death for the sin and explains that Reuben lived only because the full law had not yet been revealed.

Josephus has Jacob find Laban’s stolen gods while purifying his household and bury them at Shechem. He notes that Rachel was the only one of Jacob’s family not buried at Hebron, and explains Benjamin’s name by his mother’s sorrow. He gives Isaac 185 years, not 180, and says Rebekah was already dead when Jacob arrived.

Rabbi Jonathan says that anyone who claims Reuben sinned with Bilhah is mistaken. Because v. 22 goes straight on to say the sons of Jacob were twelve, all twelve remained equal. On this reading, after Rachel died Jacob moved his bed into Bilhah’s tent, and Reuben, defending his mother Leah’s honor, moved it; scripture counts the insult as if it were the deed.

Rashi asks why Rebekah’s nurse was with Jacob at all and answers that Rebekah had sent her to call him home, as she promised in 27:45. The place name Allon-bachuth (v. 8) means “oak of weeping,” and an old midrash heard *allon* as Greek for “another”: Jacob was mourning a second death, his mother’s. Her death went unrecorded, Rashi says, so that no one would curse the womb that bore Esau.

Rashi takes up the chronological puzzle raised in the Overview and states a rule: the Torah’s stories are not always in order. Commenting on 48:7, he adds why Rachel lay by the road rather than in a city or at Hebron: God had commanded it, so that when the exiles passed that way to Babylon she could come out and weep for them, as Jeremiah 31:15 says.

This Aramaic paraphrase calls the tower of Edar (v. 21) the place from which the King Messiah will be revealed at the end of days. The link is Micah 4:8, which addresses the “tower of the flock” (Hebrew *migdal eder*) and promises it the kingdom. Genesis itself mentions the tower only in passing, as the place Jacob camped when the Reuben episode happened.

Matthew reads Herod’s killing of the infants of Bethlehem through Jeremiah’s image of Rachel weeping for her children. The quotation works because Genesis places Rachel’s grave on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem (v. 19). Jeremiah’s Ramah lies north of Jerusalem, and 1 Samuel 10:2 puts the tomb “in the border of Benjamin,” so ancient readers already knew two possible locations.

In his memorial letter for his friend Paula, Jerome describes her pilgrimage: on the way to Bethlehem she stopped at Rachel’s tomb. He contrasts the two names of v. 18: Benoni, which he renders son of my pangs, and Benjamin, son of the right hand, the name Jacob gave in the spirit of prophecy. Paula went on from the tomb to the cave of the Nativity.

36.overview:
Esau’s family history comes in two parts. The first (vv. 1–8) names his three wives and five sons born in Canaan and tells how he moved to Mount Seir because the land could not support both brothers’ herds. The second (vv. 9–43) traces his line in Seir: the sons and grandsons who became chiefs (*alluf*, KJV “dukes”), the Horite clans who lived in Seir before them, eight kings who reigned in Edom, and a closing list of chiefs by place.

Compare the wives with earlier chapters. In 26:34 and 28:9 Esau marries Judith daughter of Beeri, Bashemath daughter of Elon, and Mahalath daughter of Ishmael. Here they are Adah daughter of Elon, Aholibamah daughter of Anah, and Bashemath daughter of Ishmael (vv. 2–3). The names and fathers do not line up, and Genesis does not explain the difference.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Verse 31 speaks of kings who reigned before Israel had a king. Tradition reads it as Moses’ prophecy or a later note; many scholars take it as written in or after Saul’s time (c. 1050 BC).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: From Esau’s marriages in the patriarchal period down to Edom’s kings, who reigned before Israel’s monarchy.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Mount Seir and the land of Edom, the highlands south and southeast of the Dead Sea; Bozrah (v. 33) and Teman (v. 34) are Edomite centers.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: 1 Chronicles 1:35–54 repeats the lists with small differences.

36.hermeneutics:
Egyptian records know Seir and Edom as herders’ country. A border official’s report in Papyrus Anastasi VI (late 13th century BC) notes that Shasu tribes from Edom were let past a frontier fort into the eastern Nile Delta to keep themselves and their flocks alive, and Ramesses III boasts of plundering the people of Seir among the Shasu (Papyrus Harris I). That is the world of v. 7, where two herding households cannot share the same pasture, and of the clan chiefs who lead Edom here before any king appears.

When did Edom first have kings? Large-scale settlement on the Edomite plateau, including the fortified capital at Bozrah (Busayra), dates mainly to the 8th–6th centuries BC. Excavations at Khirbat en-Nahas in the Faynan copper district, though, show organized mining and smelting in the 11th–9th centuries BC, which some archaeologists take as evidence of an earlier Edomite polity. The list in vv. 31–39 has no dynasty: each king comes from a different place, and none is the son of the king before him. That fits a league of chiefs more than a hereditary throne.

Several names here are places as well as people. Teman is Esau’s grandson (v. 11), a chief (v. 15), and a region (v. 34). Amos 1:12 pairs Teman with Bozrah, Job’s friend Eliphaz is a Temanite (Job 2:11), and Habakkuk 3:3 says God came from Teman. Inscriptions at Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai (c. 800 BC) invoke Yahweh of Teman. A genealogy like this one maps territory: to name a son is to name a district.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, list after list.

rows.text: Esau’s line and chiefs in Seir

notes: **Chiefs:** *alluf* (KJV “duke”) occurs 43 times in the chapter. Edom is organized by clan leaders before, around, and after its kings.
**King list formula:** “and … died, and … reigned in his stead” repeats seven times (vv. 33–39), the same pattern used later for Israel’s and Judah’s kings.
**Timna** appears three ways: as Eliphaz’s concubine and Amalek’s mother (v. 12), as a Horite chief’s sister (v. 22), and as the name of a chief (v. 40).

Esau’s *toledot* comes under two headings, 36:1 and 36:9, and closes the Jacob section before Jacob’s own heading at 37:2 opens the Joseph story. Genesis treats Ishmael the same way: the line not chosen is listed briefly (25:12–18) before the chosen line’s story resumes (25:19).

**Links:** 1 Chronicles 1:35–54 copies these lists. Deuteronomy 23:7 forbids Israel to abhor an Edomite, “for he is thy brother,” while Obadiah looks for the day when saviors “judge the mount of Esau” (Obadiah 1:21).

traditions.text: The Lord’s preface to the Doctrine and Covenants says he will come down in judgment “upon Idumea, or the world.” Idumea is the Greek form of Edom, the land this chapter maps. The usage follows Isaiah, where judgment falls on Idumea and Bozrah (Isaiah 34:5–6; 63:1), and turns Esau’s country into a name for the whole world.

Jubilees does not leave the brothers reconciled. After Isaac’s death Esau’s sons force their father into war, Jacob kills Esau with an arrow, and Edom pays tribute to Jacob’s sons. Then Jubilees copies the king list of vv. 31–39, which in Charles’s translation begins with “Balaq, the son of Beor.”

Josephus explains Idumea through the red pottage of 25:30: Esau was nicknamed Adom, “red,” and the Greeks smoothed the name to Idumea. He counts Amalek as Eliphaz’s illegitimate son by the concubine Thamna (Timna). He says Esau left Hebron to Jacob after Isaac’s death and ruled from Seir, and that Idumea kept the name of the whole country while its parts took the names of their peoples, one of them Amalekitis.

The Greek Job ends with an appendix that identifies Job with Jobab, the second king in v. 33. It names his father as Zare (Zerah), one of the sons of Esau, and his mother as Bosorrha (Bozrah), so that he is fifth from Abraham. It then repeats the opening of the Edomite king list and makes Job’s friend Eliphaz a descendant of Esau and king of the Temanites.

A Jewish historian known only from fragments quoted by Eusebius. He says Esau married Bassara of Edom and fathered Job, who lived in Uz on the border of Idumea and Arabia, and that Job was first called Jobab. Aristeas and the Greek Job appendix agree on the Jobab link but disagree on the generation: Aristeas makes Job Esau’s own son, while the appendix, counting him fifth from Abraham, makes him Esau’s grandson.

This Aramaic paraphrase makes the first king of Edom, “Bela the son of Beor” (v. 32), the prophet Balaam son of Beor of Numbers 22–24. The shared father’s name invited the link, and the Greek Job appendix and Jubilees, with their Balac and Balaq, show the names already blurring.

The Talmud imagines the wicked King Manasseh mocking verses like “Lotan’s sister was Timna” (v. 22) as pointless. It answers that Timna, a Horite noblewoman, wanted to convert and came to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who turned her away. She chose to be a concubine in Abraham’s family rather than a princess elsewhere, and her son Amalek later afflicted Israel, the price of rejecting her.

Rashi takes up the mismatched wives (see Overview) and harmonizes them. Adah is the Bashemath of 26:34, Aholibamah is Judith, renamed “Jewess” to persuade Isaac she had left idol worship, and the Bashemath of v. 3 is the Mahalath of 28:9. Mahalath, he says, means pardon: a man’s sins are forgiven on his wedding day. He also reads “daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon” as a sign that Esau’s in-laws were of irregular birth.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 36:2–3 (citing Midrash Tanchuma and Megillah 17a)

traditions.text: Rashi notices that Anah is Zibeon’s brother in v. 20 and his son in v. 24, and following the Talmud explains that Zibeon fathered Anah by his own mother. Anah, born of a forbidden union, then crossbred a donkey with a horse, which is why he is remembered for the mules (v. 24).

Both comment on v. 31. Rashi pairs Edom’s eight kings with eight kings of Israel and Judah, from Saul to Jehoshaphat, in whose days “there was no king in Edom” (1 Kings 22:47). Ibn Ezra reports a scholar who said the chapter was written in Jehoshaphat’s time and calls his book fit to be burned; he takes the “king” of v. 31 to be Moses (Deuteronomy 33:5) and notes others who read the verse as prophecy.
traditions.cite: Rashi and Ibn Ezra on Genesis 36:31

traditions.text: Augustine uses Job as proof that people outside Israel could belong to the heavenly city. Job, he says, was neither an Israelite nor a convert but of the Idumean race, born and buried in Edom. Reasoning from the book of Job itself, Augustine places him in the third generation after Israel, and holds him up as evidence that God had people among other nations.

37.overview:
Joseph, seventeen and his father's favorite, brings a bad report about his brothers, wears the coat Jacob made him, and tells two dreams in which his family bows down to him. The brothers' hatred grows with each step. When Jacob sends him to check on them, they catch him near Dothan, throw him into a dry pit, and sell him to a caravan bound for Egypt. They dip his coat in goat's blood and send it home, and Jacob mourns a son he believes a wild animal has killed. In Egypt, Joseph is sold to Potiphar.

Watch the coat. It marks Jacob's favor in v. 3, it is the first thing the brothers strip from Joseph, and it becomes the false evidence of his death. Jacob, who once deceived his own father with goat kids and his brother's clothing (27:9, 15–16), is now deceived the same way.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars date the Joseph story later.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly proposals range from the 10th to the 5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Joseph is 17 (v. 2). Dating the Exodus c. 1446 BC with 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40) puts this about 1900 BC; Ussher's reckoning gives 1728 BC.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel, the descendants of the brothers who sold Joseph.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The vale of Hebron, then Shechem and Dothan in central Canaan, on the caravan route from Gilead down to Egypt.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Psalm 105:17; Acts 7:9. The Book of Mormon recalls Joseph's torn coat (Alma 46:23–24) and Joseph “sold into Egypt” (1 Nephi 5:14; Alma 10:3).

37.hermeneutics:
The price was ordinary. Joseph goes for “twenty pieces of silver” (v. 28), twenty shekels by weight, since coins did not yet exist. Hammurabi's laws (c. 1750 BC) set twenty shekels, a third of a mina, as the payment for a slave killed by a goring ox. Kenneth Kitchen has argued that slave prices climbed over the centuries, to about thirty shekels at Nuzi and Ugarit and fifty or more under the Assyrians, so the figure fits the early second millennium. Critics reply that prices varied with a slave's age and sex, and Leviticus 27:5 also values a male aged five to twenty at twenty shekels. Either way, the brothers take the going rate for a teenage boy.

The coat set Joseph apart from working shepherds. The Hebrew *ketonet passim* is uncertain: “many colours” follows the Greek translation, while others read a long robe reaching to the hands or feet. The only other wearers in the Bible are King David's daughters (2 Samuel 13:18). A tomb painting at Beni Hasan in Egypt (c. 1890 BC) shows Asiatic visitors led by a chief named Abisha in brightly patterned garments, so fine clothing was known among Canaan's herders. Jacob's gift marks Joseph as the son who oversees and reports.

The bloody coat also works as legal evidence. Hammurabi's laws (§266) let a herdsman clear himself before the god if a lion killed an animal in his care, and Exodus 22:13 lets a keeper bring the torn remains “for witness” and owe nothing. Jacob knew the rule; with Laban he had borne such losses himself (31:39). The brothers present an exhibit and ask him to identify it, and Jacob, like a judge, gives the verdict they wanted: “torn in pieces.”

Two dreams: sheaves, then sun, moon, and eleven stars
Sent to Shechem; a stranger points him to Dothan
The plot to kill; Reuben's plan; the empty pit
Judah's plan: sold for twenty pieces of silver

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Favor, report, and dreams at home
The errand from Hebron to Dothan

notes: **The coat:** The Hebrew word for it (*ketonet*) appears 8 times, at every stage: given (v. 3), stripped off (v. 23), dipped in blood (v. 31), sent home and recognized (vv. 32–33).

**Hatred in three steps:** The brothers hate Joseph for the favoritism (v. 4), for the first dream (v. 5), and “yet the more” for his dreams and words (v. 8). Words for dream and dreaming occur 13 times in the chapter.
**Dreams in pairs:** Joseph's two dreams here begin a pattern that runs through the story: the two officers' dreams in ch. 40 and Pharaoh's two in ch. 41.

“These are the generations of Jacob” (v. 2) is the last *toledot* heading in Genesis. Jacob lives on until ch. 49, but the story now follows his sons, above all Joseph and Judah. Chapters 37–38 open the unit by sending both away from the family: Joseph down to Egypt, Judah down to Adullam (38:1).

**Looking ahead:** The dreams come true when the brothers bow before Joseph in Egypt (42:6), and Joseph reads the sale as God's doing: “God meant it unto good” (50:20). Stephen retells the sale in his defense before the council (Acts 7:9).

traditions.text: Captain Moroni rallies the Nephites as a remnant of Joseph, “whose coat was rent by his brethren into many pieces.” He then recalls words of Jacob found nowhere in Genesis: before his death Jacob saw that part of Joseph's coat had been preserved and had not decayed, and he prophesied that a remnant of Joseph's seed would likewise be preserved while the rest perished. In Genesis the torn coat is a sign of death; here a surviving scrap of it becomes a sign of survival.

Lehi learns from the brass plates that he descends from “Joseph who was sold into Egypt,” and later Nephite writers keep that label, adding that the sale was by his brothers' hands. Lehi tells his own son Joseph that the patriarch saw their day and received covenants about a branch of his descendants. For these writers the sale of Joseph is where their own family history begins.

Jubilees has the bloodied coat reach Jacob on the tenth day of the seventh month. Bilhah and Dinah die of grief, and Jacob mourns a full year. Because the brothers grieved their father that day, Israel is to afflict itself on the tenth of the seventh month and atone with a young goat, the same animal whose blood stained the coat. The sale becomes the origin of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29).

Gives Reuben a long speech against killing a brother and has him lower Joseph into the dry pit on a cord. Judah, whom Josephus calls Judas, then sells Joseph to Arab descendants of Ishmael, and Reuben, returning at night to rescue him, finds him gone. Ancient versions disagree on the price: Josephus gives twenty “pounds,” and the Greek Bible twenty pieces of gold.

One of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, farewell speeches put in the mouths of Jacob's sons. Zebulun claims he took no share of the price. Simeon, Gad, and six others bought sandals with it, refusing to eat what was the price of their brother's blood and treading it underfoot instead. The testament ties this to the law that a man who will not raise seed for his brother has his sandal loosed (Deuteronomy 25:9); compare Amos 2:6, “the poor for a pair of shoes.”

Gad confesses that he hated Joseph most for his dreams and that he and Judah sold him to the Ishmaelites for thirty pieces of gold. They hid ten and showed the other brothers twenty. The story reconciles two prices then in circulation and makes the sale a lesson about hatred and greed.

Philo tells the story literally, then as allegory, with Joseph as the type of the statesman. The coat of many colors fits, he says, because political life is many-colored, shifting with times, places, and peoples. A statesman has to adjust the way a ship's pilot adjusts to changing winds.

This Aramaic paraphrase names the “certain man” who finds Joseph wandering near Shechem (v. 15): it is the angel Gabriel in the likeness of a man. Genesis leaves the stranger anonymous, though without him Joseph might have gone home. The targum makes the hidden guidance explicit.

Rav warns that a father should never single out one son: for two selas' weight of fine wool, the coat, the brothers grew jealous, and in the end Israel went down to Egypt. Another teaching asks why v. 24 says the pit was both “empty” and had “no water.” It had no water, the answer goes, but it did have snakes and scorpions.

A Jewish writer in Egypt, known only from quotations preserved by Eusebius. In his version Joseph is never sold: he learns of his brothers' plot and asks neighboring Arabs, fellow descendants of Abraham, to take him to Egypt. There he becomes administrator of the whole country. It shows how some Jews in Egypt retold the story with Joseph in control from the start.

Writing to the church at Corinth about envy, Clement lists biblical cases: Cain and Abel, Jacob fleeing Esau, and then Joseph, whom envy caused to be “persecuted unto death, and to come into bondage.” Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and David follow. Joseph had become a standard example of what jealousy among brothers does.

Calls Joseph a figure of Christ in one point at least: he was persecuted by his brothers and sold into Egypt because of God's favor, as Christ was sold by his own people when Judas betrayed him. The brother who proposes the sale in v. 26 is Judah, whose name in Greek is Judas, the form Josephus also uses.

38.overview:
Judah leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite woman, and has three sons. The first, Er, marries Tamar and dies; the second, Onan, refuses to father a child for his dead brother and dies too. Judah sends Tamar back to her father's house to wait for the third son, Shelah, and then never gives him to her. Years later Tamar veils herself by the road to Timnath, Judah takes her for a harlot, and she asks for his signet, cord, and staff as a pledge. When Judah orders her burned for her pregnancy, she sends the pledges, and he admits, “She hath been more righteous than I.” She bears twins, Pharez and Zarah.

The story interrupts Joseph's, but a phrase ties them together. The brothers handed Jacob the bloody coat and said “know now” (37:32). Tamar hands Judah his pledges with the same Hebrew words, “discern, I pray thee” (v. 25).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Begins “at that time,” around Joseph's sale (v. 1), and runs over years; Pharez and Zarah are listed among those who go down to Egypt (46:12).

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel, and in particular Judah, whose leading clan, David's, traced its line through Pharez (Ruth 4:18–22).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Adullam, Chezib, and Timnath, in the low hills west of Hebron.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 46:12; 1 Chronicles 2:3–4; Ruth 4:12, 18; Matthew 1:3.

38.hermeneutics:
Israel's law tells a man to marry his brother's childless widow so that the first son carries the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Older law collections show the custom was wider, and its chain of duty longer. Hittite Laws §193 send the widow to her husband's brother, then to his father, then to the father's brother. Middle Assyrian Laws A §43 let a father give a dead son's wife to whichever remaining son he chooses, even a boy of ten. Against that background Judah, the head of the family, is the one who fails when he holds Shelah back. Tamar's plan lands on the next man in the Hittite chain, her father-in-law, a union Leviticus 18:15 would later forbid.

The veil did different work in different places. Middle Assyrian Laws A §40 require married women to veil in the street and forbid prostitutes to veil at all. Genesis says Judah took Tamar for a harlot “because she had covered her face” (v. 15). Whatever local custom lay behind it, the veil's job in the story is to hide who she is, so that a father-in-law who knew her face does not recognize her.

The pledge Tamar asks for is Judah's identity. Herodotus, describing Babylonians, says every man there carries a seal and a staff carved with an image of his own. Seals were rolled or pressed on clay to sign contracts, and in the Near East they were often worn on a cord; the KJV “bracelets” (v. 18) is better read as that cord. Judah hands over the equivalent of his signature and his ID, and Tamar keeps them for the one moment when they will be undeniable.

Er and Onan die; Tamar sent home to wait for Shelah
Tamar veiled by the road; Judah's signet, cord, and staff
Hirah cannot find the woman to redeem the pledge
“Let her be burnt”: the pledges, and Judah's confession
Twins: Pharez breaks out ahead of Zarah

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Judah's family: three sons, two deaths, a promise withheld

notes: **Going down:** The Hebrew verb for going down threads through the frame. The caravan goes down to Egypt (37:25), Jacob will go down to the grave mourning (37:35), Judah goes down from his brothers (38:1), and Joseph is brought down to Egypt (39:1).

**A goat and a piece of evidence:** A kid of the goats appears in both chapters, once to stain Joseph's coat (37:31) and once as Judah's promised payment (38:17, 20). Each time an object is presented to a family head for identification.
**The younger first:** As with Esau and Jacob (25:25–26), the twin who reaches out first is not born first. Pharez breaks out ahead of Zarah, and the line of David runs through Pharez.

Chapter 38 sits inside the Joseph story: 37:36 leaves Joseph sold to Potiphar, and 39:1 picks up at that same point. “At that time” (v. 1) ties it to the sale, though its events cover many years, so the narrator sets Judah's story beside Joseph's on purpose. The two brothers meet again in Egypt, where Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33).
**Looking ahead:** Jacob's blessing gives Judah the scepter (49:10), and the line through Pharez leads to David (Ruth 4:18–22).

traditions.text: Makes Tamar a daughter of Aram, not a Canaanite. Er would not lie with her because he wanted a wife from his mother's Canaanite kin, and Judah's wife later kept Shelah from marrying her. Afterward Judah repents, and the angels tell him in a dream that he is forgiven because he turned from his sin and his ignorance, and because his sons had never lain with Tamar. Jubilees also dates the twins' birth to the end of Joseph's seven years of plenty, tying the two stories together.

Judah, dying, blames wine and his Canaanite wife Bathshua, who resented Tamar for not being a Canaanite. In this telling Tamar is from Mesopotamia, as in Jubilees, and she sits by the gate in bridal dress following, Judah says, a law of the Amorites for brides. He was drunk, and gave her his staff, his girdle, and his royal crown. He warns his sons that wine leads the eyes astray.

Josephus retells the Joseph story at length but leaves this chapter out entirely. Judah's sons Phares and Zarah appear only in his list of Jacob's family going down to Egypt. Writing for Greek and Roman readers, he simply passes over it.

The Mishnah lists passages that are read aloud in the synagogue but not translated into Aramaic for the congregation, such as Reuben with Bilhah and Aaron's own account of the golden calf. The story of Tamar is not on that list: it is both read and translated. The rabbis judged Judah's confession fit for everyone to hear, embarrassing as it was for the ancestor of the kings.

This Aramaic paraphrase expands v. 25. Tamar cannot find the pledges and prays, vowing three descendants who will one day go into the fiery furnace (Daniel 3); the angel Michael opens her eyes. Judah reasons that it is better to be ashamed in this world than before his fathers in the next, and recalls his own words to Jacob, “Know now the robe of thy son.” A voice from heaven then declares that the matter came from God.

Asks why Tamar did not name Judah outright, and answers that she would rather be burned than shame him in public. From her the rabbis draw a rule: better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to humiliate another person publicly. The same page says Tamar had kept her face covered in Judah's house, which is why he did not know her, and that kings and prophets came from her.

Asks why this story breaks into Joseph's. Following the midrash, he answers that the brothers demoted Judah when they saw their father's grief: had Judah told them to bring Joseph home, they would have obeyed him. So Judah “went down from his brethren” in rank as well as in place.

Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Thamar, the first of four women in it, followed by Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah. Israel had already remembered her as a founding mother: the elders at Bethlehem blessed Boaz's house to be like the house of Pharez, “whom Tamar bare unto Judah” (Ruth 4:12).

Reads the twins as two peoples. Zarah, whose hand with the scarlet thread came out first, stands for faith before circumcision, as in Abraham; he withdrew so that Pharez, the age of circumcision and the law, could be born first. Zarah then came after, as faith without circumcision returned with Christ. The scarlet thread he takes as a sign of the passion.

Preaching on Matthew 1:3, he imagines a hearer objecting to a genealogy that recalls an unlawful union. His answer: if Christ were a mere man, silence would be fitting, but he came for the very purpose of bearing our disgraces. The list also shows that even the patriarchs were under sin. He then takes the midwife's question at Pharez's birth as one of the dark sayings of Scripture.

Faustus the Manichaean used Judah and Tamar to attack the patriarchs and Christ's descent from them. Augustine replies that Scripture records evil without approving it, then reads the story as a figure: Tamar changing her clothes is the Church called from the nations. The ring, bracelets, and staff she receives stand for being called, justified, and glorified (Romans 8:30).

39.overview:
In Egypt, Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, buys Joseph. Because the LORD is with Joseph, everything he handles prospers, and soon he runs the whole household. Potiphar's wife presses him day after day to lie with her. He refuses: his master has trusted him with everything but her, and he will not “sin against God.” One day, with no one else in the house, she grabs his garment; he leaves it in her hand and runs. She shows the garment to the servants and then to her husband as proof of an assault, and Potiphar puts Joseph in the king's prison. There the keeper soon puts him in charge.

For the second time, a garment taken from Joseph is turned into false evidence. His brothers used his coat to prove a death (37:31–33); his master's wife uses his cloak to prove a crime. Both times the person shown the garment believes it.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Between Joseph's sale at 17 (37:2) and his release at 30 (41:46). Ussher's reckoning places the sale in 1728 BC; the traditional early-Exodus reckoning, about 1900 BC.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel, a people who would themselves become servants in Egypt.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The house of an Egyptian court official, then the prison “where the king's prisoners were bound” (v. 20).

39.hermeneutics:
Egyptians knew this plot. Papyrus d'Orbiney in the British Museum, copied about 1215 BC, preserves the *Tale of Two Brothers*. The young Bata lives in the house of his elder brother Anubis. Anubis's wife invites him to lie with her; he refuses, telling her she is like a mother to him. Afraid he will talk, she smears herself with grease to look beaten and tells her husband the boy attacked her, and Anubis goes out to kill him. An Israelite hearing Genesis 39 would recognize a familiar Egyptian scene. In the tale the sun god rescues Bata on the spot; Joseph is not rescued, and the LORD is with him in prison instead.

Foreign slaves in Egyptian households were ordinary. Papyrus Brooklyn 35.1446, from the late Middle Kingdom (c. 1740 BC), lists the 95 servants of one Theban household, and about 45 have Asiatic, that is Semitic, names. Large estates were run by a steward, an “overseer of the house,” a regular Egyptian title. Joseph's rise from bought foreigner to manager of everything “save the bread which he did eat” (v. 6) fits how such households worked.

Joseph's words also match the region's legal language. Egyptian marriage contracts and texts from Ugarit call adultery “the great sin,” and in Genesis Abimelech uses the same phrase for it (20:9). Joseph calls it “this great wickedness” (v. 9), terms his mistress's own world would recognize. Then he adds what her world would not: the wrong is against Potiphar's trust, and it is “against God.”

structure.summary: Inclusio: “the LORD was with Joseph” frames the chapter (vv. 2–6, 21–23).

open.text: The LORD with Joseph; all prospers in Potiphar's house

close.text: The LORD with Joseph; all prospers in the prison

rows.text: Day after day she asks; he refuses
The garment left in her hand
The garment as evidence, told twice

notes: **The divine name:** The LORD (YHWH) is named 8 times here, all inside the frame (vv. 2, 3 twice, 5 twice, 21, 23 twice), and never in the scene with Potiphar's wife, where Joseph speaks of “God.” In all of chs. 37–50 the name occurs only 12 times: the other four are in ch. 38 and at 49:18.

**Two versions:** The word for garment (*beged*) comes 6 times in vv. 12–18. She tells the servants their master “hath brought in an Hebrew unto us” (v. 14), then tells her husband it was the servant “which thou hast brought” (v. 17).
**Hand:** Potiphar puts everything into Joseph's hand (vv. 4, 6, 8), the garment is left in her hand (vv. 12–13), and the keeper puts the prisoners into Joseph's hand (v. 22).

Chapter 39 resumes the Joseph story where 37:36 left it, repeating that Potiphar, captain of the guard, bought him (v. 1). It opens the unit that runs from prison to palace (chs. 39–41). Joseph falls twice, from favored son to slave and from steward to prisoner, before he rises in ch. 41.
**Links:** Set right after ch. 38, Joseph's refusal stands beside Judah's lapse. Stephen sums up these years in a line: the patriarchs sold Joseph, “but God was with him” (Acts 7:9).

traditions.text: Explains why Joseph refused: he remembered the words of Abraham that Jacob used to read to his sons, that death is ordained in heaven for the man who lies with another man's wife, and the sin is written in the eternal books. The woman pleads for a full year. At the end she shuts the doors and holds him, and he breaks through the door to escape; Potiphar sees the broken door along with the garment.

Joseph's own account stretches the trial over seven years of fasting and prayer. The woman, here from Memphis, first claims him as an adopted son, then offers to give up her idols if he will yield, then threatens to kill her husband and marry him, and sends him food laced with charms. At last she seizes his garments and he flees naked. He counts ten temptations, all of them endured.

Potiphar has Joseph taught the learning fit for a free man. His wife waits for a public festival when women went out in crowds, pleads sickness to stay home, and makes her offer with both promises and threats. In prison, Josephus adds, Joseph made no defense and left his case with God.

Gives Joseph a speech that explains Jewish sexual ethics to Greek readers. Other nations let young men visit prostitutes, he says, but among the Hebrews a harlot may not even live, and they come to marriage having known no other woman. Even if no one saw, his own face and conscience would testify against him.

The dying priest Mattathias urges his sons to remember the deeds of their fathers, and Joseph is on the list. Joseph, he says, “in the time of his distress kept the commandment,” and so became lord of Egypt. The refusal in Potiphar's house and the later rise are joined as cause and result, and Joseph stands in a line of the faithful with Abraham, Phinehas, and Daniel.

A Greek Jewish book that retells Genesis as the work of personified Wisdom, without naming anyone. When the righteous man was sold, Wisdom did not forsake him: she “went down with him into the pit,” stayed with him in bonds, and brought him the scepter of the kingdom. She also showed his accusers to be liars, a vindication Genesis itself never narrates for Potiphar's wife.

Two rabbis dispute what Joseph went into the house to do in v. 11: one says his real work, the other that he had given in. The rescue, in this reading, came at the last moment, when the image of his father appeared at the window. It reminded him that his brothers' names would be engraved on the high priest's ephod and asked if he wanted his erased.

This Aramaic paraphrase fills several gaps in the chapter. Joseph refuses her day after day so that he will not share her guilt on the day of the great judgment in the world to come, and on the fatal day he enters the house to check his account tablets, the plainer of the two readings the Talmud weighs for v. 11. It also explains why Potiphar did not execute a slave accused of assault: he consulted the priests, who examined the evidence and found it was only egg white, so Joseph went to prison instead of to his death.

Explains why the story of Tamar comes just before this one: both women acted, the midrash says, with a purpose. Potiphar's wife had foreseen by astrology that she was to be the ancestress of Joseph's children but did not know whether through herself or her daughter. On 41:45 Rashi identifies Potiphera, whose daughter Joseph marries, with Potiphar himself.

The pagan critic Celsus had listed episodes of the Joseph story to ridicule them. Origen points out that Celsus skipped the one that shows virtue: Joseph refusing his mistress's allurements and threats. Joseph, he says, outdid Bellerophon of Greek legend, who faced a similar false charge, since Joseph chose prison over wrongdoing and stayed silent, entrusting his cause to God.

In a handbook on conduct for clergy, Ambrose uses the cloak as a lesson about speech. Joseph fled and left his garment “that he might hear nothing inconsistent with his modesty,” since the one who listens encourages the one who speaks. Elsewhere he says Joseph was a slave but not wretched, since he mastered his mistress's lust.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 1.18.76; 2.5.20

40.overview:
Pharaoh's chief butler and chief baker offend him and are put in the prison where Joseph serves. On the same night each has a dream. The butler sees a vine with three branches whose grapes he presses into Pharaoh's cup; Joseph tells him that in three days Pharaoh will restore him, and begs him to mention Joseph to Pharaoh. The baker sees three baskets of baked goods on his head, with birds eating from the top one; in three days, Joseph says, Pharaoh will hang him and the birds will eat his flesh. On Pharaoh's birthday both readings come true, and the butler forgets Joseph.

Before he hears either dream, Joseph asks, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (v. 8). He claims no technique of his own. The chapter then ends with that gift apparently wasted: the one man who could help him forgets, and Joseph waits two more years.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Two years before Joseph stands before Pharaoh at 30 (41:1, 46), so Joseph is about 28. Ussher dates the officers' dreams to 1717 BC.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The prison in the house of the captain of the guard (v. 3), then Pharaoh's birthday feast (v. 20).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 41:9–13 (the butler's retelling); Psalm 105:18–19.

40.hermeneutics:
Egyptians wrote dream interpretation down. Papyrus Chester Beatty III in the British Museum, copied around 1220 BC and probably compiled centuries earlier, lists dreams line by line: “if a man sees himself in a dream” doing something, then a verdict, good or bad, then a meaning. Looking out of a window, for example, is good: his cry will be heard. Many entries turn on a pun between the dream and its meaning. The officers' complaint that “there is no interpreter” (v. 8) fits that world, since in prison they have no access to the experts and their books. Joseph needs neither. His readings come from details inside each dream, three branches and three baskets, and he credits God.

The butler was a court official, not a waiter. In New Kingdom Egypt the royal butler was a personal attendant of the king, later sent on missions far from the palace, and in the Ramesside period many who held the title had foreign names. A man close enough to hand Pharaoh his cup was close enough to speak in his ear. That is why Joseph asks him to “make mention of me unto Pharaoh” (v. 14).

The baker's sentence was worse than death. Egyptian religion held that the dead needed a preserved, buried body to live on; tombs and embalming existed to secure it. To be hanged and left for the birds (v. 19) meant losing the afterlife along with life. An Egyptian listener would hear Joseph's second reading as the harshest sentence he could pronounce.

Two dreams in one night; “interpretations belong to God”
The butler's vine: restored in three days; “think on me”
The baker's baskets: hanged in three days
Pharaoh's birthday: one restored, one hanged
The chief butler forgets Joseph
Two full years later, Pharaoh dreams

structure.summary: Parallel panels (A B C / A′ B′ C′) inside a frame: two dreams, two readings, two outcomes.

open.text: Two officers in prison, two dreams; “interpretations belong to God”

left.label: A
left.text: Butler's dream: vine, three branches, Pharaoh's cup

right.label: A′
right.text: Baker's dream: three baskets, birds eating

left.label: B
left.text: Three days: Pharaoh will lift up thy head

right.label: B′
right.text: Three days: Pharaoh will lift up thy head from off thee

notes: **Lift up the head:** The phrase comes three times: for the butler (v. 13), for the baker with “from off thee” added (v. 19), and for both on the birthday (v. 20). The same words mean restoration for one man and execution for the other.
**Threes:** The Hebrew word for three occurs 8 times: three branches, three baskets, and three days for each.
**The break in the pattern:** Only the butler's panel carries a plea, “think on me” (vv. 14–15). The frame's last line answers it: he “forgat him” (v. 23).

The middle chapter of the prison-to-palace unit. It opens in the prison where ch. 39 ended (v. 3) and sets up ch. 41. The butler's forgetting keeps Joseph in prison until Pharaoh dreams, and his remembering “at the end of two full years” (41:1, 9) gets him out.
**Looking back and ahead:** Joseph's own dreams (ch. 37) were about himself. Here, for the first time, he interprets other men's dreams, and in ch. 41 he will interpret a king's.

traditions.text: A hymn that retells Israel's history from Abraham to the Exodus adds a detail Genesis lacks: Joseph's feet were hurt with fetters, and he was laid in iron. It also gives the prison years a meaning, calling them the time until his word came, when “the word of the LORD tried him.” Genesis shows a trusted prisoner who runs the place; the psalm remembers chains. Then the king sent and loosed him, which the psalm treats as God's doing from first to last.

Notes that Joseph had already been in prison two years when the officers arrived, and calls them Pharaoh's two eunuchs, the same title it gives Potiphar. It tells the dreams in a single sentence and dwells instead on the butler's forgetting: he did not remember to tell Pharaoh what Joseph had foretold, “for he forgot.” The next chapter opens with Pharaoh's dreams, so the two years pass without a word.

The keeper, struck by Joseph's diligence and dignity, loosens his bonds and feeds him better than the other prisoners, and the butler, chained beside him, confides his dream because Joseph seems the wisest of them. In his reading Joseph praises wine as God's gift, a pledge of trust among men that ends quarrels and drives away grief. The baker carries two baskets of loaves and a third of delicacies, and Joseph says he would rather have announced good news. On the king's birthday the baker is crucified, as foretold.

Before the officers arrive, Philo has Joseph reform the whole prison. The keeper hands over the real work to him, and his teaching and example so change the inmates that they stop calling the place a prison and call it a house of correction. For Philo, Joseph is already the model statesman, governing a prison before he governs Egypt. In his version the vine grows from three roots, and the baker is told he will be crucified and beheaded.

Asks why the officers' offense follows “after these things.” Since Potiphar's wife had made Joseph the talk of Egypt, God turned people's attention to the two officers, and they became the means of Joseph's release. Their offenses, following the midrash, were small: a fly in Pharaoh's cup and a pebble in his bread.

Explains the two extra years in prison. Joseph, says this Aramaic paraphrase of v. 23, had turned from the mercy above and put his trust in the chief butler, so the butler forgot him until God's appointed time came. Rashi gives the same reading from the midrash, citing Psalm 40:4: blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust. The plea “think on me” (v. 14) is read as a lapse of faith.
traditions.cite: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 40:23; Rashi on Genesis 40:23

traditions.text: Collects rabbinic readings of the butler's vine. Rabbi Eliezer takes the three branches as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Rabbi Joshua objects that a dream shows only what is still to come, and reads them as Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. Others see Jerusalem with its Temple, king, and high priest; the well, the cloud, and the manna in the wilderness; or the three pilgrimage festivals. The dream becomes a lens on Israel's whole history.

The pagan critic Celsus had cited the dreams of the butler, the baker, and Pharaoh, and Joseph's rise to second place in Egypt, as if the story were absurd on its face. Origen asks what absurdity there is in it, even read only literally. He adds that the narrative is attractive in itself, quite apart from its figurative meaning, and that no fair critic could find fault with it. The exchange shows that by the second century outsiders were reading the Joseph chapters closely enough to attack them.

In a sermon on Joseph, Ambrose makes the two officers a warning to royal servants: their standing hangs on the king's will, and a slight offense can bring ruin. He declines to discuss the baker's dream at all, saying its end recalls a man whose death makes him shudder; his translator identifies him as Calligonus, a court chamberlain who had threatened Ambrose and was later executed. The butler's pride in his office was itself a dream, Ambrose says, since all worldly power is one. In Joseph's plea to be remembered he hears Christ speaking through a servant, and in Joseph's prison he sees Christ descending to loose the bonds of the dead.

41.overview:
Two years later Pharaoh dreams twice: seven lean cows eat seven fat ones, and seven thin ears of grain swallow seven full ones. None of Egypt's magicians can explain it. The butler at last remembers Joseph, who is shaved, dressed, and brought up from the dungeon. Joseph tells Pharaoh that God has shown him seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, and advises storing a fifth of the harvest. Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt and gives him his ring, fine linen, a gold chain, a new name, and a wife, Asenath. Joseph fills the cities with grain, has two sons, and when the famine comes, all lands come to Egypt to buy.

Notice the names Joseph gives his sons. Manasseh means God “hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house” (v. 51). Joseph seems ready to leave his family behind, just as the famine is about to bring them to his door.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Joseph is 30 (v. 46). Ussher dates his rise to 1715 BC; the early-Exodus reckoning (Exodus c. 1446 BC, 430 years in Egypt) places it about 1885 BC.

historicalContext.label: First audience
historicalContext.text: Israel; the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh traced themselves to the two sons born here (vv. 50–52).

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Pharaoh's court, and On (Greek Heliopolis), city of the sun god, home of Joseph's father-in-law (v. 45).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Psalm 105:20–22; Acts 7:10–11. The Book of Mormon recalls Joseph preserving his family from famine (1 Nephi 5:14) and traces Lehi to Manasseh (Alma 10:3).

41.hermeneutics:
Pharaoh's “magicians” (*hartummim*, v. 8) carry an Egyptian title. Most scholars derive the word from the title of the chief lector priest, the temple scholar who read the sacred books and knew ritual and dream lore. Egyptians treated a king's dream as a message from the gods: on the Dream Stela of Thutmose IV, set between the paws of the Sphinx, the god promises the throne to the sleeping prince. So Pharaoh calls the experts first, and when the readers of the sacred books fail, a foreign slave from the prison succeeds.

Joseph's installation follows Egyptian court practice. The king's signet ring let him seal in Pharaoh's name, fine linen was the dress of the elite, and a gold collar was the reward pharaohs hung on favored officials; tomb reliefs at Amarna show the king showering an official with gold collars from a palace window. Joseph also receives an Egyptian name and a wife from a priestly family. Egyptologists have proposed meanings for Zaphnath-paaneah, such as “the god speaks and he lives,” but none is certain. Asenath (perhaps “belonging to Neith”) and Poti-pherah (commonly “he whom Ra gave”) are better understood.

Egypt's food depended on the Nile flood, and a run of low floods meant famine. That is why the cows come up “out of the river” (v. 2), the source of both plenty and want. The Famine Stela on Sehel Island near Aswan, carved in the Ptolemaic period (probably 2nd century BC), tells of seven years of low Nile under King Djoser, ended after the god Khnum appeared to the king in a dream. It is far later than Joseph and is no record of his famine, but it shows seven lean years as an Egyptian way of telling a famine story.

The chief butler remembers the Hebrew in prison
Joseph brought from the dungeon; Pharaoh retells his dreams
“The dream is one”: seven years of plenty, seven of famine
Joseph's plan: officers, and a fifth stored in the cities
Set over Egypt: ring, linen, chain, chariot, name, wife
Joseph, thirty, gathers grain beyond counting
Two sons: Manasseh and Ephraim
The famine begins; all lands come to Joseph

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. Inside it, Pharaoh's dream is told twice (below).

rows.text: Pharaoh's dreams; the experts fail; the butler remembers
Joseph before Pharaoh: the dream retold, read, and answered with a plan

left.label: A
left.text: Narrator: seven fat cows eaten by seven lean

right.label: A′
right.text: Pharaoh: lean cows worse than any in Egypt, no fatter after eating

left.label: B
left.text: Narrator: seven thin ears swallow seven full

right.label: B′
right.text: Pharaoh: the thin ears also withered; none could declare it

notes: **Sevens:** The Hebrew word for seven occurs 28 times in the chapter, four times seven.

**Told twice:** Pharaoh's retelling adds his own horror at the lean cows and the detail that they looked no better after eating. Joseph explains that the doubling itself has meaning: the dream was doubled “because the thing is established by God” (v. 32).

**God's name at court:** *Elohim* (God) occurs 9 times. Joseph uses it six times before Pharaoh, Pharaoh picks it up (vv. 38–39), and it ends the chapter in the names of Joseph's sons (vv. 51–52). The personal name YHWH does not appear.

Chapter 41 closes the prison-to-palace unit. It opens two years after ch. 40 and ends with “all countries” coming to Egypt for grain (v. 57), which brings Joseph's brothers in ch. 42. Joseph's clothes trace his path: the coat stripped (37:23), the garment left behind (39:12), and now a change of raiment (v. 14) and Pharaoh's fine linen (v. 42).
**Looking ahead:** The famine brings the brothers to bow before Joseph (42:6), and Jacob later adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons (48:5).

traditions.text: Lehi finds on the brass plates that Joseph “was preserved by the hand of the Lord” so that he might save Jacob's household from famine. Moroni's abridgment of Ether draws the parallel out: as God was merciful to Joseph's father so that he would not perish, he brought a remnant of Joseph's seed out of Jerusalem so that they would not perish. Lehi's journey is read as a second preservation of Joseph's family.

The two sons born in v. 50–52 matter in Restoration scripture. Amulek traces Lehi's line to Manasseh, son of Joseph, and the Doctrine and Covenants speaks of “the richer blessing upon the head of Ephraim and his fellows” in the gathering of Israel. The births at the end of this chapter become the roots of two latter-day lineages.

Has a herald cry “El El wa Abirer” before Joseph's chariot and adds that Joseph ruled without pride, took no bribes, and judged with no respect of persons, so that Pharaoh's kingdom had no Satan in it. It gives his new name as Sephantiphans and makes his wife the daughter of Potiphar, priest of Heliopolis and chief cook, so the father-in-law is Joseph's former master. In the good years, it says, one measure yielded eighteen hundred.

In his telling, Pharaoh saw both dreams and their interpretation in the night, then forgot the interpretation, so Joseph's task is to recover it. Pharaoh lets Joseph use his seal and wear purple, and names him Psothom Phanech, which Josephus says means “the revealer of secrets.” Asenath is the daughter of Petephres, a priest of Heliopolis.

Lists the seal, the sacred robe, the golden circlet, the second chariot, and the herald, and says the new name referred to Joseph's skill with dreams. Then he allegorizes the chariot: the statesman rides second because he stands between private citizen and king. He serves the people as his true master.

Onkelos renders Zaphnath-paaneah as the man to whom hidden things are revealed, close to Josephus's gloss, and turns the herald's cry (*avrekh*, v. 43) into a title: the king's father, that is, his counselor. Rashi passes on a rabbinic debate over that word. Rabbi Judah split it into father in wisdom and tender in years, and Rabbi Jose ben Dormaskit protested that it can only come from the word for knees, as in the KJV's “Bow the knee.”
traditions.cite: Onkelos on Genesis 41:43, 45; Rashi on Genesis 41:43

traditions.text: Pharaoh's astrologers object that a slave cannot rule; a king must know the seventy languages. That night the angel Gabriel teaches Joseph all of them, adding a letter of God's name to his own so that he can learn them; the Hebrew of Psalm 81:5 spells his name Yehoseph. The next day he answers Pharaoh in every language Pharaoh tries.

A romance that answers the question of how Joseph could marry an Egyptian priest's daughter. Aseneth first scorns him, then repents, throws her gold and silver gods out of her window to the poor, and is visited by a heavenly messenger. Joseph, who will not marry before she turns to his God, asks Pharaoh for her, and Pharaoh declares her betrothed to Joseph from eternity.

Solves the same problem another way. Asenath was really the daughter of Dinah, conceived when Shechem took her (ch. 34). Jacob hung a golden plate with God's name around the child's neck and sent her away; the angel Michael carried her to Egypt, where Potiphera's childless wife raised her. Joseph's Egyptian bride turns out to be Jacob's granddaughter.

A Syriac bishop in Persia lists Joseph's life as a pattern of Jesus'. Joseph stood before Pharaoh at thirty, and Jesus was about thirty at his baptism; Joseph fed Egypt with bread, and Jesus feeds the world with the bread of life. Joseph's marriage to the daughter of a pagan priest stands for Christ taking a Church from the Gentiles.

Holds up Joseph as the model of prudent generosity. Joseph opened the granaries to all but sold the grain instead of giving it away, Ambrose says, so that there would be enough for everyone and people would not stop working their land. He contrasts Joseph with hoarders who hold grain back for higher prices.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.16.79–83; 3.6.42

traditions.date: 1st century BC; epitome c. 2nd–4th century AD
traditions.text: A Roman historian's account of the Jews, preserved in Justin's summary. Joseph, youngest of the brothers, was sold to foreign merchants because they feared his abilities, mastered the arts of magic in Egypt, and was “the first to establish the science of interpreting dreams.” He foresaw a famine years ahead and saved Egypt by having grain stored. Trogus then makes Moses Joseph's son.

42.overview:
Famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons to Egypt for grain, keeping Benjamin at home. They bow to the ground before the governor without knowing him. Joseph knows them at once. Speaking harshly through an interpreter, he calls them spies, jails them for three days, then keeps Simeon and sends the rest home with grain, their silver secretly put back in their sacks, and an order to bring their youngest brother. At home Jacob refuses: Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and Benjamin will not go.

Watch what each side remembers. When the brothers bow, Joseph remembers his dreams (v. 9). Under pressure, the brothers remember the pit: “we saw the anguish of his soul” (v. 21), a detail chapter 37 never told. Joseph, listening, turns away and weeps. The guilt surfaces before the test is even explained.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly estimates for the Joseph story vary widely.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Early in the seven-year famine, a year or so before Jacob's move to Egypt. Ussher dates that move to 1706 BC; counting back from 1 Kings 6:1 and Exodus 12:40 gives about 1876 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. Inside the story Joseph speaks through an interpreter (v. 23), so the brothers assume he cannot follow their talk.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jacob's camp in Canaan (near Hebron, 37:14) and the place in Egypt where Joseph sold grain; the text names no city.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Acts 7:11–12. In the Book of Mormon, 1 Nephi 5:14 says Joseph was preserved so that he might preserve Jacob's household from famine.

42.hermeneutics:
Canaan's crops depended on rain; Egypt's depended on the Nile flood. A drought in the hills could leave the Nile valley untouched, so Canaanites in hard years went down to Egypt, as Abram did (12:10). Egyptian records show the traffic. A tomb painting at Beni Hasan (c. 1890 BC) shows a party of 37 Asiatics with donkeys arriving under a leader named Abisha, and a border official in Papyrus Anastasi VI (c. 1200 BC) reports letting herders from Edom past the fortress at Tjeku to the pools of Per-Atum “to keep them alive.” Ten brothers arriving with their donkeys would have looked ordinary.

That same border was watched closely. Egypt guarded its eastern approach with forts, and the *Story of Sinuhe* has its hero hiding from the watchmen on the “Walls of the Ruler,” built to keep Asiatics out. A group of foreign men asking questions could plausibly be scouting. Joseph's charge, that they came to see “the nakedness of the land,” means its weak points, and an Egyptian official would have heard it as a serious accusation, not a pretext.

Joseph also swears “by the life of Pharaoh” (vv. 15–16). Egyptian legal oaths were taken on the life of the king, so the phrase is part of his disguise: he talks the way an Egyptian official talks. The famine itself has an Egyptian echo in the Famine Stela on Sehel Island, a Ptolemaic inscription that sets seven years of low Nile in the reign of King Djoser.

Before the governor: the bow, the spy charge, three days' ward
Simeon held; the brothers confess their guilt over Joseph
Silver found in one sack on the road home
The report to Jacob; silver in every sack
Jacob refuses to send Benjamin; Reuben's offer rejected

structure.summary: Parallel panels: the brothers' report to Jacob (vv. 29–35) retells the scene in Egypt (vv. 7–28). Not a chiasm.

left.label: B
left.text: True men, twelve brothers, one is not

left.label: C
left.text: Leave one brother, bring the youngest

right.label: C′
right.text: The terms as they report them

notes: The report edits the scene. The three days in prison and Simeon's binding drop out, and the brothers add a promise that they may “traffick in the land” (v. 34), which the governor never made in vv. 18–20.

**Recognize:** the Hebrew root *nakar* comes four times in vv. 7–8. Joseph recognizes them, “made himself strange” (same root), recognizes them, and they do not recognize him. The root links back to 37:32–33 (“know now whether it be thy son's coat”) and 38:25–26 (Tamar's “discern”).
**Spies** (*meraggelim*) occurs seven times (vv. 9, 11, 14, 16, 30, 31, 34).

Chapters 42–45 form one movement inside the account headed “These are the generations of Jacob” (37:2). It opens with Jacob sending his sons down for grain and closes when he resolves to go down himself (45:28). Two journeys shape it: this one, and the return trip of 43–44 that ends in Joseph's self-revelation.

**Links:** Jacob's fear that they will “bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” (v. 38) echoes his vow in 37:35 to go down to the grave mourning. Stephen retells this first journey in Acts 7:11–12.

traditions.text: Lehi reads a genealogy on the brass plates and learns he descends from Joseph, the son of Jacob who was sold into Egypt. Nephi states the purpose of that sale in one line: Joseph “was preserved by the hand of the Lord,” so that he could keep Jacob's household from perishing in the famine. The Book of Mormon reads the grain journeys as the point of Joseph's suffering, the same reading Joseph himself gives in Genesis 45:5–7.

Dates the famine to the year 2171 from creation and adds that no rain fell at all. It also explains why Egypt held out: ordinary Egyptians had watched Joseph store grain and stored their own. Jacob's refusal gets a homely reason. Benjamin might catch a fever on the road, and his mother bore only two sons.

Gives Joseph a gentler first offer: the brothers may stay and send for Benjamin by letter. In Philo the brothers say justice, quiet for a while, has now woken up against them. Reuben answers that the one demanding Joseph's blood is “not man, but either God, or reason, or the law of God.”

Has Joseph argue that no private man could raise so many handsome sons, so they must be strangers posing as brothers. Josephus also says what Joseph was after: news of his father and of Benjamin, because he feared they had done to Benjamin what they had done to him. Reuben speaks for the brothers and later reproaches them for repenting too late.

traditions.date: 2nd century BC, with later Christian additions
traditions.text: One of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, deathbed speeches put in the mouths of Jacob's sons. Simeon confesses that envy made him want to kill Joseph. When the governor bound him as a spy, he says, he knew he was suffering justly and did not complain. Rashi, below, gives a similar reason for why Simeon was the one held.

Jacob told his sons not to enter the city by a single gate, so that so many handsome brothers would not draw the evil eye. That is why they come “among those that came” (v. 5). In the midrash Joseph uses the ten gates against them: honest brothers travelling together would have come in together.

Asks why v. 1 says Jacob “saw” there was grain when v. 2 says he heard it, and answers from the midrash that he glimpsed in a dim vision that his hope lay in Egypt, without learning it was Joseph. Jacob says “get you down,” not “go,” and the Hebrew letters of that word add up to 210, read as the years Israel would spend in Egypt. The brothers are called “Joseph's brethren” in v. 3, Rashi says, because they now regretted the sale and meant to find and ransom him.

Explains why Joseph knew them but they did not know him: they already had beards when he left, and he did not. Following the midrash, he names the interpreter of v. 23 as Joseph's son Manasseh. Simeon was taken because he had thrown Joseph into the pit, and Joseph wanted him separated from Levi; once the others left, Rashi says, Joseph released him and fed him.

Stephen, on trial in Jerusalem, retells the story: the dearth hits Egypt and Canaan, “our fathers found no sustenance,” and Jacob sends them “first.” The recognition comes only on the second trip. Stephen's larger point is a pattern in which Israel's fathers first fail to recognize the deliverer God sends.

Takes v. 6, Joseph as the one who “sold to all the people,” as a lesson for clergy handing out alms. Joseph could have given Egypt's grain away but chose to sell it. Given free to a few, it would have run out for the many; sold, it reached everyone, and no one stopped farming in the hope of free bread.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.16.79

traditions.text: Asks how an upright man like Joseph could swear “by the life of Pharaoh” to a threat he did not fully carry out. His answer: Joseph did keep one brother until Benjamin came, and the threat that they are spies means they will be treated as spies if their story proves false. He also notes that the dream of sun and moon bowing (37:9–10) could not be fulfilled literally, since Joseph's mother was already dead.

43.overview:
The grain runs out, and Jacob tells his sons to go back to Egypt. Judah tells him they cannot go without Benjamin and pledges himself as surety for the boy. Jacob gives in, sending gifts, double silver, and a prayer to God Almighty. In Egypt the brothers are led into Joseph's house and fear a trap, but the steward tells them not to be afraid and brings out Simeon. Joseph sees Benjamin, blesses him, and leaves the room to weep. At the meal the brothers find themselves seated in order of age, and Benjamin's portion is five times larger than theirs.

The hinge is Judah's pledge (v. 9). The brother who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) now stakes himself on Rachel's other son, and Jacob, who has clung to Benjamin, lets go: “If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” (v. 14).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly estimates for the Joseph story vary widely.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The second year of the famine (45:6), just before Jacob's move to Egypt, which Ussher dates to 1706 BC; counting back from 1 Kings 6:1 and Exodus 12:40 gives about 1876 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jacob's household in Canaan, then Joseph's own house in Egypt, where he dines apart from both his Egyptian guests and the Hebrews (v. 32).

43.hermeneutics:
The narrator explains the three tables in v. 32: eating with Hebrews was “an abomination unto the Egyptians.” Greek visitors met the same wall centuries later. Herodotus reports that no Egyptian would kiss a Greek, use a Greek's knife, spit, or cauldron, or eat the meat of a clean bull cut with a Greek knife, because cows were sacred to Isis and foreigners did not keep the rules that protected them. Read with that in mind, the seating is ordinary Egyptian purity practice. The brothers eat in a great man's house, yet they remain outsiders at his table, and Joseph, eating alone, keeps up the role of an Egyptian lord who cannot share a table with them.

Jacob's gift is a sample of what a drought-stricken hill country could still offer: balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds (v. 11). These are tree and shrub products, not grain, and Canaan exported them to Egypt. The Uluburun shipwreck (c. 1300 BC) carried about 150 Canaanite jars, most holding resin of the *Pistacia* (terebinth) tree, and jars of the same clay found at Amarna in Egypt were used to carry the same resin. The gift also has an edge. Balm, myrrh, and spices are what the Ishmaelite caravan was carrying to Egypt when the brothers sold Joseph to it (37:25). They now carry the same goods down themselves, to the brother they sold.

breakdown.label: The food runs out; Judah pledges himself for Benjamin
Jacob sends gifts, double silver, and Benjamin
Brought to Joseph's house: fear, the steward's reassurance, Simeon freed
Joseph sees Benjamin, blesses him, and weeps in private
The meal: separate tables, seating by age, Benjamin's fivefold portion

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three places.

rows.text: The doorway of Joseph's house: fear of a trap
Inside: gifts, tears, and the meal

notes: **Present** (*minchah*, the gift for a superior) comes four times (vv. 11, 15, 25, 26), carrying the brothers from Canaan to Joseph's feet.
**Bowing:** the brothers bow twice (vv. 26, 28), and now there are eleven of them, the number of the stars in Joseph's second dream (37:9).
**Yet alive:** Joseph's question about his father, “Is he yet alive?” (v. 27), first raised in v. 7, will be the first thing he asks when he reveals himself (45:3).

This is the second of the two journeys in chapters 42–45. The visit begins here and runs straight into the cup episode of chapter 44, so the chapter break falls in the middle of a single stay in Egypt. The banquet is the calm before the last test.
**Links:** Judah's “of my hand shalt thou require him” (v. 9) is the pledge he will cite to Joseph in 44:32, and Jacob's blessing later gives Judah the leadership among his brothers (49:8–10).

traditions.text: Dates the second journey to the first day of a month in the year after the famine began, and keeps Reuben's offer and Judah's pledge, with Judah promising to bear the blame “all the days of my life.” Jacob's gift becomes stacte, almonds, terebinth nuts, and pure honey. Benjamin's portion is seven times larger than his brothers'.

Gives Judah a longer speech to his father: nothing can happen to Benjamin except by God's appointment, and keeping him home only puts Simeon at risk. Jacob weeps over his sons, and Josephus says the lament lasted a whole day. When Joseph learns the youngest is Benjamin, he answers that the God over all is his protector, then withdraws to weep. At the meal the brothers are seated as they sat at their father's table, and Benjamin's portion is only double.

Pictures the brothers so afraid of being charged with stealing the returned silver that they defend themselves before anyone accuses them. At the meal, Philo says, Joseph served each group by its own national customs, thinking it wrong to overturn ancient laws at a banquet. The brothers, seated by age, marvel that Egyptians know how to honor the eldest and the youngest. Philo adds that the table was plain, since Joseph would not feast lavishly while others were starving.

A Jewish writer in Egypt whose work survives in quotations preserved by Eusebius. He solves the puzzle of Benjamin's fivefold portion with arithmetic: Benjamin's five plus Joseph's own two make seven, matching Leah's seven children. Rachel's house thus received as much as Leah's, and Demetrius applies the same reasoning to Benjamin's five changes of clothing in 45:22.

Explains how Joseph knew the birth order. He struck his goblet as if divining and called out the sons of each mother in turn, then seated Benjamin beside himself, since both had lost their mother. The five portions were Benjamin's own plus gifts from Joseph, Asenath, Manasseh, and Ephraim. And “they drank”: the brothers, and Joseph, had not drunk wine since the day of the sale.

Reads Jacob's “your other brother” (v. 14) as an unknowing prophecy that included Joseph. He hears in the divine name *El Shaddai* the word for “enough,” and has Jacob pray that God say “enough” to his troubles, which he lists: Laban, Esau, Rachel, Dinah, Joseph, Simeon, and now Benjamin. Rashi also reads Judah's plea in v. 8, that they may live, as a promise that Jacob's own spirit would live again, as it does in 45:27.

Supplies the conversation behind Joseph's sudden tears in v. 30. Joseph asks Benjamin about his sons, and Benjamin explains that he named all ten for the brother he lost: Bela because Joseph was “swallowed up,” Becher because he was the firstborn of their mother, Ashbel because he was taken captive, Huppim because neither brother saw the other's wedding canopy, and so on through the list in 46:21. Hearing his own story in his nephews' names, Joseph has to leave the room.

Hears a confession of humiliation in the brothers' opening words at the door, “we came indeed down” (v. 20): men used to feeding others now had to beg for food. The steward's answer names two sources of the treasure in their sacks, their own God and the God of their father, and Rashi takes them as two kinds of merit. If their own merit was not enough, their father's would carry them.

This Aramaic translation, read aloud in synagogues, spells out the “abomination” of v. 32. The Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews because the Hebrews ate the animals the Egyptians worshiped. The explanation fits what Herodotus says about sacred cattle (see Hermeneutics), and Rashi gives the same reason for the shepherds of 46:34.

Takes up two moral puzzles. The steward's “I had your money” (v. 23) sounds like a lie, so Augustine looks for a hidden sense: silver tested and found good is the Lord's word, purified seven times (Psalm 12:6). And when his Latin Bible says the brothers drank and “were drunk” with Joseph, he insists that in Scripture the word can mean “filled,” as when God makes the earth drunk with rain (Psalm 65:9).

44.overview:
Joseph sends the brothers home with full sacks, their silver returned again, and his own silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. His steward overtakes them on the road and accuses them of theft. Sure of their innocence, they offer death for the thief and slavery for the rest, and the cup turns up in Benjamin's sack. They tear their clothes and go back together. Before Joseph, Judah confesses that God has found out their guilt, then pleads at length: he retells the first visit, his father's grief, and his own pledge, and asks to stay as a slave so the boy can go home.

The test rebuilds chapter 37. Once more the brothers can walk away free while Rachel's son becomes a slave in Egypt, and Joseph even offers them that way out (v. 17). Judah's speech (vv. 18–34) refuses it, and that refusal is the turning point of the whole story.

44.hermeneutics:
The steward calls the silver cup the one “whereby indeed he divineth” (v. 5), and Joseph asks whether they did not know that a man like him “can certainly divine” (v. 15). Divining with a cup of liquid is real ancient practice. Old Babylonian omen texts read the shapes that oil makes when poured onto water in a bowl, and much later Egyptian handbooks, such as the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden (3rd century AD), describe vessel divination in detail. To the brothers, then, the missing object was more than tableware: it was the sacred instrument of the man who read Pharaoh's dreams, and its theft explains how he “found out” the thief. The narrator reports these claims but never shows Joseph using the cup. Israel's law later forbids divining (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10), and the claim reads best as part of Joseph's Egyptian mask.

The penalties fit ancient law. The Laws of Hammurabi (c. 1750 BC) put to death anyone who steals the property of a temple or of the palace, and the one who receives it too (§6). So when the brothers offer death for the thief and slavery for themselves (v. 9), they name the punishment such a theft could bring. Joseph's ruling sounds lenient by comparison: only the guilty man will stay, as a slave, and the rest may go home in peace (v. 17). That leniency is the trap. It gives the brothers a lawful way to do again what they did to Joseph.
