structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence and ends in a long speech.

rows.text: The verdict: the others may go

notes: **Father** comes 14 times in Judah's speech (vv. 18–34) and “my lord” 7 times. Judah keeps putting the old man in front of the Egyptian lord, without knowing that the lord is the old man's son.
**The lad** (*na'ar*) appears seven times in vv. 22–34, Judah's word for Benjamin as he moves from report to plea.

**An echo of 31:32:** the brothers' oath, “With whomsoever of thy servants it be found, both let him die” (v. 9), repeats Jacob's rash vow over Laban's stolen gods, which also put Rachel's life at stake without his knowing it.

Chapter 44 finishes the second journey begun in 43:1 and brings the tests of chapters 42–44 to their climax. Joseph's response follows without a pause (“Then Joseph could not refrain himself,” 45:1), so the chapter break falls between Judah's last word and Joseph's tears.
**Links:** Judah's pledge here makes good on his words in 43:9, and Jacob's blessing later gives Judah the place his brothers will praise (49:8–10).

traditions.text: Makes the cup gold and says nothing about divining. He states Joseph's purpose plainly: to see whether the brothers would stand by Benjamin or leave him and go home. In his version a troop of horsemen overtakes them, and Judah's plea becomes a long speech that appeals to Joseph's own good nature: the governor who saved them from famine once should not now destroy them, and they would all accept punishment if the boy could go free.

Calls the cup the most beautiful of Joseph's silver drinking cups and, like Josephus, drops the divining. Judah is “the fourth in age,” bold but modest. Philo then explains the whole sequence as three tests: the spy charge, the banquet where Joseph watched their faces for envy at Benjamin's portion, and the theft charge, which would show most clearly how they felt about Rachel's son.

Also removes the divining. Joseph's line becomes a question of taste: do they not know that a man delights in his cup, as he does in this one? Judah's speech is cut to its core, and Joseph reveals himself when he sees that the brothers are “all accordant in goodness one with another.” Jubilees, Philo, and Josephus all left out the divination of vv. 5 and 15.

The standard Aramaic translation does not have Joseph divine at all. In vv. 5 and 15 it says he “examines” or “tests” with the cup, so his claim becomes a boast of investigating skill. Rashi takes the same line: Joseph meant that a man of his standing could work out by reasoning who had taken it.

The verb for Judah's approach in v. 18 is read three ways: he came near ready for battle, for conciliation, or for prayer, and Rabbi Elazar says he was ready for all three. The midrash pictures Judah's anger so loud that it was heard far away and nearly shook Egypt. In one exchange Joseph asks why he did not show this concern when he sold his brother for twenty pieces of silver.

Judah's “God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants” (v. 16) puzzles readers, since the brothers did not steal the cup. The midrash, followed by Rashi, has them say that they know they did nothing wrong here, but the Creditor has found an occasion to collect his debt. The old sin against Joseph, not the cup, is what God has found. The brothers' argument in v. 8, that men who returned found silver would hardly steal, is counted among the ten arguments from the lesser to the greater in the Torah.

Notes that the steward searched from the eldest down so that no one would suspect he knew where the cup was. Judah's “thou art even as Pharaoh” (v. 18) is read both as honor and as a veiled threat: Pharaoh was struck with plague for holding Sarah one night (12:17). Judah presses harder than the others, Rashi says, because he alone had bound himself as surety.

Reads Judah's speech line by line for what it does not say. “His brother is dead” (v. 20) is an untruth spoken out of fear, since Judah thought that admitting Joseph was alive would bring the demand to produce him too. The warning that the lad would die if he left his father (v. 22) means the brothers feared Benjamin would die on a journey, as his mother had. And Jacob's grief in v. 29 is grief for three: Benjamin comforted him for Rachel and Joseph, so losing him would be like losing all three in one day.

Asks whether Joseph lied when he claimed to divine, and answers that he spoke in play, and that a jest is not a lie. The harder question is why so wise a man kept his brothers in fear so long. Augustine's answer is that every delay was meant to make their final joy, on recognizing the brother they thought they had lost, all the greater.

traditions.date: 1st century BC (epitome by Justin, c. 2nd–4th century AD)
traditions.text: A Roman historian whose account of the Jews survives in Justin's abridgment. He calls Joseph the youngest of the brothers, sold to foreign merchants because they feared his abilities. In Egypt Joseph made himself “master of the arts of magic,” founded the science of interpreting dreams, and foresaw the dearth, so that Egypt would have perished without him. Outsiders, in other words, remembered Joseph the way his steward describes him in v. 5.

45.overview:
Joseph sends everyone else out of the room, weeps so loudly that the Egyptians hear, and says, “I am Joseph.” His brothers are too terrified to answer. He draws them close and explains: they sold him, but God sent him ahead of them to preserve life, and five years of famine remain. He tells them to bring Jacob down to live near him in Goshen, then embraces Benjamin and kisses them all. Pharaoh adds wagons and the best of Egypt. Jacob does not believe the news until he sees the wagons; then his spirit revives.

Notice that Joseph never pretends the sale did not happen. He says “whom ye sold” (v. 4) before he says anything about God. Forgiveness here does not erase the wrong; it sets the wrong inside a larger purpose, a reading Genesis repeats in 50:20.

historicalContext.text: The second year of the famine, with five years still to come (v. 6). Ussher dates Jacob's move to Egypt to 1706 BC; counting back from 1 Kings 6:1 and Exodus 12:40 gives about 1876 BC.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Acts 7:13–14. In the Book of Mormon, 1 Nephi 5:14 gives the same purpose: Joseph was preserved to preserve his father's household from famine.

45.hermeneutics:
Joseph describes his rank in three phrases: “a father to Pharaoh,” “lord of all his house,” and “ruler throughout all the land” (v. 8). These sound like the titles of an Egyptian court, and the brothers would have heard them that way. Egyptian officials could carry the honorific “god's father,” and the steward of the palace estate, the “overseer of the house,” was one of the great offices of state. For the brothers, the words described a man near the top of the Egyptian state. For the reader, Joseph's point is that God put him there (vv. 8–9), and that the rank exists to feed his family.

The offer of Goshen (v. 10) fits what archaeology shows of the eastern Delta. Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, ancient Avaris, uncovered a large settlement of people of Canaanite culture there from about 1800 BC, with Canaanite-style houses, burials, and pottery; it later became the capital of the Hyksos, foreign kings who ruled northern Egypt. The eastern Delta was Egypt's border country, where newcomers from Canaan could live as herders near the route home. Pharaoh's generous welcome (vv. 17–20) is unusual in its warmth, but settling a Semitic family in that region would not have surprised an Egyptian.

structure.summary: Inclusio: the chapter opens and closes on whether someone is “yet alive.”

close.text: “Joseph is yet alive … Joseph my son is yet alive”

rows.text: “I am Joseph your brother”: God sent me

notes: The Hebrew pairing *od … chai* (“yet … alive”) marks the frame: Joseph's question (v. 3), the brothers' report (v. 26), and Jacob's answer (v. 28). It picks up Joseph's questions in 43:7 and 43:27 and returns once more in 46:30.

**Sent:** the verb *shalach* comes three times in vv. 5–8, each time with God as the one who sends (“not you … but God,” v. 8). It then comes three more times for what Joseph sends home (vv. 23, 24, 27).
“I am Joseph” is said twice (vv. 3, 4). The second adds “your brother, whom ye sold.”

Chapter 45 closes the section on the brothers in Egypt (42–45). The tests end, the family is reconciled, and Jacob decides to go down (v. 28), which sets up the journey that opens the last section at 46:1.

**Links:** Joseph gives the same reading after Jacob's death: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (50:20). Psalm 105:17 compresses it into one line: God “sent a man before them, even Joseph.”

traditions.text: Lehi finds on the brass plates a genealogy showing that he descends from Joseph, “who was sold into Egypt.” Nephi adds that Joseph was preserved by the Lord so that he might save Jacob and his household from famine, the same purpose Joseph names in vv. 5–7. Through Lehi, the Book of Mormon peoples count themselves among the posterity Joseph says God preserved.

Joseph reveals himself when he sees the brothers “all accordant in goodness one with another,” and Jubilees adds that he spoke to them in the Hebrew tongue. He tells them the Lord sent him ahead so that many people might live. Joseph sends his father clothing, silver, and ten asses laden with grain. Jacob's answer is simpler than in Genesis: it is enough for him if Joseph lives.

Has Joseph send the Egyptians away so that no stranger would learn of the brothers' shame. Philo's Joseph forgives them outright and tells them they need no one to plead for them. He calls God, not the brothers, the author of what happened, because God wanted Joseph to be the servant of his gifts to the human race in its time of need.

Gives Joseph a speech of praise. Everything was done to try their love for their brother, and he now finds them better men than he expected. What they did to him happened by God's will, and he thanks them for having, without knowing it, carried out God's intentions. Pharaoh then sends wagons full of grain, gold, and silver.

Abba Kohen Bardela reads v. 3 as a warning about the judgment. Joseph was the youngest of the brothers, and they could not stand before his rebuke; how much less will anyone stand when God rebukes each person according to what he is. The midrash adds that when Joseph said “come near,” he showed them he was circumcised, proof that this Egyptian lord was one of them.

Rabbi Elazar notices that “neck” in v. 14 is plural in Hebrew. Joseph, it says, wept over the two Temples that would stand in Benjamin's territory and be destroyed, and Benjamin wept over the sanctuary at Shiloh in Joseph's territory. Benjamin's five changes of clothing (v. 22) point ahead to Mordecai, his descendant, who would leave the king's presence in five royal garments (Esther 8:15). Joseph's appeal to Benjamin's eyes in v. 12 is read as a pledge: as he holds nothing against Benjamin, who had no part in the sale, so he holds nothing against them, and his mouth speaks what is in his heart.

traditions.date: 2nd century BC, with later Christian additions
traditions.text: In this deathbed speech Joseph tells his sons what he endured so as not to shame his brothers. When they came to Egypt, he says, he gave back their money, did not reproach them, and comforted them, and after Jacob's death he loved them even more. Simeon's testament in the same collection agrees that Joseph bore no malice.
traditions.cite: Testament of Joseph 17; Testament of Simeon 4

traditions.text: A Persian Christian writing in Syriac, he sets Joseph beside Jesus point by point: the beloved son, sent to his brothers, cast into the pit, raised to rule. When Joseph made himself known, his brothers were abashed and afraid; so, Aphrahat says, when Jesus is revealed in majesty at the last time, those who rejected him will be dismayed. He and Abba Kohen Bardela, in Genesis Rabbah, both read v. 3 as a preview of judgment.

Preaching on Stephen's speech, he calls Joseph's sale a type of Christ: the brothers mistreated the one who came to bring them food. When they came to buy grain and depended on him for everything, Joseph made himself known and also made them known to Pharaoh, then brought them into the land. They were saved, Chrysostom says, by the brother they had injured. Without knowing it, he adds, the brothers helped fulfill the very promise they had tried to defeat.

His Latin Bible has Joseph say God sent him to preserve “a remnant” (v. 7), which troubles him, since the whole family was alive. He reads it as pointing to Paul's “remnant according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5). As Joseph was handed over by his brothers to the Egyptians, Christ was handed over to the Gentiles, so that a remnant of Israel would share in salvation.

46.overview:
Jacob sets out with everything he owns and stops at Beer-sheba to offer sacrifices. God speaks to him in a night vision: do not fear going down to Egypt; I will make you a great nation there, I will go down with you, and I will bring you up again. The family travels in Pharaoh's wagons, and a list names the seventy souls of Jacob's house. Judah goes ahead to Goshen, where Joseph meets his father and weeps on his neck a long while. Joseph then coaches his brothers to tell Pharaoh they are herdsmen, so they will be settled apart in Goshen.

Watch Beer-sheba. Isaac had been told not to go down into Egypt (26:2), and Abraham's descent in famine had ended badly (12:10–20). Jacob goes only after God promises to go with him and bring him back. The move to Egypt is permitted, and it is also an exile with a promised return.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime; scholarly estimates for the Joseph story vary widely.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Jacob was 130 when he arrived (47:9). Ussher dates the descent to 1706 BC; counting back from 1 Kings 6:1 and Exodus 12:40 gives about 1876 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: From Beer-sheba in the Negev to Goshen in Egypt's eastern Delta. The Greek Septuagint places the meeting at Heroopolis, “in the land of Rameses” (vv. 28–29).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 1:1–5; Deuteronomy 10:22; Acts 7:14–15. In the Book of Mormon, Ether 13:7 recalls that Joseph brought his father down into Egypt.

46.hermeneutics:
Joseph tells his brothers to stress their trade, “for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians” (v. 34). Egypt had plenty of herds of its own, so the scorn seems aimed at a way of life: herders who moved with their flocks, especially foreign ones from the eastern desert. Egyptian border records show such herders being let into the pastures of the eastern Delta in hard times; Papyrus Anastasi VI reports Edomite herders admitted near Per-Atum to keep them and their cattle alive. Herodotus later describes an Egyptian herding group, the swineherds, as barred from the temples and marrying only among themselves. Joseph turns that kind of prejudice into protection. If Pharaoh hears “herdsmen,” the family will be placed at a distance, in pasture land near the border, where they can stay together and remain a separate people.

Seventy was a conventional number for a complete family. In the Ugaritic Baal myth, the goddess Athirat has “seventy sons,” meaning the whole company of the gods, and the Bible gives Gideon and Ahab seventy sons each (Judges 8:30; 2 Kings 10:1). Genesis reaches seventy only by counting with some care (see Structure), and the number does more than total heads. The whole house of Israel, a nation in small, goes down into Egypt together.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves from journey to list to reunion.

rows.text: The names of those who came into Egypt

notes: **The counts:** the list names 32 living descendants under Leah (Er and Onan died, v. 12) against her total of 33, then 16 for Zilpah, 14 for Rachel, 7 for Bilhah. Each maid's line is half her mistress's.

**66 and 70:** the 69 named, minus Joseph and his two sons already in Egypt, give the 66 of v. 26. Adding Joseph's house and Jacob gives 70 (v. 27). Rabbinic readers instead count Jochebed, born on arrival (Numbers 26:59). The Greek Septuagint adds five descendants of Manasseh and Ephraim in v. 20 and reads 75, the figure Stephen uses (Acts 7:14).
**Frame:** the list opens with the names of those “which came into Egypt” (v. 8) and closes on the same words (v. 27).

Chapter 46 opens the last section of the Joseph story (46–50): the family settles in Egypt, Jacob blesses his sons, and Jacob and Joseph both die there. It begins with the decision announced in 45:28.

**Links:** Exodus opens with the words of v. 8 (Exodus 1:1) and repeats the seventy (Exodus 1:5). God's promise to bring Jacob up again (v. 4) is kept for his body at his burial (50:13) and for his people in the Exodus foretold to Abraham (15:13–14).

traditions.text: Moroni, abridging the Jaredite record, draws a parallel with this chapter: “as Joseph brought his father down into the land of Egypt,” and Jacob died there, so the Lord brought a remnant of Joseph's seed out of Jerusalem. God was merciful to Joseph's father so that he would not perish, and he is merciful to Joseph's descendants in the same way. The Book of Mormon reads Lehi's journey as a second rescue of Joseph's house.

Amulek traces his line to Lehi, who “was a descendant of Manasseh,” the son of Joseph. Manasseh is one of the two sons listed in v. 20 as born to Joseph in Egypt, which ties Lehi's family to Joseph's Egyptian household and to a son born before the famine years (41:50).

Says Jacob was afraid to go down, remembering his dream at Bethel, and waited seven days at Beer-sheba hoping for a vision. While he waited he kept the harvest feast of first fruits with old grain, since none had grown. God appeared on the sixteenth of the month, and Jacob set out that same day.

traditions.source: Book of Jubilees on the seventy
traditions.text: Gives a different list, with extra sons for Dan who died the year they arrived, and still reaches seventy. It adds that five of the seventy died in Egypt childless, and that Er and Onan, who died in Canaan, were counted among the seventy nations of the Gentiles. The family of seventy is set against the seventy nations of the world.

Has Jacob afraid at Beer-sheba that Egypt's wealth would tempt his descendants to settle there and forget Canaan. He lists all seventy names, not counting Jacob, and says he does so to answer those who claimed the Jews were Egyptians by origin. Father and son meet at Heroopolis, as in the Septuagint, and Josephus explains the shepherd plan: Egyptians were forbidden to tend sheep.

Asks who has ever handed someone sixty-six cups and then three more and called it seventy. The answer is Jochebed, Levi's daughter, the mother of Moses: conceived in Canaan and born at the gates of Egypt, she completes the count. Rashi uses her to fill out Leah's thirty-three as well.

God says “fear not” because Jacob grieved at leaving the land, and “I will bring thee up” promises burial there. Jacob sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac, naming Isaac rather than Abraham, because honoring one's father comes before honoring one's grandfather. On v. 34 Rashi explains the shepherds' disgrace: Egyptians treated sheep as gods.

Fills in the meeting from the midrash. Judah was sent ahead (v. 28) to set up a house of study before Jacob arrived, and Joseph harnessed his own chariot to honor his father. Only Joseph is said to weep on the other's neck; the rabbis explain that Jacob was reciting the Shema at that moment. Jacob's “now let me die” (v. 30) becomes relief: he had feared God would hold him responsible for Joseph's death, and now he would die only once, in this world.

A Jewish chronicler in Egypt, preserved by Eusebius, who works out the ages: Joseph was thirty when he rose to power, then governed seven years of plenty and two of famine. Why did he wait nine prosperous years before sending for his father? Because Jacob and his sons were shepherds, and to Egyptians shepherding was a disgrace, as Joseph's own instructions in vv. 33–34 show.

Another Jewish writer quoted by Eusebius, who makes Joseph a culture hero of Egypt. He says Jacob and his sons came with great possessions and were settled in Heliopolis and Sais, where these “Syrians” multiplied. Josephus also places the family's pasture at Heliopolis.
traditions.cite: Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 9.23; Josephus, Antiquities 2.7.6

traditions.text: Works through the Greek count of seventy-five, which includes Joseph's grandsons and great-grandsons. They could not have been born when Jacob arrived, since Ephraim and Manasseh were still boys. So he takes “entered Egypt” to cover the whole span of Joseph's life, which Genesis says saw Ephraim's children to the third generation (50:23).

Asks why Scripture praises the patriarchs as shepherds from their youth (v. 34). Ruling over animals is just, he says, because God gave humans dominion over them (1:26). Rule of one human over another came only through sin or misfortune, as when Joseph was sold by his brothers.

47.overview:
Joseph presents five of his brothers to Pharaoh, and then his father. The brothers ask to stay in Goshen as shepherds, and Pharaoh gives them the best of the land. Jacob blesses Pharaoh and gives his age: 130 years of “pilgrimage,” few and evil beside his fathers' years. As the famine deepens, Joseph sells grain to the Egyptians for their money, then their livestock, then their land and their own service, and sets a standing tax of one fifth of the harvest. Seventeen years later Jacob, near death, makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan.

Watch who becomes whose servant. Jacob's sons call themselves Pharaoh's servants as a courtesy and are given a “possession” in Egypt (v. 11). The Egyptians become Pharaoh's servants in fact and give up their fields (vv. 19–25). Israel gains ground in Egypt while Egypt sells itself to its king, and still Jacob wants his bones carried home.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Jacob enters Egypt at 130 (v. 9): 1706 BC by Ussher's reckoning, or about 1876 BC counting 430 years (Exodus 12:40) back from an Exodus about 1446 BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Pharaoh's court, then Goshen in the eastern Nile Delta, called “the land of Rameses” in v. 11.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Acts 7:14–15 summarizes the descent. In the Book of Mormon, 1 Nephi 5:14 and Ether 13:7 recall Joseph preserving Jacob's household in Egypt.

47.hermeneutics:
Egypt's eastern border was used to herders arriving in hard times. A wall painting in the tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan (about 1890 BC) shows a party of 37 *Aamu*, “Asiatics,” led by a chief named Abisha, entering Egypt with their donkeys and goods. Papyrus Anastasi VI, a frontier official's report from about 1200 BC, records letting Shasu herders from Edom past the fort at Tjeku to the pools of Per-Atum in the eastern Delta, to keep them and their flocks alive. The brothers' request in v. 4 is that kind of request, and Pharaoh's answer settles them on the same frontier. His offer to make capable men “rulers over my cattle” (v. 6) names a real post; Egyptian officials carried the title overseer of cattle.

In Egypt the crown and the temples held much of the farmland, and the farmers who worked it paid part of each harvest. Temples ran their own estates and fed their staff from offerings. Herodotus, who visited in the 5th century BC, says Egypt's priests “do not consume or spend anything of their own” (2.37) and counts them among the few Egyptians with special land privileges (2.168). Genesis describes the same arrangement in its own terms: the priests eat a portion from Pharaoh and keep their fields (v. 22). A first hearer would recognize the system, a king who owns the land and a people who sow it for a share, and would hear vv. 20–26 as the story of how it began.

Jacob blesses Pharaoh: “few and evil” years
The family settled in Rameses and fed

Joseph buys the land; a fifth to Pharaoh
Israel multiplies; Jacob lives seventeen more years
Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Israel received at court and settled
Egypt sold to Pharaoh for bread

notes: **Two kinds of servants:** “Servants” (*avadim*) occurs 5 times. Jacob's sons use it three times as a courtesy (vv. 3–4) and receive a possession (v. 11); the Egyptians use it of themselves in earnest (vv. 19, 25) and lose their land.
**Repetition to watch:** Pharaoh is named 24 times. “Bread” runs through vv. 12–19 (6 times), and in vv. 18–26 “land” in the sense of farmland (*adamah*) comes 12 times.
The short report in vv. 27–28 sets Israel's growth in Goshen right beside Egypt's loss, before the deathbed scene begins.

The last subsection of the Joseph story runs from the descent into Egypt (46:1) to Joseph's death (50:26), all under the heading “the generations of Jacob” (37:2). Verse 28 echoes that heading: Joseph was seventeen when the story began, and now Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt near him. Verses 29–31 open Jacob's deathbed, which runs to 49:33.

**Forward:** A people who are Pharaoh's servants and a crown that owns the land set the stage for Exodus, where a new king makes Israel itself serve “with rigour” (Exodus 1:8–14). Jacob's oath is kept in 50:5–13.

traditions.text: Lehi finds his genealogy on the brass plates and learns he descends from Joseph, who was “preserved by the hand of the Lord” so that he could save Jacob and his household from famine. The verse reads chapters 45–47 as a single act of providence and makes it part of Lehi's own family history. Elsewhere the Book of Mormon traces Lehi through Manasseh.

Moroni, summarizing Ether's prophecy, draws a parallel between Joseph's household and Lehi's. As Joseph brought his father down into Egypt, where he died, so the Lord brought a remnant of Joseph out of Jerusalem so that it would not perish. Jacob's last years in Egypt, reported in vv. 27–31, become a pattern for a branch of Joseph preserved in a new land.

Retells the chapter briefly and fills a gap Genesis leaves. During the seven years of famine the Nile had not flooded except on a few places along its banks; when it rose again, Joseph gave the people seed to sow in the eighth year. Jubilees keeps the fifth for the king and counts Jacob's 147 years as exactly three jubilees.

Quotes v. 9 to show that every wise man in Moses' books is a sojourner. Souls, he says, are sent down from heaven to earth as to a colony, and Jacob mourns his sojourn in the body because his true homeland is heavenly; Abraham (23:4) and Moses say the same of themselves. Hebrews 11:13 calls the patriarchs “strangers and pilgrims on the earth” in a similar way.
traditions.cite: On the Confusion of Tongues 77–80; Hebrews 11:13

traditions.text: Places Jacob's family in Heliopolis, where the king's shepherds grazed, rather than Goshen, and has Pharaoh admire Jacob's age. He also softens Joseph's land policy: once the river overflowed again, Joseph went city to city and gave the people their land back as their own, asking only a fifth of the crop, which won the king more goodwill. The tax, he adds, lasted until Egypt's later kings, and like Jubilees he ties the famine to the Nile failing to rise.

Asks why Joseph presented only five of his brothers (v. 2) and answers that he chose the least robust-looking, so that Pharaoh would not press strong men into his army. The rabbis then argued over which five, matching them against the sons whose names Moses repeats or does not repeat in his blessing of the tribes (Deuteronomy 33). Rashi sets the Palestinian and Babylonian lists side by side.
traditions.cite: Genesis Rabbah 95:4; Bava Kamma 92a; Rashi on Genesis 47:2

traditions.text: Takes Jacob's parting blessing in v. 10 as the usual farewell to a ruler, then adds a midrash from Tanchuma: Jacob blessed Pharaoh that the Nile would rise whenever he approached it, since Egypt is watered by the river and not by rain. On v. 21 he explains why Joseph moved the Egyptians from city to city: once everyone was a newcomer, no one could sneer at Joseph's brothers as strangers.

Reads the “kindness and truth” Jacob asks for in v. 29 as kindness to the dead, the only kind that can expect nothing back. He gives three reasons Jacob refused burial in Egypt, one being that the Egyptians might worship at his grave. At v. 31 he cites a proverb, bow to the fox in his hour, for the father bowing to his powerful son, and reads “the bed's head” as Jacob giving thanks that all his sons had stayed faithful.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Genesis 47:29, 31 (Genesis Rabbah 96; Megillah 16b; Sifre)

traditions.text: Remembers the dying Jacob as a man of faith who blessed Joseph's sons and worshipped “leaning upon the top of his staff.” That follows the Greek Septuagint of v. 31. The Hebrew consonants *mth* can be read *mittah*, bed, as in the later Hebrew vowels, or *matteh*, staff, as the Greek translators read them. Rashi's bed and Hebrews' staff come from the same three letters.

Reports a royal land settlement from the Egyptian side. His informants told him that King Sesostris divided the country among all Egyptians in equal plots and drew his revenue from a yearly tax on them, sending surveyors to reassess any plot the river carried away. He gives no famine and no fifth, but his Greek readers learned, as readers of v. 26 did, that Egypt's farmland answered to the crown. He even guessed that Greek land-measuring, geometry, began with those royal surveys.

48.overview:
Joseph hears that his father is sick and brings his two sons. Jacob recalls God's promise to him at Luz, claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon, and remembers burying Rachel by the road to Bethlehem. When the boys are brought close, Joseph places the elder, Manasseh, at Jacob's right hand, but the nearly blind old man crosses his arms and lays his right hand on Ephraim. Joseph tries to move it; Jacob refuses, saying the younger will be greater. He ends by giving Joseph one portion more than his brothers.

The chapter quietly settles the birthright. By adopting two grandsons, Jacob gives Joseph two tribes, the double share that belonged to a firstborn, and 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 says plainly that Reuben's birthright went to the sons of Joseph. Rachel's firstborn takes the place of Leah's.

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: The Joseph Smith Translation (1830–1833) expands vv. 5–11 into a blessing on Joseph as the deliverer of his family and a future light to Israel.

historicalContext.label: Date of events

historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jacob's sickbed in Egypt. He looks back to Luz, that is Bethel (28:19; 35:6–12), and to Rachel's grave near Bethlehem.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Hebrews 11:21; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 on the birthright; JST Genesis 48:5–11.

48.hermeneutics:
Babylonian law gave a spoken declaration of sonship legal force. In the Laws of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC), if a man said “My sons” to the children his slave woman bore him and counted them with his wife's sons, they shared his estate after his death; if he never said it, they did not (§§170–171). Jacob's “they are mine” in v. 5 works the same way. Said before witnesses, it moves Ephraim and Manasseh from grandsons to heirs, and v. 6 marks the limit: any later sons of Joseph inherit only under their brothers' names.

The same laws let a father favor one son with a gift beyond the equal shares. A field, orchard, or house given by deed to a son “whom he prefers” stayed with that son, and only then was the rest of the estate divided (§165). Jacob does something like this twice, giving Joseph a portion above his brothers (v. 22) and setting Ephraim over Manasseh (vv. 14–19). Israel's own law later fenced in that freedom. A man with a loved wife and an unloved one may not make the loved wife's son his firstborn over the true firstborn, who keeps the double portion (Deuteronomy 21:15–17). That is close to what Jacob does for Rachel's son over Leah's Reuben, and a hearer who knew the rule would notice how often Genesis turns on fathers choosing against the order of birth.

“Who are these?”: Jacob kisses and embraces the boys
Crossed hands: Jacob blesses Joseph through his sons
Joseph objects; Ephraim set before Manasseh
Promise of return; Joseph's extra portion

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Jacob blesses them, the younger first

notes: **The order of names:** The narrator lists Manasseh first (v. 1). Jacob names Ephraim first (v. 5), and the scene ends “he set Ephraim before Manasseh” (v. 20).

**Repetition to watch:** “Right hand” (*yamin*) comes 5 times in vv. 13–18, every time in the struggle over whose head it rests on. The verb “bless” (*barak*) comes 6 times, from God blessing Jacob at Luz (v. 3) to the formula Israel will use, “God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh” (v. 20).
Jacob's dim eyes (v. 10) recall Isaac's (27:1), but this time the old father is not deceived; he crosses his hands “wittingly” (v. 14).
Chapters 48 and 49 are two deathbed scenes inside Jacob's burial requests (47:29–31; 49:29–33). Chapter 48 deals with Joseph's line alone; chapter 49 turns to all twelve sons.

**Echoes:** The younger-over-elder pattern runs through Genesis, from Isaac and Jacob to Perez and Zerah (38:27–30). Ephraim's precedence returns in 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 and Jeremiah 31:9, “Ephraim is my firstborn.” The “portion” of v. 22 is the Hebrew *shechem*, and Joseph's bones are finally buried at Shechem in the ground Jacob bought (Joshua 24:32).

traditions.text: Expands Jacob's words. The adopted boys are called after Jacob's name, “therefore they were called Israel,” and Joseph's later sons belong to the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob then blesses Joseph as the son God raised up to save the house from famine: his brothers will bow to his seed for generations, and his descendants will deliver Israel from captivity and bring salvation when the people are bowed down under sin.

Amulek traces his line through Nephi and Lehi to Manasseh, Joseph's elder son, and Lehi had found his descent from Joseph on the brass plates. Latter-day Saints therefore read Jacob's prayer that the boys “grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth” (v. 16) as reaching the Americas. The Book of Mormon itself names only Manasseh.

An apostle, reporting what Joseph Smith had told the early elders, said that Lehi's record on the lost 116 pages made Ishmael's family Ephraimite. Lehi's and Ishmael's children intermarried, so both of Joseph's sons were represented in the Book of Mormon peoples, fulfilling Jacob's words that his name be “named on them.” The present Book of Mormon does not give Ishmael's tribe.

D&C 133 pictures the returning tribes bringing their treasures to the children of Ephraim and ends with “the richer blessing upon the head of Ephraim and his fellows,” language that follows Jacob's choice in v. 19. D&C 27:5 calls the Book of Mormon the record of the stick of Ephraim, from Ezekiel 37:16–19, where Joseph's stick is in Ephraim's hand.

Folds chapters 48–49 into one sentence: before he died Jacob blessed his sons, told them what would befall them in Egypt and in the last days, and gave Joseph two portions in the land. That reads v. 22's single “portion” as the double share, as the Talmud later does. Jubilees adds that Jacob handed all his books, and his fathers' books, to Levi to preserve.

Compresses chapters 48–49 into a few lines. The dying Jacob praises Joseph for not holding his brothers' wrongs against them, then commands his sons to admit Ephraim and Manasseh into their number and divide Canaan with them. Josephus thus moves Joseph's forgiveness, which Genesis saves for 50:15–21, into Jacob's mouth.

Uses this chapter to prove that a birthright means a double portion. Reuben lost his birthright and it went to Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1), and v. 5, “Ephraim and Manasseh, as Reuben and Simeon,” shows that Joseph's sons received two full shares. A baraita adds that Jacob's “sword” and “bow” in v. 22 mean prayer and petition, the same reading the Targum Onkelos puts into its translation.
traditions.cite: Bava Batra 123a; Targum Onkelos on Genesis 48:22

traditions.text: Hears an apology in v. 7. Jacob asks Joseph to carry him to Canaan though he did not carry Rachel even to Bethlehem, and explains that God commanded the roadside grave. Centuries later, when the exiles passed that road, Rachel would weep for her children and be answered, as in Jeremiah 31:15–17.

Explains the odd question “Who are these?” (v. 8), when Jacob already knew the boys. Citing Tanchuma, he says the divine presence left Jacob as he foresaw wicked kings among their descendants, Jeroboam and Ahab from Ephraim, Jehu from Manasseh. On v. 16 he reads the verb “grow” as “multiply like fish,” which are fruitful and hidden from the evil eye.

Reads the crossed hands as prophecy. Jacob “saw in spirit the type of the people to arise afterwards” and laid his right hand on the younger son, so that the later people, the Christians, would be first and heirs of the covenant. Barnabas pairs the scene with Rebekah's twins, where the elder serves the younger.

Traces the laying on of hands after baptism back to this blessing. Jacob's hands, laid on Ephraim and Manasseh and crossed one over the other, drew the shape of the cross and so foretold the blessing that would come through Christ. For Tertullian the Spirit then descends on the baptized as the dove came down after the Flood and on Christ.

Treats Joseph's sons like Isaac's: the elder stands for the Jews, the younger for the Christians. Manasseh will become “a people,” Ephraim “a multitude of nations” (v. 19), and Augustine reads the two promises as Israel by descent and the whole world of Abraham's seed by faith.

49.overview:
Jacob gathers his twelve sons and speaks to each in turn, in poetry. Reuben loses the firstborn's place for going up to his father's bed; Simeon and Levi are cursed for their anger and scattered. Judah receives the lion, the sceptre, and a future of wine and plenty, and the next sons get short sayings tied to their land or character. Joseph's is the richest: “a fruitful bough,” blessed from heaven above and the deep below. Then Jacob charges them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham, Isaac, and Leah, draws his feet into the bed, and dies.

The sayings are called blessings (v. 28), yet the first three are rebukes. With the three eldest passed over, leadership falls to Judah, the fourth son, and to Joseph, the eleventh. Those two names carry Israel's later history: the kings come from Judah, and Joseph's line becomes the heart of the northern tribes.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text; Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Jacob dies at 147 (47:28): 1689 BC by Ussher's reckoning, or about 1859 BC on an early-Exodus reckoning.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew poetry, full of rare words and puns on the sons' names (Judah and “praise,” Dan and “judge,” Gad and “troop”). “Shiloh” in v. 10 is one of the Bible's best-known puzzles.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Jacob's deathbed in Egypt. His burial charge points to the cave Abraham bought at Machpelah near Hebron (23:17–20).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Moses' blessing of the tribes (Deuteronomy 33). The published JST excerpts show no change to this chapter, though JST Genesis 50:24 names “the Messiah who is called Shilo.”

49.hermeneutics:
Deathbed words carried legal weight in the ancient Near East. In a lawsuit from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (15th–14th century BC), a man named Tarmiya claimed a wife his dying father had given him by taking his hand and speaking. His brothers contested it, and the court upheld the dying man's spoken word. Jacob's sayings are that kind of act. They do more than predict; they assign rank and inheritance, which is why Reuben's loss of the firstborn's place (vv. 3–4) could later be cited as settled (1 Chronicles 5:1).

Judah's saying (vv. 8–12) speaks the region's royal language. The lion was a royal animal from Egypt, where the king could be shown as a lion-bodied sphinx, to Assyria, where Ashurbanipal had his lion hunts carved on the palace walls at Nineveh. The mount fits as well. A governor at Mari advised King Zimri-Lim (18th century BC) to honor his kingship by riding a litter and mules rather than a horse, and David has Solomon set on his own mule to be proclaimed king (1 Kings 1:33). A hearer would take the lion, the sceptre, and the tethered ass's colt as kingship, and the rest of the saying as the plenty that comes with it: vines so common a donkey is tied to one, wine as plentiful as wash water, teeth white with milk.

Simeon and Levi: cursed anger, scattered in Israel
Judah: the lion, the sceptre, and Shiloh
Zebulun by the sea; Issachar under the burden
Dan the judge and serpent; a prayer for salvation
Gad, Asher, and Naphtali
Joseph: the fruitful bough and the everlasting hills
Benjamin the wolf; the twelve tribes blessed
Burial charge; Jacob is gathered to his people

structure.summary: An ordered sequence of twelve sayings, grouped by mother, inside a narrative frame. Not a chiasm.

close.text: The twelve tribes blessed; burial charge; death

rows.text: Leah's six: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar
The handmaids' four: Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali

notes: **Order:** Leah's sons come in birth order, except that Zebulun precedes Issachar (compare 30:17–20). The handmaids' sons run Bilhah, Zilpah, Zilpah, Bilhah (Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali), so Bilhah's two enclose Zilpah's.
**Weight:** Judah (vv. 8–12) and Joseph (vv. 22–26) take 119 of the 254 Hebrew words in vv. 3–27. Gad, Asher, and Naphtali get one verse each.

**Blessing:** The noun *berakhah* comes 5 times in Joseph's saying (vv. 25–26) and once more in v. 28. The one line spoken to God, “I have waited for thy salvation, O LORD” (v. 18), breaks into the sayings after Dan.

The poem is Jacob's last act. Verses 29–33 close the deathbed scene that opened at 47:29 with the same request, burial with his fathers, and Jacob's death sets up the burial and the closing scenes of ch. 50, the end of “the generations of Jacob” begun at 37:2.

**Echoes:** Moses blesses the tribes again before his own death (Deuteronomy 33), and his blessing of Joseph repeats “the head of Joseph” and “him that was separated from his brethren” (33:16). Judah's lion returns as a title of Christ, “the Lion of the tribe of Juda” (Revelation 5:5).

traditions.text: In Joseph's expanded prophecy, the prophet who will deliver Israel from Egypt is set apart from “the Messiah who is called Shilo.” The JST thus takes Jacob's “Shiloh” (v. 10) as a title of the Messiah, the reading the Targums and the Qumran commentary below also give. The published JST excerpts show no change to Genesis 49 itself.

Nephi calls Lehi's family a branch broken off from the house of Israel, and the Lord tells Jacob, Nephi's brother, that he led them out of Jerusalem to raise up a righteous branch from the loins of Joseph. Latter-day Saints read Joseph's fruitful bough “whose branches run over the wall” (v. 22) as that branch carried over the sea. The Book of Mormon does not quote v. 22 directly.

Describing the return of the lost tribes from the north, the revelation says the boundaries of the everlasting hills will tremble at their presence. The phrase echoes v. 26, where Jacob's blessings on Joseph reach “unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills,” and the same passage ends with the richer blessing on the head of Ephraim, Joseph's son.

traditions.date: 2nd century BC, with later Christian additions
traditions.text: A Jewish expansion of this chapter in which each son of Jacob gives his own deathbed testament. Reuben fills in the story behind v. 4: he saw Bilhah bathing, later found her drunk and asleep, and an angel revealed his sin to Jacob. Judah tells his sons that God gave him the kingdom and Levi the priesthood and set the kingdom beneath the priesthood, and that his kingdom will pass to foreigners “until the salvation of Israel shall come.”
traditions.cite: Testament of Reuben 3:11–15; Testament of Judah 21:1–5; 22:2

traditions.text: A Dead Sea Scrolls commentary that comments on several of Jacob's sayings. On v. 10 it says a ruler will not depart from the tribe of Judah until the righteous Messiah comes, the branch of David, to whom and to whose seed the kingship of his people is given forever. It is the earliest surviving messianic reading of Shiloh.

The Aramaic translations read v. 10 as a promise of the Messiah. Onkelos renders “until Shiloh come” as until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs. Pseudo-Jonathan says kings and rulers will not cease from Judah “till the time that the King the Meshiha shall come,” and adds scribes teaching the law among Judah's descendants.

Explains why v. 1 promises to tell “the last days” and then does not. Jacob wanted to reveal the end, but the divine presence left him, and he feared one of his sons was unworthy, as Ishmael and Esau had been. His sons answered with the words of the Shema, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one, and Jacob responded with the praise of God's glorious kingdom that Jews still say quietly after the Shema. Rashi gives the first part of this reading on v. 1.

Takes the sceptre of v. 10 as Judah's authority even after David's line stopped ruling: the exilarchs who governed the Jews of Babylon, and the scholarly princes of the land of Israel, Hillel's descendants. Shiloh he reads with Genesis Rabbah and Onkelos as the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs. He adds a midrash that splits the word into *shai lo*, “a gift to him,” from Psalm 76:11.

Finds Israel's later history in single lines. Dan's serpent that makes the rider fall backward (v. 17) is Samson, who brought down the Philistines on the roof without touching them. The “everlasting hills” of v. 26 mean a blessing without boundaries: Jacob alone was told he would spread west, east, north, and south (28:14), while Abraham and Isaac were shown only the land. D&C 133 uses the same phrase for a gathering that reaches past every border.

Quotes vv. 10–11 in the Greek form, “until He come for whom it is reserved,” as a prophecy of Christ. He argues that the Jews had their own rulers until Jesus came and lost their land to Rome soon after his crucifixion. The foal bound to the vine points to the colt tied at the village entrance, and the robe washed in the blood of the grape to his passion.

Reads Judah's lion as Christ choosing his own death. The lion lying down (v. 9) is his death, the lion's title shows the death was voluntary, and “who shall rouse him up?” means no one raised him but himself. The robe washed in wine is the church, cleansed in his blood.

50.overview:
Joseph weeps over his father and has him embalmed, and Egypt mourns him seventy days. With Pharaoh's leave, a great company of Egyptian officials, chariots, and horsemen goes up with Jacob's family, mourns seven days at the threshing floor of Atad, and buries Jacob in the cave of Machpelah. Back in Egypt the brothers fear that Joseph has only been waiting for their father to die. They send him a message in Jacob's name and fall down as his servants. Joseph weeps, refuses to put himself in God's place, and promises to provide for them. He lives to 110, makes Israel swear to carry his bones out when God visits them, and is laid in a coffin in Egypt.

The brothers' bow fulfills Joseph's first dream (37:7) at last, and he answers it with the sentence the whole story has been building toward: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (v. 20).

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: The Joseph Smith Translation (1830–1833) adds vv. 24–38, Joseph's prophecy of Moses and of a latter-day seer named Joseph. Lehi quotes a parallel form from the brass plates (2 Nephi 3:4–22).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Jacob dies 1689 BC and Joseph 1635 BC by Ussher's reckoning. On an early-Exodus reckoning Joseph dies about 1805 BC, 71 years after the family entered Egypt.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Egypt; the threshing floor of Atad “beyond Jordan”; the cave of Machpelah near Hebron.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 13:19 and Joshua 24:32 (Joseph's bones); Hebrews 11:22; Acts 7:15–16.

50.hermeneutics:
Embalming was Egyptian, not Israelite. Herodotus (2.86) describes the costliest method: the brain and organs removed, the body packed in natron for seventy days, then wrapped in linen and placed in a wooden case shaped like a man. Diodorus (1.91) says the treatment with oils and spices took over thirty days, and that all Egypt mourned a dead king for seventy-two days (1.72). Genesis falls between them, with forty days for the embalming and seventy days of Egyptian mourning (v. 3), close to royal honors. That Jacob is embalmed at all, by Joseph's own “physicians,” shows how far the family now belongs to Egypt's court, even while Jacob insists on a grave in Canaan.

Egyptian texts treat 110 years as the full life of a blessed man. The sage Ptahhotep closes his Instruction by saying he reached “fivescore and ten years” because the king favored him for doing right (Gunn's translation, 1906). Joseph dies at exactly that age (vv. 22, 26). The patriarchs before him lived longer by Genesis' count (Abraham 175, Isaac 180, Jacob 147), so Joseph's span reads as an Egyptian ideal fulfilled. Joshua, the next great leader from Joseph's tribe of Ephraim, also dies at 110 (Joshua 24:29).

Pharaoh permits the burial journey

Joseph's long life and great-grandchildren
Joseph's oath about his bones; his death

structure.summary: A loose frame (inclusio): the chapter opens and closes with an embalming in Egypt. Not a chiasm.

open.text: Jacob dies; embalmed and mourned in Egypt

close.text: Joseph dies; embalmed and coffined in Egypt

rows.text: Jacob carried up and buried in Canaan

rows.label: B
rows.text: The brothers' plea and Joseph's answer

rows.label: C
rows.text: Joseph's oath: carry my bones up

notes: **The frame:** “Embalm” (*chanat*) appears 4 times, three for Jacob (vv. 2–3) and once for Joseph (v. 26). Jacob is buried in Canaan at once; Joseph's body stays in Egypt, waiting, which leaves the book open.
**Oaths:** “Bury” comes 7 times in vv. 5–14, and “swear” 4 times (vv. 5, 6, 24, 25). Jacob's oath is kept in the first half; Joseph's is laid on Israel in the last verses.
**Evil turned:** “Evil” (*ra'ah*) comes 3 times (vv. 15, 17, 20), the last answered by “good.” Joseph's “God will surely visit you” (vv. 24, 25) doubles the verb both times (*paqod yifqod*).

The last chapter of Genesis closes “the generations of Jacob” begun at 37:2. Jacob's burial ends the deathbed scene of 47:29–49:33; vv. 15–21 close the brothers' story that began with their hatred in ch. 37; vv. 22–26 end the book with Joseph's bones still in Egypt.

**Forward:** Exodus opens by naming the sons who came to Egypt and noting Joseph's death (Exodus 1:1–6). Moses takes the bones when Israel leaves, quoting Joseph's oath (Exodus 13:19), and they are buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

traditions.text: Joseph's last words grow into a prophecy. He goes to his grave with joy, because the Lord has promised a righteous branch from his loins and a prophet, “not the Messiah who is called Shilo,” to deliver Israel from Egypt. Israel will be scattered again, and a branch broken off and carried into a far country will be remembered when the Messiah is made known to them in the latter days.

The prophecy names three men. A choice seer from Joseph's loins will bring forth the Lord's word, and “his name shall be called Joseph,” after his father's name. The deliverer from Egypt will be called Moses and will be nursed by the king's daughter, and his spokesman will be Aaron. The JST also ends the chapter with Israel keeping Joseph unburied so he could be laid in his father's sepulchre.

Lehi quotes Joseph's prophecy from the brass plates to his own son Joseph, almost line for line with the JST: the choice seer, the writings of Joseph's seed and Judah's seed growing together, the seer named for himself and his father. The Book of Mormon form leaves Aaron unnamed and adds a spokesman for the latter-day seer. It presents the prophecy as part of the record Lehi's family carried away from Jerusalem.

Divides Joseph's 110 years: seventeen in Canaan, ten as a servant, three in prison, and eighty ruling Egypt under the king. It explains why his bones stayed behind: war broke out between Egypt and Canaan and the gates of Egypt were closed. During a later war the Israelites carried the bones of all Jacob's other sons to the cave at Hebron.

traditions.date: 2nd century BC, with later Christian additions
traditions.text: Simeon's testament tells the same story as Jubilees from another angle. His bones were taken up to Hebron secretly during a war, but the Egyptians guarded Joseph's bones in the royal tombs, because their sorcerers said darkness would cover the land when those bones left. Benjamin's testament dates the secret reburial of the brothers to the ninety-first year after Israel entered Egypt.
traditions.cite: Testament of Simeon 8; Testament of Benjamin 12

traditions.text: Retells the burial at Hebron “at a great expense” and the brothers' fear in a sentence each, and praises Joseph for using his authority with moderation. He says the brothers' descendants later carried their bodies to Hebron, while Joseph's bones waited for the Exodus. Jubilees and the Testaments say the same, though Acts 7:16 places the fathers' tomb at Shechem.

The Mishnah sees measure for measure: Joseph buried his father with great honor, so Moses himself carried Joseph's bones. The Talmud enlarges the funeral. Esau blocks the burial at Machpelah, claiming the last place in the cave, and Naphtali, “a hind let loose” (49:21), runs back to Egypt for the deed until Hushim son of Dan strikes Esau down.

Fills in what happened to Joseph's coffin. The Egyptians made a metal casket and sank it in the Nile so the river would be blessed. At the Exodus, Serah daughter of Asher, the last of her generation, showed Moses the place, and when Moses called on Joseph to keep his oath, the coffin rose to the surface.

Notes that Genesis never records Jacob giving the command the brothers quote in vv. 16–17. Citing the Talmud, Rashi says they altered the facts for the sake of peace, since Jacob never suspected Joseph, and that they sent Bilhah's sons, who had been Joseph's companions as a boy (37:2).

Lists Joseph among the heroes of faith for one act only: dying in Egypt, he spoke of the Exodus and “gave commandment concerning his bones.” His burial plan is read as confidence in a promise he would not live to see.

Stephen's speech compresses Genesis 46–50 into two verses: Jacob went down into Egypt and died, he and the fathers, and they were carried to Sychem (Shechem) and laid in the tomb Abraham bought from the sons of Emmor. He merges the cave Abraham bought at Hebron with the plot Jacob bought at Shechem (33:19), where Joshua 24:32 buries Joseph. Genesis itself keeps the two purchases apart.

Uses the end of Genesis as a hinge in his history of the city of God. After Jacob and Joseph died, he counts 144 years until Israel left Egypt, years in which the nation grew beyond belief despite the slaughter of its sons. Then Moses, hidden from the killers of infants and adopted by Pharaoh's daughter, leads that nation out.
